text: A map of AI before the vocabulary gets in the way: reasoning, learning, perception, generation, and action. How the pieces connect MENTAL MODEL What artificial intelligence includes — from question to evidence 01 Frame the task State the input, output, decision, and cost of failure. 02 Choose a capability Search, prediction, generation, perception, or 03 Test the behavior Use evidence that matches the intended use. 04 Operate the system Monitor exceptions, feedback, and changing conditions. Frame the task → Choose a capability → Test the behavior → Operate the system. Each transition is a place where an assumption can be inspected before the next layer of the system compounds it. Start with the task Artificial intelligence studies systems that perform tasks involving perception, reasoning, learning, or decision-making. A system can search a game tree without learning anything. A classifier can learn from labeled examples without generating text. A language model can generate fluent text without checking whether its claims are true. These are different capabilities and need different tests. The nested families Machine learning is one approach to AI: fit behavior from data. Deep learning uses layered neural networks to learn representations. Generative models learn to produce samples such as text, images, audio, or molecular structures. An agent combines a policy or model with observations, tools, and an environment in which actions have consequences. These categories overlap; they do not form a leaderboard. Training and inference Training changes learned parameters using an objective and data. Inference applies a trained system to new inputs. A prompt usually changes the input context, not the model weights. Retrieval supplies external information. Fine-tuning updates parameters. A production application may use all four and must track which component caused a result. What to learn first Understand how computers represent and move data, then the mathematics of vectors, uncertainty, and gradients. Learn a small supervised learning pipeline before studying transformers. After that, choose a branch: build applications, train models, optimize hardware, study multimodal systems, or evaluate risks. Each branch builds on the same shared foundations. Worked example Problem Candidate approach Useful test Find a route Graph search Path cost and constraints Predict equipment failure Supervised learning Recall at an acceptable false-alarm rate Answer a policy question Retrieval plus generation Evidence support and abstention Control a robot Perception, planning, control Task success and physical constraint violations What goes wrong Treating “AI” as synonymous with a chatbot hides the engineering choices. A deterministic rule can be more suitable than a learned model when the desired behavior is known exactly. Check your understanding Does adding a document to an LLM prompt train the model? Reveal the explanation No. It conditions this inference request. A training step requires a learning objective and a parameter update. An operating model for what artificial intelligence includes The first design decision is not “which model?” It is whether the task needs a learned approximation at all. A rule, database query, calculator, optimizer, retrieval system, classifier, and generative model each fail in different ways. The most useful AI systems make those boundaries visible rather than pretending one component can do every job. The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test. Worked system: choose the smallest component that owns the decision A support portal receives a question about a customer’s current invoice. A language model can explain the result, but it should not invent the amount. The correct path is a database query for the authoritative balance, a calculator for deterministic arithmetic, retrieval for the applicable policy text, and a generative component only for the explanation. Each tool has a distinct contract and failure mode; combining them into “ask the model” hides those boundaries. Start by naming the input, intended decision, source of truth, acceptable abstention, and cost of a harmful error. Then choose the smallest component that can own each part. This is the core architectural move in AI systems: models are useful approximators, while identity, permissions, records, arithmetic, and irreversible actions usually belong to components with explicit guarantees. Five lenses for reading any AI claim Capability. What behavior was demonstrated, on what task, and under which conditions? A benchmark score and a compelling demo answer a limited capability question; they do not prove the system can operate reliably in an open workflow. System. What data, memory, retrieval, tools, evaluators, and human interventions make the behavior possible? A model is one component inside a larger causal chain. Reliability. What happens at the edge: rare inputs, long sequences, missing evidence, distribution shifts, malicious text, or a failing dependency? Product quality is usually dominated by these paths rather than the median example. Economics and infrastructure. What hardware, energy, capital, organization, and supply chain are required for the claimed capability to exist at scale? A feature that works in a controlled demo can face an entirely different constraint when multiplied across millions of requests. Power and legitimacy. Who supplies the data, owns the infrastructure, absorbs errors, and has a route to contest a decision? This is not an ethical afterthought. It shapes which objectives are optimized, which failures are visible, and which systems are permitted to operate. The Perspective volume applies these lenses to the people, fault lines, physical constraints, and prediction record surrounding AI. The technical library explains how systems work; the perspective work asks what their builders believe, what evidence would change a view, and what the system is actually allowed to decide. Keeping both in one field library makes it harder to confuse capability with inevitability. Notebook: Trace a byte budget Write an acceptance test before choosing a model. For each intended action, define the available evidence, an acceptable abstention path, the human or system allowed to act, and what counts as a harmful error. items = 1_000_000 bytes_per_item = 4 working_set = items * bytes_per_item print(f"{working_set / 2**20:.1f} MiB") # Now include every copy, index, and temporary buffer. Capability is only one layer of an AI system A model converts an input representation into an output representation. A useful system must also decide what information enters that model, what authority follows from its output, and how failures become visible. Treating the model as the entire product hides the parts that usually determine reliability. Capability layer. Test whether the learned component can classify, rank, retrieve, generate, perceive, plan, or control under a stated distribution. A successful demonstration establishes possibility. It does not establish a stable failure rate. System layer. Trace acquisition, preprocessing, model execution, retrieval, tools, storage, authentication, interface, and monitoring. Each boundary can corrupt meaning even when every component returns a technically valid result. Decision layer. Define who or what acts on the output. A recommendation shown to an analyst has a different risk boundary from an automatic payment, code deployment, medical escalation, or physical motion. Evidence layer. Match evidence to the claim. Unit tests support implementation claims. Held-out evaluations support behavioral claims. Controlled experiments support causal claims. Field operation supports reliability and economic claims. The gotcha. Teams often improve model quality while the product remains unchanged because the binding constraint sits in retrieval, workflow integration, latency, permissions, or user trust. Five lenses for reading any AI claim Capability. Ask exactly what input produced what output, under which tools, prompt, sampling settings, time budget, and human assistance. Reliability. Ask for the denominator: how many trials, which failures, what variance across seeds and subgroups, and how the system handles an unsupported request. Infrastructure. Count memory, compute, network traffic, data movement, queueing, and service dependencies. A model that fits on one accelerator may still need a distributed serving system to meet demand. Economics. Compare cost per accepted task at equal quality. Include retries, review, retrieval, storage, network transfer, idle capacity, and incidents. Power. Identify who controls data, compute, distribution, labor, standards, and the right to challenge a decision. Technical capability does not determine how benefits and costs are allocated. The gotcha. A benchmark result can be correct and still fail to support the much larger social or commercial claim attached to it. From task statement to operating system A disciplined AI project begins with an observable decision rather than a model family. Write down the input available at decision time, the output contract, the actor who consumes it, the cost of each error, and the fallback when evidence is missing. This turns a vague wish for intelligence into an engineering boundary. Rules and programs. Use deterministic logic when the world is closed, the rules can be stated, and violations must fail hard. Tax calculations, schema checks, access control, and protocol parsing belong here. Search and optimization. Use an explicit objective and constraints when the system must choose among alternatives. Route planning, scheduling, resource allocation, and satisfiability can often provide checkable solutions. Statistical prediction. Use learned models when patterns must be inferred from examples and uncertainty is expected. Define the target population and loss before selecting the estimator. Retrieval. Use indexes when the answer already exists in a corpus and provenance matters. A generator can express retrieved evidence, but it should not replace the retrieval test. Generation. Use generative models when the output space is too open to enumerate. Constrain format, ground claims, and keep consequential actions behind explicit authorization. The gotcha. Selecting a general model first encourages the project to absorb tasks that a database, calculator, or verifier could perform more cheaply and reliably. The lifecycle changes the system after launch Training freezes one relationship between data, parameters, and objective. Deployment introduces users, incentives, new distributions, and feedback. The deployed system can change its own future inputs: recommendations affect clicks, moderation affects what is posted, and automated decisions affect who appears in later training data. Data generation. Record how examples entered the dataset, who was excluded, when labels became available, and which policy created the observed behavior. Evaluation. Protect a held-out set from model selection. Add slices, counterexamples, adversarial cases, latency, cost, and calibration that reflect the operating decision. Release. Version weights, tokenizer, prompts, preprocessing, retrieval index, tool policy, and runtime as one compatible artifact set. A model-only rollback can preserve the incident. Monitoring. Measure input drift, outcome drift, abstention, tool authorization, queue time, and user-impacting failure. Logs should minimize sensitive content while retaining enough causal structure for diagnosis. Retirement. Define how a model, index, or dataset stops serving, how dependent systems migrate, and how retained data is deleted or archived. The gotcha. Feedback collected from a deployed policy is selected by that policy. Treating it as an unbiased sample can reinforce mistakes while dashboards appear to improve. The field is a stack of contracts Layer Primary contract Typical evidence Characteristic failure Hardware Execute supported operations within capacity Kernel correctness, bytes, latency, energy Bandwidth or memory ceiling Numerics Approximate mathematical operations within tolerance Error bounds, finite checks, conditioning Overflow, underflow, cancellation Model Map a defined input distribution to useful outputs Held-out tasks, slices, calibration Shift, shortcut, confabulation Application Assemble evidence, tools, and permissions End-to-end tests and traces Wrong context or excess authority Organization Assign ownership, review, and incident response Runbooks, audits, field outcomes No accountable decision owner Society Allocate benefits, costs, and recourse Distributional and institutional evidence Concentrated power or unchallengeable harm The gotcha. Success at one layer cannot certify the layer above it. Correct matrix multiplication does not prove a useful model; a useful model does not prove a legitimate decision.

Begin with the physical and logical foundations: binary numbers, instructions, memory, storage, and the CPU. How the pieces connect MENTAL MODEL Bits, bytes how computers work — from question to evidence 01 Encode Represent a value as bits and a datatype. 02 Move Fetch it through storage, RAM, cache, and registers. 03 Execute Apply instructions using CPU or accelerator units. 04 Persist Write results with an explicit format and lifetime. Encode → Move → Execute → Persist. Each transition is a place where an assumption can be inspected before the next layer of the system compounds it. From voltage to information Digital circuits interpret ranges of electrical states as 0 and 1. A bit stores one binary choice. Eight bits form a byte and encode 256 distinct patterns. Meaning comes from an agreed representation: the same bits can be interpreted as an integer, a character, or part of a floating-point number. A program is data plus instructions A processor fetches instructions, decodes them, operates on registers, and reads or writes memory. Modern CPUs overlap work, predict branches, and cache recently used data. A thread is an instruction stream with its own execution state. Multiple cores can execute multiple streams; dependencies still limit what can happen simultaneously. The storage hierarchy Registers are small and close to arithmetic units. Caches retain likely-to-be-reused memory. RAM holds a running program’s working set. SSDs persist files but are much slower for fine-grained access. Moving a model from disk to RAM to GPU memory is real work, even if a framework hides the transfers. Units that prevent expensive mistakes A decimal GB is 10^9 bytes; a GiB is 2^30 bytes. Bandwidth is data per second; latency is time until a result arrives. Frequency counts clock cycles per second, not completed useful operations. Model parameter count measures stored learned values, not token capacity or reasoning ability. Worked example An 8-billion-parameter model with one 16-bit value per parameter needs 8×10^9×2 = 16 GB, or about 14.90 GiB, for weights alone. Runtime buffers and a KV cache consume additional memory. A 16 GB device is therefore not guaranteed to fit it. What goes wrong Confusing Gb with GB introduces an eightfold error. Assuming all installed memory is available ignores the operating system, other processes, and runtime allocations. Check your understanding How many distinct patterns fit in 12 bits? Reveal the explanation 2^12 = 4,096 patterns. This says nothing about their meaning until an encoding is chosen. An operating model for bits, bytes & how computers work Every apparent software abstraction eventually becomes a memory layout and a sequence of instructions. A model checkpoint is bytes on storage; loading it establishes tensors in memory; inference schedules arithmetic; a response becomes network bytes. This path explains why loading, serialization, and copying can be more important than FLOPS for small workloads. The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test. Worked system: loading a model is a data-movement problem Consider a 7-billion-parameter model stored in a two-byte format. The weights alone occupy roughly 14 billion bytes before file metadata, alignment, runtime allocations, or a key-value cache. Opening the file does not make it runnable: storage reads move bytes into main memory; the framework interprets those bytes as tensors; a GPU runtime may then copy or map them into device memory; only then can arithmetic begin. The slowest stage is often not multiplication. A local machine with a fast GPU can still feel slow because the checkpoint is on a slow external drive, because memory pressure forces paging, or because the model is copied twice by an accidental dtype conversion. That path also explains why an apparent “out of memory” error is a structural diagnosis. Ask which allocation is live at the failure: immutable weights, a growing KV cache, temporary activations, a duplicate host copy, or an allocator reservation. Lowering batch size may hide the symptom, but it does not identify the owner of the bytes. The useful habit is to make a ledger before changing hardware: count elements, choose a dtype, multiply by bytes per element, then name the location and lifetime of each allocation. Notebook: Trace a byte budget For any performance or capacity claim, name the representation, bytes per element, working-set size, storage location, and transfer path. Those five facts prevent most unit mistakes. items = 1_000_000 bytes_per_item = 4 working_set = items * bytes_per_item print(f"{working_set / 2**20:.1f} MiB") # Now include every copy, index, and temporary buffer. Move What would show that this boundary failed? Fetch it through storage, RAM, cache, and registers. Execute What would show that this boundary failed? Apply instructions using CPU or accelerator units. Persist What would show that this boundary failed? Write results with an explicit format and lifetime. The gotcha. Passing each component check separately does not prove the composed path preserves identity, units, ordering, or authority. One bit pattern, several meanings A bit pattern has no intrinsic type. The consuming instruction decides whether it represents an unsigned integer, two's-complement integer, floating-point value, text, address, or flags. Unsigned integers spend every pattern on magnitude. An n-bit value covers 0 through 2ⁿ−1 and usually wraps modulo 2ⁿ. IEEE 754 trades uniform spacing for dynamic range. Sign, exponent, and significand encode ordinary values plus NaN, infinities, signed zero, and subnormals. UTF-8 encodes Unicode code points as bytes. A visible grapheme may contain several code points, so byte length and character count differ. The gotcha. Reinterpreting bytes changes meaning without converting value. Memory is a hierarchy Registers, caches, RAM, and storage trade capacity against latency and bandwidth. Dense scans exploit locality; pointer chasing and random page access often do not. Caches move lines. Reading one field fetches nearby bytes, and unrelated writes on one line can create false sharing. Virtual memory translates and protects addresses. Page tables and translation caches add another locality boundary. Capacity includes live intermediates. Parameters coexist with activations, gradients, optimizer state, workspaces, padding, and copies. The gotcha. A parameter file can fit while the running model fails at its memory peak. Instructions expose physical cost Compilers lower source into an instruction set. Pipelines overlap stages, out-of-order execution finds independent work, vector units operate on lanes, and atomic operations coordinate selected shared updates. Dependencies set the parallel ceiling. More cores cannot accelerate a serial chain. Memory ordering belongs to correctness. An atomic counter does not protect a multi-step invariant. Formats preserve meaning across machines. Endianness, sizes, schema versions, units, and checksums need explicit contracts. The gotcha. Successful parsing proves structure, not semantic compatibility.

Learn the programming concepts that connect ordinary code to numerical computing. How the pieces connect MENTAL MODEL Python, arrays vectorized thinking — from question to evidence 01 Specify shapes Name every axis and its semantic meaning. 02 Transform Use array operations with an explicit dtype. 03 Validate Assert shape, range, finiteness, and alignment. 04 Measure Benchmark representative sizes and allocations. Specify shapes → Transform → Validate → Measure. Each transition is a place where an assumption can be inspected before the next layer of the system compounds it. Names, values, and mutation A Python name refers to an object. Assignment can create another reference rather than another copy. Lists are flexible containers; numerical arrays store elements with a dtype and shape. Mutating an array view can modify the original storage, so understand whether an operation returns a view or a copy. Shape is part of the contract A batch of 32 feature vectors with 128 features has shape (32,128). A weight matrix of shape (128,10) maps it to (32,10). Write dimensions next to each intermediate. Broadcasting expands compatible dimensions conceptually; it may avoid copying inputs but still produce a very large output. Vectorization and the runtime Calling an array operation delegates loops to compiled numerical code. This reduces Python interpreter overhead and can use SIMD or GPU kernels. It does not make the computational complexity disappear. A vectorized pairwise distance calculation over a million points may still allocate an impossible trillion-entry result. Build reproducible experiments Use isolated environments and record dependency versions. Set seeds when comparing runs, but do not assume identical results across hardware or kernels. Keep preprocessing, model code, data versions, and evaluation settings together. Assertions about shapes and finite values catch errors closer to their source. Worked example import numpy as np x = np.array([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]]) w = np.array([[2.], [-1.]]) y = x @ w assert y.shape == (2, 1) print(y.ravel()) # [0. 2.] What goes wrong Elementwise multiplication (*) and matrix multiplication (@) answer different questions. A computation can run without a shape error and still broadcast along the wrong axis. Check your understanding What is the result shape of (8,16) @ (16,4)? Reveal the explanation (8,4). The matching inner dimension is summed over; the outer dimensions remain. An operating model for python, arrays & vectorized thinking Numerical programming is a discipline of contracts. A tensor shape is not decoration: it records which examples, positions, features, heads, or channels an operation is acting on. Most subtle errors occur when an operation is legal under broadcasting but semantically applies an axis in the wrong role. The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test. Worked system: the broadcast that silently changes the experiment Suppose a batch of four examples has shape [4, 3] : four rows and three features. You intend to subtract one mean per feature, so the mean must have shape [3] and broadcasts across rows. If you instead compute a mean with shape [4, 1] , Python and NumPy will still produce a legal [4, 3] result—but it subtracts one value per example. There is no exception because both operations are mathematically defined. The failure is semantic: the array library cannot know whether your first axis means examples, time, heads, or channels. Use a tiny matrix whose expected result can be calculated by hand. Print every shape at an operation boundary, assert finiteness after divisions or exponentials, and name axes in comments or a typed tensor library. This is not defensive ceremony. In ML code, a silently broadcast loss can improve while training the wrong objective, and a transposed attention tensor can return plausible values with the wrong positions interacting. Notebook: Trace a byte budget Keep a tiny hand-calculated input beside every new operation. Print shapes and a few values, then compare the vectorized result to a simple loop before scaling it. items = 1_000_000 bytes_per_item = 4 working_set = items * bytes_per_item print(f"{working_set / 2**20:.1f} MiB") # Now include every copy, index, and temporary buffer. Names, identity, and ownership Assignment binds a name to an object; it does not promise a copy. This matters when configurations, containers, iterators, and numerical views carry mutable state across experiments. Identity differs from equality. is tests shared identity; == compares values. Mutable defaults persist across calls. Create per-call state inside the function. Shallow copies retain nested aliases. Define which layer owns mutation. Generators are consumable state. An exhausted iterator can produce an empty evaluation pass without an exception. The gotcha. A fixed seed cannot control hidden mutation from an earlier run. Shape, dtype, strides, and offset define an array An ndarray is a view over a buffer. Shape gives logical extents; strides give byte steps; dtype determines representation and arithmetic. Reshape may change only metadata. An incompatible layout forces a copy. Transpose usually changes strides. A later kernel may materialize contiguous storage. Basic slicing often returns a view. Advanced indexing commonly returns a copy. Broadcasting aligns axes from the right. It can avoid copying an input while allocating a huge output. The gotcha. Compatible dimensions do not prove compatible axis meanings. Vectorization changes the cost model Array operations move loops into compiled kernels. Fusion avoids intermediates; batching amortizes overhead; reductions introduce ordering and numerical choices. Benchmark synchronization boundaries. Reading an accelerator scalar may wait for queued work. Keep a slow oracle. Verify optimized operations against a transparent implementation on tiny inputs. Test invariants. Assert shape, finiteness, normalization, masking, and expected transformations. The gotcha. A one-line expression can allocate several arrays and perform quadratic work.

Estimate how work grows before trying to make it faster with hardware. How the pieces connect MENTAL MODEL Algorithms, complexity data structures — from question to evidence 01 Define input scale Count records, edges, dimensions, and sequence length. 02 Choose representation Use an array, index, graph, cache, or stream. 03 Find dependencies Separate parallel work from reductions and sequential state. 04 Measure reality Include allocation, locality, I/O, and constants. Define input scale → Choose representation → Find dependencies → Measure reality. Each transition is a place where an assumption can be inspected before the next layer of the system compounds it. Count growth, then constants Big-O describes an asymptotic upper bound, not a measured runtime. Scanning n records is O(n); comparison sorting is typically O(n log n); forming all pairwise similarities is O(n²). Constant factors, memory locality, and parallelism determine actual performance at a particular size. Choose the representation Arrays provide compact indexed storage. Hash tables give expected constant-time lookup under suitable assumptions. Trees organize ordered searches. Graphs represent relationships; adjacency lists are efficient for sparse edges, while dense matrices can be convenient for highly connected structures. Dependencies control parallelism Independent outputs can run concurrently. A reduction, such as summing a million values, needs a combination step but can use a logarithmic-depth tree. A recurrence that requires the previous state creates a sequential dependency. Concurrency describes overlapping progress; parallelism describes simultaneous execution. Time-space tradeoffs Caching spends memory to avoid repeated computation. Recomputing activations saves training memory but increases work. Tiling moves small reusable chunks into fast storage. Approximate nearest-neighbor indexes trade exact retrieval guarantees for speed and memory efficiency. Always state which resource the optimization spends. Worked example Doubling sequence length makes a dense attention score matrix four times larger: 4,096² becomes 8,192². At two bytes per element, a single unbatched, single-head score matrix grows from 32 MiB to 128 MiB. Memory-efficient attention changes materialization, while exact dense attention still involves quadratic pair interactions. What goes wrong An O(n) algorithm is not always faster than an O(n log n) one at small n. Benchmark representative sizes and include preprocessing, transfers, and allocations. Check your understanding If pairwise work is O(n²), what happens when n triples? Reveal the explanation The leading quadratic work grows by a factor of nine. Fixed overhead and other terms may make measured time differ. An operating model for algorithms, complexity & data structures Complexity is a way to eliminate impossible designs before implementation. It does not replace profiling. A quadratic algorithm can be ideal at small scale, and an asymptotically elegant method can lose because it creates scattered memory access or expensive setup. The right procedure is to estimate growth, then measure the actual operating range. The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test. Worked system: why attention makes sequence length expensive A standard attention layer compares each token with every other token. At sequence length n , the score matrix has n² entries. Doubling a prompt from 4,000 to 8,000 tokens creates four times as many pairwise scores; it does not merely add another 4,000 operations. The same pattern appears in all-pairs similarity search, dense graph algorithms, and naive duplicate detection. Complexity tells you which axis will dominate before a profiler can. But asymptotic notation is only the beginning. An implementation that never materializes the full score matrix can change memory behavior radically while preserving the mathematical result. A hash index can turn a scan into an expected constant-time lookup while introducing build cost and collisions. A practical design asks two questions together: what grows fastest as the input changes, and what does one unit of that work mean in bytes, cache misses, network round trips, or kernel launches on the actual machine? Notebook: Trace a byte budget Write one back-of-the-envelope calculation for every large intermediate. Count elements, bytes per element, and operations. Growth covers work, space, communication, and span Complexity rules out impossible designs before profiling. Work counts operations; span counts the longest dependency chain; communication counts bytes, messages, and synchronization rounds. Worst-case bounds protect tail behavior. Good average performance can coexist with an adversarial outage. Amortized analysis prices a sequence. Occasional resizing can still yield constant average append cost. Lower bounds expose changed assumptions. Beating a general bound usually changes keys, error tolerance, preprocessing, or the query. The gotcha. Big-O hides constants and units; calculate bytes or operations at the intended scale. Data structures purchase operations with layout Arrays favor indexed scans and locality. Middle insertion requires movement. Hash tables favor exact lookup. They spend ordering and collision management. Trees preserve ordered operations. Balance maintains logarithmic depth. Graph storage follows density. Adjacency lists cost O(V+E); matrices cost O(V²). Indexes trade build cost for queries. Approximate indexes also trade recall for speed. The gotcha. A lookup bound ignores iteration, cache misses, serialization, and operation mix. AI complexity starts with named tensor axes Dense attention couples positions quadratically. Doubling length creates four times the pairwise scores. Autoregressive decoding retains a serial dependency. Batching adds parallel work across requests. Retrieval separates recall from ranking. A fast index supplies candidates; a slower model reranks a bounded set. Checkpointing trades arithmetic for memory. Recomputed activations reduce stored state. The gotcha. A faster kernel changes nothing when queues, transfers, retrieval, or tokenization dominate.

Understand processes, files, asynchronous work, and the distributed systems underneath AI applications. How the pieces connect MENTAL MODEL Operating systems, networks concurrency — from question to evidence 01 Receive A request arrives with identity, deadline, and payload. 02 Queue Admission control decides whether work can begin. 03 Execute CPU, GPU, storage, and tools make progress asynchronously. 04 Commit Return or persist an idempotent, observable result. Receive → Queue → Execute → Commit. Each transition is a place where an assumption can be inspected before the next layer of the system compounds it. Processes and resource ownership An operating system schedules processes, protects address spaces, and manages files and devices. Threads in one process share memory; processes communicate through pipes, sockets, shared memory, or files. Shared state requires coordination to prevent races. More workers can increase overhead or oversubscribe CPU cores. Asynchrony is not completion An asynchronous API returns before the requested work finishes. A future, event, or synchronization boundary lets code wait for completion. GPU kernel launches are often asynchronous. Timing only the launch measures submission overhead rather than the kernel’s full execution. Networks introduce partial failure A request may time out even though the server completed it. A retry can repeat an action. Idempotency keys, deadlines, bounded retries, and durable task state help control this ambiguity. Distinguish a transport connection, a protocol such as HTTP, and an application’s contract. Throughput, latency, and queues Throughput measures completed jobs per unit time. Latency measures how long a job takes. Under load, queue time can dominate service time. Report percentiles, particularly p95 or p99, because averages can hide slow requests. Backpressure limits incoming work when downstream capacity is saturated. Worked example If an endpoint can complete 20 requests per second but receives 30 every second, its queue grows by about 10 per second until requests are rejected, timed out, or capacity changes. Faster model kernels will not help if requests actually wait on a slow database. What goes wrong Using unbounded retries or queues turns a recoverable slowdown into a resource outage. Measure the full request path, not only the model invocation. Check your understanding Why can a retried tool call create two orders? Reveal the explanation The first request may have committed before the response was lost. Retrying without an idempotency mechanism repeats the external action. An operating model for operating systems, networks & concurrency Distributed systems fail by being ambiguous. A timeout says the caller did not receive an answer; it does not say whether the server acted. A robust design therefore carries identity, deadlines, idempotency, cancellation, and durable state through the path rather than treating retries as harmless. The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test. Worked system: a timeout is not a cancellation A user presses “generate report.” The browser sends a request with a ten-second deadline. At nine seconds, the server has written the report request to a queue; at ten seconds, the browser disconnects. Did the request succeed? From the user’s perspective it failed because no response arrived. From the worker’s perspective it may still run and email a report. Retrying without an idempotency key can therefore produce two reports, two charges, or two writes to a database. The design response is concrete. Give the request a stable identifier; store its state durably; make the worker accept duplicate deliveries without duplicating the effect; propagate cancellation only where cancellation is safe; and expose a status endpoint that separates “not started,” “running,” “completed,” and “failed.” These are not cloud-service niceties. Any AI workflow that calls tools, spends money, or takes time needs the same distinction between a lost response and an unperformed action. Notebook: Trace a byte budget Draw the request path and mark every boundary where work can be queued, retried, canceled, or committed. Then test each boundary with a forced delay and a repeated request. items = 1_000_000 bytes_per_item = 4 working_set = items * bytes_per_item print(f"{working_set / 2**20:.1f} MiB") # Now include every copy, index, and temporary buffer. Return or persist an idempotent, observable result. The gotcha. Passing each component check separately does not prove the composed path preserves identity, units, ordering, or authority. Processes, threads, and async tasks fail differently A process owns an address space. Threads share it. Async tasks usually share a thread and yield at suspension points. Each model defines isolation, communication, and cancellation boundaries. Locks protect invariants. Holding one during I/O can serialize unrelated work. Async overlaps waiting. It does not make CPU-heavy work parallel. Cancellation requires cooperation. Stopping a caller does not undo a database commit, tool call, or accelerator kernel. The gotcha. Tests must force contested schedules, cancellation, and exhaustion. Queues make overload explicit A queue absorbs bursts but cannot create capacity. When arrival exceeds sustainable service, waiting grows until rejection, timeout, or failure. Bound queues. Shed work before memory exhaustion chooses the outcome. Measure queue time separately. Busy workers can coexist with unacceptable user latency. Propagate backpressure. A slow consumer does not help if producers retry into another buffer. Choose fairness. FIFO, priority, quotas, and aging distribute waiting differently. The gotcha. Throughput can improve while p99 latency violates the promise. Networks create ambiguous outcomes A timeout cannot distinguish a slow server, lost request, lost response, or work committed after the deadline. TCP is an ordered byte stream. Applications define messages and commits. Retries need deadlines, jitter, and idempotency. Deduplication must share a transaction with the effect. Ordering has a scope. One connection may preserve order while the whole system does not. Trace the complete request. Separate queue, retrieval, prefill, decode, tool, and commit time. The gotcha. Exactly-once behavior usually combines at-least-once delivery with transactional deduplication.

The language of model representations: vectors, matrices, projections, rank, and singular values. How the pieces connect MENTAL MODEL Linear algebra: vectors to decompositions — from question to evidence 01 Represent Choose coordinates, shapes, and a basis. 02 Transform Apply a matrix as a linear map. 03 Measure Use dot products, norms, projections, and rank. 04 Compress Retain useful directions with low-rank structure. Represent → Transform → Measure → Compress. Each transition is a place where an assumption can be inspected before the next layer of the system compounds it. Vectors encode measurements A vector is an ordered collection of numbers. Its coordinates only have meaning relative to a representation. Addition combines coordinates; scalar multiplication rescales them. The Euclidean norm measures length. A dot product combines coordinatewise products into one value, useful for similarity and linear prediction. Matrices are linear maps A matrix maps an input vector to an output vector through weighted sums. Multiplication composes maps. Transposition exchanges rows and columns. An embedding table uses a row lookup, while a neural layer typically multiplies features by a learned weight matrix and adds a bias. Rank and subspaces Rank measures the number of independent directions a matrix maps to. Correlated features can reduce effective dimensionality. Orthogonal vectors have zero dot product. Projecting onto a subspace discards information outside it; whether this is useful depends on which information matters for the task. Decompositions explain compression The singular value decomposition writes a matrix as UΣVᵀ, separating input directions, strengths, and output directions. Keeping the largest singular values gives a low-rank approximation under standard matrix norms. LoRA parameterizes an update as a product of two thin matrices; it does not require the original matrix to be low rank. Worked example For a=[1,2] and b=[3,4], a·b=11. Their norms are √5 and 5, giving cosine similarity 11/(5√5)≈0.984. A large cosine means similar direction in this representation; it is not proof that two sentences make the same claim. What goes wrong Similarity depends on the embedding model and normalization. Confusing linear independence with statistical independence mixes two different concepts. Check your understanding How many parameters are in a rank-8 update A×B for a 4,096×4,096 weight matrix? Reveal the explanation 4,096×8 + 8×4,096 = 65,536, compared with 16,777,216 for the full matrix. An operating model for linear algebra: vectors to decompositions Linear algebra becomes useful when you read each symbol as a transformation of a space rather than a grid of arithmetic. A row of a weight matrix asks one learned question of an input; a column describes how one input coordinate contributes across outputs. Matrix multiplication composes these questions into layers. The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test. Worked system: a recommendation is a projection Imagine representing a song as a vector whose coordinates encode learned musical properties. A listener history can also be aggregated into a vector. A simple recommender scores each candidate song by a dot product with that history: coordinates aligned with the listener’s preferences add positive evidence; opposed coordinates subtract it. Normalizing vectors turns the score into cosine similarity, which emphasizes direction over magnitude. The model does not need human-readable coordinates for the geometry to matter. Low-rank structure gives the same system an economic advantage. If a large interaction matrix is well approximated by a few latent directions, the model can store and compute with compact factors instead of one parameter per user–song pair. The caveat is equally important: the approximation preserves the directions favored by the objective, so rare tastes and poorly represented communities can lose detail. A singular-value plot is therefore both an engineering tool and a question about whose variation the system is willing to discard. Notebook: Check the quantity before trusting it When reading an equation, annotate every object with its shape and ask what each axis means. If a multiplication has no interpretation in terms of mapping or aggregation, the notation has become disconnected from the model. import numpy as np x = np.array([2., -1.]) W = np.array([[1., 3.], [0., -2.]]) y = W @ x print("shape", y.shape, "value", y) # Write units and axis meanings beside every array. Transform What would show that this boundary failed? Apply a matrix as a linear map. Measure What would show that this boundary failed? Use dot products, norms, projections, and rank. Compress What would show that this boundary failed? Retain useful directions with low-rank structure. The gotcha. Passing each component check separately does not prove the composed path preserves identity, units, ordering, or authority. Vectors represent states, not arrows by default A vector is an element of a space whose operations obey specific rules. Coordinates appear only after choosing a basis. The same abstract vector can have different coordinate lists in different bases, which is why a basis change can expose structure without changing the represented object. Vector spaces define legal combination. Addition combines states and scalar multiplication changes scale. Images, audio windows, token embeddings, model parameters, and probability tables can all be vectors once their coordinate assumptions are explicit. A basis is a coordinate system. Basis vectors span the space and remain linearly independent. Every vector has one coordinate representation in that basis. Learned representations choose coordinates that make downstream transformations useful. Subspaces describe constrained variation. The column space contains outputs a matrix can produce. The null space contains inputs erased by the transformation. Rank counts independent directions preserved by the map. Affine operations add translation. A neural layer usually computes Wx+b. The matrix is linear; the bias shifts the origin. Calling the whole layer linear is common shorthand but mathematically imprecise. The gotcha. A coordinate has no stable meaning outside its basis. Comparing individual embedding dimensions across independently trained models usually has no invariant interpretation. Matrix multiplication composes transformations If A maps inputs into an intermediate space and B maps that representation into an output space, BA performs both maps in order. The shared inner dimension is the interface contract. Order matters because matrix multiplication is generally not commutative. Rows ask questions. Each row forms a dot product with the input. It measures alignment with one learned direction and becomes one output coordinate. Columns show contribution. A column describes how one input basis direction influences every output coordinate. Reading rows and columns this way turns a grid of numbers into a map between representations. Batched multiplication adds leading axes. Libraries apply products across batches, heads, or spatial positions. Shape notation should identify these axes because broadcasting can replicate a matrix without copying it. Associativity creates implementation choices. A(BC) and (AB)C are mathematically equal when shapes allow, but intermediate sizes and rounding differ. Compilers choose contraction orders to reduce work or memory. The gotcha. Compatible shapes do not guarantee a correct semantic contraction. Label every axis before trusting a high-rank tensor expression. Inner products create geometry An inner product turns two vectors into a scalar and defines length, angle, and orthogonality. The ordinary dot product is one inner product. Other positive-definite forms encode different geometry by weighting directions differently. Norms measure size. The Euclidean norm follows from the dot product. L1 and max norms measure different properties and induce different nearest points. Regularization and robustness claims depend on the selected norm. Cosine similarity removes magnitude. Dividing a dot product by both norms measures directional alignment. It is undefined for a zero vector and can hide confidence or frequency information stored in magnitude. Projection finds the represented component. Orthogonal projection decomposes a vector into a component inside a subspace and a perpendicular residual. Least squares uses this geometry when no exact solution exists. Gram matrices collect pairwise products. XᵀX records feature relationships; XXᵀ records sample relationships. Forming either explicitly can square a large dimension and worsen conditioning. The gotcha. Similarity in an embedding space comes from the training objective and data. Proximity does not automatically mean factual equivalence, causality, or fairness. Linear systems and least squares The equation Ax=b asks for an input whose transformation equals the target. A unique solution requires the map to preserve enough independent directions. When observations conflict or outnumber parameters, least squares minimizes the squared residual norm. Elimination reveals structure. Row operations preserve the solution set while reducing a system to triangular form. Pivoting avoids division by dangerously small values and improves numerical behavior. Overdetermined systems project. Least squares projects b onto the column space of A. The residual is orthogonal to every column, yielding the normal equation AᵀAx=Aᵀb. Normal equations can be unstable. Forming AᵀA squares the condition number and can lose precision. QR or SVD costs more arithmetic but preserves more numerical information. Regularization changes the question. Ridge regression adds a parameter-norm penalty. It stabilizes poorly determined directions while introducing bias, creating an explicit bias-variance tradeoff. The gotcha. Never form a matrix inverse merely to solve a system. Use a factorization that exploits structure and reports numerical failure. Decompositions expose useful axes A decomposition rewrites one transformation as simpler factors. The factors reveal directions, scaling, rotation, triangular structure, or low-rank approximation and usually provide a better computational route than direct symbolic manipulation. QR separates orientation and scale. An orthogonal factor preserves lengths while a triangular factor supports efficient substitution. QR is a reliable default for least squares. Eigenvectors describe invariant directions. An eigenvector keeps its direction under a square transformation while its eigenvalue gives the scale. Defective or non-normal matrices may lack a stable eigenbasis. SVD works for rectangular matrices. Singular value decomposition expresses a map as orthogonal input directions, nonnegative scales, and orthogonal output directions. Truncation gives the best low-rank approximation under common norms. Condition number predicts sensitivity. The ratio of largest to smallest relevant singular value estimates how much input or rounding error can be amplified. A formally solvable equation can still be unreliable. The gotcha. A small singular value may represent noise or a rare but essential direction. Validate compression on the downstream task, not only reconstruction error. Attention is linear algebra with data-dependent weights A transformer projects token representations into queries, keys, and values. Query-key dot products create pairwise scores. Softmax turns each row into nonnegative weights summing to one, and a weighted sum of values produces a context-dependent representation. Projection defines comparison spaces. Learned matrices decide which features queries ask for, keys advertise, and values transmit. Multiple heads repeat the process in smaller subspaces. Scaling controls magnitude. Dividing scores by the square root of head width keeps their variance from growing with dimension under common initialization assumptions. Masking changes legal interactions. A causal mask prevents positions from using future tokens. Padding masks remove nonexistent positions. A mask bug can leak answers while training loss looks excellent. Output projection mixes heads. Concatenated head outputs return through a learned map to model width. Residual paths and normalization then change both representation and optimization behavior. The gotcha. Attention weights are internal routing coefficients. They are not automatically faithful explanations of what caused the final prediction. A numerical checklist for linear algebra code Annotate shapes and axes. Record the semantic role of every dimension beside equations and assertions. Track dtype and device. Know where conversion, copying, accumulation, and synchronization occur. Avoid explicit inverses. Choose a solver matched to symmetry, sparsity, definiteness, and conditioning. Measure residuals. Check both forward error and how well the computed result satisfies the original equation. Test invariants. Orthogonal matrices preserve norms; probability rows sum to one; covariance matrices should remain symmetric positive semidefinite within tolerance. Use tiny exact cases. Compare optimized kernels against hand-computed examples before scaling dimensions. The gotcha. A result can have the expected shape, finite values, and low runtime while remaining mathematically wrong because one axis, transpose, or normalization convention was misidentified.

Understand what a derivative measures and how a network assigns responsibility for error. How the pieces connect MENTAL MODEL Calculus, gradients the chain rule — from question to evidence 01 Forward pass Compute intermediate values and the loss. 02 Local derivatives Record how each operation changes nearby values. 03 Backward pass Apply the chain rule from loss to parameters. 04 Update Use the gradients with a controlled optimizer step. Forward pass → Local derivatives → Backward pass → Update. Each transition is a place where an assumption can be inspected before the next layer of the system compounds it. A derivative measures local change For a scalar function, the derivative describes how the output changes for a small change in input. It is a local approximation, not a prediction over an arbitrary distance. A gradient collects partial derivatives with respect to many parameters. Its negative points toward steepest local decrease under Euclidean geometry. The chain rule connects operations For y=f(g(x)), dy/dx=f′(g(x))g′(x). A computation graph makes the intermediate values explicit. Backpropagation applies this rule backward, reusing intermediate derivatives. It computes gradients; an optimizer separately decides how to update parameters. Jacobians and vector-Jacobian products For a vector output, the Jacobian contains derivatives of every output with respect to every input. Materializing it can be expensive. Reverse-mode differentiation propagates vector-Jacobian products from a scalar loss, which is efficient when there are many parameters but one objective. Curvature and numerical checks Second derivatives describe how slopes change. Curvature makes one learning rate behave differently along different directions. Finite differences approximate gradients and can validate small implementations, but cancellation and step-size choice matter. Non-differentiable points often use an agreed subgradient. Worked example Let prediction ŷ=wx and loss L=(wx−y)². For x=2, y=5, and w=1, the prediction is 2, loss is 9, and dL/dw=2(wx−y)x=−12. A step of 0.1 gives w=2.2 and the new loss is 0.36. What goes wrong A negative gradient does not guarantee a finite step decreases the loss. Detaching a tensor or converting it to a Python number can break the computation graph. Check your understanding Does backpropagation itself change weights? Reveal the explanation No. It computes derivatives. An optimizer uses them, potentially with momentum, adaptive statistics, weight decay, or other rules. An operating model for calculus, gradients & the chain rule Backpropagation is an accounting method for responsibility. Each local derivative answers how an output would respond to a small input change; the chain rule sends that responsibility through the graph. It does not understand a task or select a learning rate. Those are modeling and optimization decisions made around it. The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test. Worked system: trace one error backwards Take a one-parameter model ŷ = w × x with one observation x = 3 , target y = 12 , and squared loss L = (ŷ − y)² . At w = 2 , the prediction is 6 and the loss is 36. The derivative follows the graph: changing w changes ŷ by x ; changing ŷ changes the loss by 2(ŷ−y) . Thus dL/dw = 2(6−12)×3 = −36 . A small positive update to w moves the prediction toward 12. This miniature example contains the full backpropagation pattern. The loss contributes a local signal, each operation multiplies it by its local derivative, and parameter gradients accumulate where paths meet. It also shows why scale matters: if activations or derivatives become very large or very small across many layers, the update can explode or vanish. Gradient clipping, normalization, initialization, residual connections, and learning-rate schedules exist to keep this accounting process numerically usable. Local derivatives What would show that this boundary failed? Record how each operation changes nearby values. Backward pass What would show that this boundary failed? Apply the chain rule from loss to parameters. Update What would show that this boundary failed? Use the gradients with a controlled optimizer step. The gotcha. Passing each component check separately does not prove the composed path preserves identity, units, ordering, or authority. Derivatives are local linear models A derivative describes the best linear approximation near one point. For a scalar function it is a slope; for many inputs the gradient collects partial derivatives; for vector outputs the Jacobian records every local input-output sensitivity. Directional derivatives test one perturbation. The dot product of a unit direction with the gradient predicts first-order change along that direction. The chain rule composes local maps. Reverse-mode automatic differentiation propagates one scalar loss backward through a graph and is efficient when parameters greatly outnumber outputs. Subgradients extend selected nonsmooth cases. ReLU and absolute value lack a unique derivative at a point, so libraries choose a valid convention that supports optimization. Finite differences provide an independent check. Compare a directional derivative with symmetric perturbations across several step sizes; steps that are too large incur approximation error, while tiny steps suffer cancellation. The gotcha. A gradient is local. It does not identify a global optimum, a causal effect, or a safe step size. Backpropagation is a memory and graph computation The forward pass creates intermediate values. The backward pass applies vector-Jacobian products in reverse dependency order. Frameworks retain enough graph state to compute those products. Broadcasting reverses through reduction. A value broadcast across positions receives the sum of gradient contributions from those positions. In-place mutation can invalidate saved values. Autodiff needs the version used during the forward computation. Gradient accumulation is additive. Clear buffers deliberately or microbatches and repeated backward calls accumulate state. Checkpointing recomputes intermediates. It lowers activation memory and spends additional arithmetic. The gotcha. A finite gradient can still be wrong because the loss, mask, reduction, or detached path encodes the wrong computation.

Reason about uncertain events, conditional evidence, distributions, and estimates from samples. How the pieces connect MENTAL MODEL Probability, statistics uncertainty — from question to evidence 01 Define event State the population, outcome, and time horizon. 02 Model uncertainty Choose conditional variables and assumptions. 03 Estimate Use samples with known selection and dependence. 04 Decide Combine uncertainty with costs and thresholds. Define event → Model uncertainty → Estimate → Decide. Each transition is a place where an assumption can be inspected before the next layer of the system compounds it. Probabilities describe a model of uncertainty A probability is between zero and one, and mutually exclusive exhaustive outcomes sum to one. A random variable assigns values to outcomes. Discrete variables use probability masses; continuous variables use densities whose integrals over intervals give probabilities. A density itself can exceed one. Conditioning changes the question P(A|B) means probability of A given B. Bayes’ rule connects it to P(B|A), P(A), and P(B). Independence means observing one variable does not change the distribution of the other under the model. Correlation captures a narrower kind of association. Mean, variance, and sampling Expectation is a probability-weighted average. Variance describes dispersion around the mean. A sample mean estimates a population mean, with uncertainty depending on sample size and dependence. Duplicated records do not provide as much independent evidence as new observations. Interpret intervals carefully A frequentist confidence procedure has a specified long-run coverage under assumptions. A Bayesian credible interval summarizes a posterior under a likelihood and prior. Neither fixes dataset bias. Evaluation uncertainty includes sampling variation, annotation disagreement, and shifts between test data and deployment. Worked example Suppose a rare event occurs in 1% of cases. A detector catches 90% of events but flags 5% of non-events. Out of 10,000 cases it finds about 90 true positives and 495 false positives. Only 90/585≈15.4% of alerts are true positives. What goes wrong Confusing P(alert|event) with P(event|alert) ignores the base rate. A precise estimate on an unrepresentative dataset can be precisely wrong. Check your understanding Does a 95% accurate classifier prove useful when 99% of cases are negative? Reveal the explanation No. Always predicting negative already achieves 99% accuracy. Examine precision, recall, decision costs, and the actual class distribution. An operating model for probability, statistics & uncertainty Probability is useful because it forces a conditional statement. “The model is 90% accurate” is incomplete without the population, label definition, base rate, threshold, and time period. A probability estimate supports a decision only if it is calibrated enough for the decision costs and remains valid after deployment shifts. The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test. Worked system: an alert is a decision under a base rate Suppose an account-abuse detector flags 100 accounts in a day. If 80 are truly abusive, its precision is 80%; if there were 160 abusive accounts in total, its recall is 50%. Those two facts immediately suggest different interventions: a costly manual review process may tolerate low recall but needs high precision; an automated block may demand an even lower false-positive rate; a low-friction warning can be used at a different threshold. Accuracy alone conceals all of this because legitimate accounts are usually the overwhelming majority. Calibration matters when a score is presented as a probability. Among accounts given a 0.20 risk score, roughly one in five should be abusive if the score is calibrated for that population and time period. A model can rank cases well yet be poorly calibrated after a policy or user population changes. That is why probability is not just a number from a model—it is a claim about a conditional frequency, a population, and a decision that must survive deployment. Verification questions for probability, statistics & uncertainty Boundary Question Evidence Define event What would show that this boundary failed? State the population, outcome, and time horizon. Model uncertainty What would show that this boundary failed? Choose conditional variables and assumptions. Estimate What would show that this boundary failed? Use samples with known selection and dependence. Decide What would show that this boundary failed? Combine uncertainty with costs and thresholds. The gotcha. Passing each component check separately does not prove the composed path preserves identity, units, ordering, or authority. Probability statements require a population and conditioning set A probability is defined relative to a model or sampling process. The useful question is never merely “what is the probability?” It is “for which population, given which information, measured at what time?” Base rates shape posterior conclusions. A highly accurate detector can produce mostly false alarms when the event is rare. Conditional independence is an assumption. Factoring a joint distribution makes inference tractable and can be badly wrong when the omitted dependence carries signal. Calibration and ranking differ. A model can rank examples well while its reported probabilities remain systematically too high or low. Selection changes the estimand. Logged users, labeled cases, and completed outcomes may exclude exactly the cases a deployed policy affects. The gotcha. More samples reduce random error around the quantity sampled; they do not remove selection bias or repair the wrong target. Uncertainty belongs around comparisons A sample statistic varies across possible samples. Standard errors, confidence intervals, posterior intervals, and resampling methods express different uncertainty claims and depend on different assumptions. Dependence reduces effective sample size. Repeated events from one user, adjacent time points, and near-duplicate documents do not provide independent evidence. Multiple testing creates discoveries by chance. Searching many metrics, slices, checkpoints, and prompts requires correction or a protected confirmation set. Effect size answers a different question from significance. A tiny operationally irrelevant change can become statistically clear with enough data. Distribution shift changes the target. An interval computed under yesterday's sampling process does not guarantee coverage after policy or population change. The gotcha. A narrow interval around a biased estimate communicates precision without accuracy.

Turn a mathematical objective into a stable training process. How the pieces connect MENTAL MODEL Optimization numerical stability — from question to evidence 01 State objective Encode what improves and what constraints apply. 02 Differentiate Compute or estimate a direction of local change. 03 Step Apply a learning rate and optimizer state. 04 Diagnose Inspect loss, gradients, stability, and validation. State objective → Differentiate → Step → Diagnose. Each transition is a place where an assumption can be inspected before the next layer of the system compounds it. Objectives encode preferences A loss assigns a penalty to predictions. Optimization searches parameters that lower it. The training objective is a proxy for the actual goal: a lower loss need not imply safer answers or better user outcomes. Constraints and regularization express additional preferences about solutions. Gradient descent and minibatches Full-batch descent computes a gradient over the dataset; stochastic methods estimate it from samples or minibatches. Small batches use less memory but produce noisier estimates. Momentum smooths updates, while adaptive methods scale coordinates using gradient statistics. Learning rate often matters more than a fashionable optimizer. Conditioning and scaling An ill-conditioned problem is much more sensitive along some directions than others. Feature scaling, initialization, normalization, and suitable parameterization can improve the optimization landscape. Clipping limits unusually large gradients but does not explain why they appeared. Finite precision is part of the algorithm Floating-point addition is not associative. Overflow, underflow, and cancellation can alter results. Compute log-sum-exp by subtracting the largest input before exponentiation. Mixed precision saves memory and increases supported arithmetic throughput but needs appropriate accumulation and loss scaling when necessary. Worked example import math logits = [1000., 1001., 1002.] m = max(logits) logsumexp = m + math.log(sum(math.exp(x-m) for x in logits)) print(round(logsumexp, 3)) # 1002.408 What goes wrong If loss becomes NaN, inspect inputs, activations, gradients, optimizer state, and overflow. Reducing the learning rate blindly may hide a data or numerical bug. Check your understanding Why subtract the largest logit inside softmax? Reveal the explanation It leaves the normalized probabilities unchanged but ensures exponent inputs are nonpositive, preventing large positive exponentials from overflowing. An operating model for optimization & numerical stability An optimizer searches the objective you gave it, including accidental shortcuts in the data. Training curves are therefore evidence about the combined system of model, data, loss, numerical precision, and update rule. A stable decreasing training loss is necessary for many models but is not evidence of a useful deployed behavior. The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test. Worked system: a lower training loss can be a worse model Train two models on the same labeled dataset. Model A has a small capacity and settles at modest training loss; Model B has enough capacity to drive training loss nearly to zero. If validation loss improves with A but worsens with B, B has learned details that do not transfer to unseen data. The optimizer did exactly what it was asked to do: reduce the objective on the examples supplied. Generalization is not an optimizer guarantee; it comes from the data, representation, regularization, split design, and selection procedure around optimization. Use curves as instruments. Plot training and validation loss on the same scale, inspect gradient norms, and mark changes in learning rate or data. If loss becomes non-finite, find the first activation, gradient, or operation that did so. If training is stable but validation stalls, investigate labels, leakage, augmentation, capacity, and the metric before adding more epochs. The point is not to memorize a list of optimizers; it is to observe which part of the closed loop is carrying the failure. The objective defines what improvement means Optimization searches a mathematical objective under constraints. Model behavior follows the combined objective, data, parameterization, and algorithm, including shortcuts the designer did not intend. Convexity separates local from global structure. For a convex objective every local minimum is global; neural-network objectives generally lack this guarantee. Conditioning controls directional difficulty. Narrow curved valleys make one learning rate too small along one direction and unstable along another. Regularization changes the fitted solution. Connect uncertainty, prediction loss, coding, and the limits of what a benchmark tells you. How the pieces connect MENTAL MODEL Information theory, entropy compression — from question to evidence 01 Define distribution Specify outcomes and conditioning context. 02 Score predictions Compare assigned probability with observations. 03 Compress Use predictable structure to reduce code length. 04 Interpret Separate likelihood from usefulness and truth. Define distribution → Score predictions → Compress → Interpret. Each transition is a place where an assumption can be inspected before the next layer of the system compounds it. Surprise and entropy The information content of an outcome with probability p is −log p. Rare outcomes carry more surprise. Entropy averages surprise under a distribution. With base-two logarithms the unit is bits; natural logarithms give nats. Entropy depends on what is being modeled and conditioned on. Cross-entropy scores a predictor Cross-entropy averages −log q(x) when outcomes are drawn from p but predicted using q. It equals entropy of p plus KL divergence from p to q where defined. Minimizing it rewards probability on observed outcomes, but a model can still assign high likelihood to harmful or factually false text if it appears in data. Compression and language modeling A better probability model can encode predictable symbols more efficiently. Language model perplexity is the exponential of average negative log likelihood in nats. Comparing perplexity across tokenizers or datasets without controlling their definitions is misleading because the prediction units differ. Mutual information and representations Mutual information measures dependence between variables: how much knowing one reduces uncertainty about another. A compressed representation is useful if it retains information needed for the downstream task. Compression alone does not guarantee meaningful, causal, or fair features. Worked example A fair coin has entropy 1 bit. A coin that always lands heads has entropy 0. A predictor assigning 0.9 to an event that occurs receives −ln(0.9)≈0.105 nats of loss; assigning 0.01 receives about 4.605 nats. What goes wrong Entropy of a model’s output distribution measures its uncertainty under its own beliefs. An confidently wrong model can have very low entropy. Check your understanding If token loss is 2 nats, what is perplexity? Reveal the explanation e²≈7.39. Interpret it only with the same tokenization, dataset, and loss accounting. An operating model for information theory, entropy & compression Information measures uncertainty under a distribution, not intelligence or factuality. Cross-entropy teaches a predictor to place probability mass on observed data. It does not directly optimize factual grounding, causal reasoning, safety, or a downstream task unless those are represented in data and the objective. The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test. Worked system: lower cross-entropy, wrong comparison Two language-model evaluations report losses of 1.9 and 2.1. It is tempting to declare the first model better, but the numbers are incomparable if tokenizers differ: one system may divide the same text into more prediction events. The dataset, normalization, token unit, and evaluation protocol define the quantity. Cross-entropy measures the code length assigned to observations under one stated distribution; it does not directly measure factuality, helpfulness, or usefulness in a downstream workflow. Use the measure where it is strong. On a fixed corpus and tokenizer, loss exposes whether a model assigns more probability to held-out text. Then add the task-specific checks loss cannot express: evidence support, safety boundaries, cost, latency, and user success. An information measure is a precise instrument; it becomes misleading when asked to stand in for every product property. A lower number across different token units is not a direct capability comparison. import numpy as np x = np.array([2., -1.]) W = np.array([[1., 3.], [0., -2.]]) y = W @ x print("shape", y.shape, "value", y) # Write units and axis meanings beside every array.
