Information measures depend on a distribution Entropy measures expected uncertainty under one distribution. Cross-entropy measures the expected code length when observations follow one distribution and predictions use another. KL divergence measures their excess coding cost and is asymmetric. Zero-probability assignments are catastrophic. An observed event given probability zero has infinite log loss, which is why numerical implementations clip or use stable logits. Conditional entropy measures remaining uncertainty. Mutual information is the reduction in uncertainty about one variable after observing another. Differential entropy is coordinate-dependent. Continuous entropy can be negative and does not behave like the discrete quantity under rescaling. Tokenization changes the unit. Per-token language-model losses cannot be compared directly across different token vocabularies and segmentation rules. The gotcha. Lower cross-entropy on fixed text measures predictive compression, not truth, reasoning, safety, or task value. Compression connects prediction to representation A predictor that assigns high probability to likely events can encode them with shorter descriptions. This link explains why next-token prediction learns structure, while also marking what the objective leaves unspecified. Source coding exploits statistical regularity. The attainable average code length approaches entropy only under stated source assumptions and sufficiently capable codes. Lossy compression defines a distortion measure. The rate-distortion tradeoff depends on which differences the metric treats as costly. Bottlenecks can discard nuisance variation. Compression helps only when the discarded information is irrelevant to the downstream task. Minimum description arguments include the model. A compact residual paired with an enormous decoder is not a compact explanation. The gotcha. Calling a representation “compressed” is incomplete until the retained task, acceptable distortion, decoder, and total storage cost are stated.

Build trustworthy training and evaluation datasets from raw records. How the pieces connect MENTAL MODEL Data collection, quality lineage — from question to evidence 01 Collect Record source, permissions, time, and unit of observation. 02 Validate Check schema, content, gaps, duplicates, and labels. 03 Version Freeze inputs, transformations, and split identity. 04 Maintain Track drift, corrections, access, and retirement. Collect → Validate → Version → Maintain. Each transition is a place where an assumption can be inspected before the next layer of the system compounds it. Define the unit of data A row might represent an event, person, document, conversation, or device. Decide the unit of prediction and the time at which features would actually be known. Keep stable identifiers so related records can be grouped and traced. A target derived from future outcomes must not leak into features. Quality is task-specific Validate schema, ranges, missingness, duplicates, timestamps, encoding, and class balance. Inspect representative raw examples after each transformation. A perfectly formatted dataset may omit the very cases that matter most. Maintain separate tests for structural validity and semantic correctness. Lineage makes results explainable Record source, collection date, consent or permitted-use metadata where relevant, transformation versions, and dataset hashes. When a source changes, lineage identifies affected examples and models. Version labels and splits as well as raw inputs. Preserve the difference between original observations and synthetic examples. Dataset documentation Describe intended use, collection process, known gaps, language coverage, annotator instructions, and maintenance responsibility. Document who is missing. Restrict access to sensitive records and minimize retention. A model card cannot compensate for unknown training data provenance. Worked example For a support-ticket classifier, split by customer or conversation when related messages share content. If a follow-up response includes the final resolution, using that response to predict the original ticket’s priority would give the model information unavailable at prediction time. What goes wrong Deduplicating only exact strings misses paraphrases and templates. Conversely, aggressive deduplication can remove legitimate minority patterns. Check your understanding Why version the train/test split? Reveal the explanation A changed split changes what success means. Without a fixed split identity, model comparisons can accidentally compare different tasks. An operating model for data collection, quality & lineage Data work is system design, not a preparatory chore. Labels reflect a process, sources change, and rows may represent related events rather than independent samples. A dataset that cannot explain where a record came from, when it was available, and how it was transformed cannot support a reliable model comparison. The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test. Worked system: the label that arrives from the future A support-ticket system wants to predict escalation at the moment a ticket is created. The final resolution, agent notes, and later customer messages may be excellent predictors—but none exists when the original decision is made. Including them creates a model that looks strong offline and fails at the exact moment it is meant to help. This is temporal leakage, and it survives ordinary random train/test splits because both halves can contain information from the future relative to their rows. Build the dataset around an explicit “as-of” time. For every field, record when it became available, who produced it, and whether it can be revised. Split by time or by entity when the deployment demands it. A clean schema is not enough: the semantic lifetime of a value is part of the model. Notebook: Make the split an explicit artifact Treat a data contract like an API contract: validate it automatically and assign an owner. Store a small, reviewed fixture set of raw examples to catch semantic regressions that schema tests miss. train_ids = set(train["record_id"]) assert not train_ids set(test["record_id"]) assert train["event_time"].max() = cutoff # Fit transformations only after this boundary exists. Version: Freeze inputs, transformations, and split identity. 4. Maintain: Track drift, corrections, access, and retirement. The gotcha. A small inspection script proves only the quantities it prints. Preserve units, shapes, versions, and the input fixture beside its output. A rigorous way to practice Collect. Record source, permissions, time, and unit of observation. Validate. Check schema, content, gaps, duplicates, and labels. Version. Freeze inputs, transformations, and split identity. Maintain. Track drift, corrections, access, and retirement. Treat a data contract like an API contract: validate it automatically and assign an owner. Store a small, reviewed fixture set of raw examples to catch semantic regressions that schema tests miss. Validate What would show that this boundary failed? Check schema, content, gaps, duplicates, and labels. Version What would show that this boundary failed? Freeze inputs, transformations, and split identity. Maintain What would show that this boundary failed? Track drift, corrections, access, and retirement. The gotcha. Lineage must answer what happened to one record A usable lineage chain connects source identity, collection time, consent or license, schema version, transformations, labels, splits, and every derived artifact. The unit of observation sets independence. Rows can describe events from the same person, device, document, or session and must often remain in one split. Event time differs from processing time. Backfills and late arrivals can make a feature available in a warehouse long before it would have existed at prediction time. Deletion must propagate. Removing raw data while retaining features, embeddings, caches, exports, and training subsets does not complete the lifecycle. Version content, not only paths. Immutable hashes and manifests distinguish two datasets written to the same location. The gotcha. Turn raw observations into model inputs without contaminating evaluation. How the pieces connect MENTAL MODEL Features, preprocessing leakage — from question to evidence 01 Split first Create time-aware or group-aware evaluation partitions. 02 Fit on train Learn imputers, vocabularies, and scalers only there. 03 Transform Apply identical frozen logic to later data. 04 Serve Validate features and monitor changed distributions. Split first → Fit on train → Transform → Serve. Each transition is a place where an assumption can be inspected before the next layer of the system compounds it. Fit transforms only on training data Imputers, scalers, vocabularies, target encoders, and feature selectors can learn information from data. Fit them within each training split, then apply them to validation data. A pipeline keeps preprocessing coupled to model fitting so cross-validation repeats the correct sequence. Represent missing and categorical values Missingness can be informative, accidental, or structurally required. Choose imputation based on the measurement process, and optionally retain a missingness indicator. One-hot encoding works for modest cardinality. Target encoding needs careful cross-fitting to avoid injecting labels into inputs. Respect time and grouping For forecasting, train on the past and validate on later periods. For patient records, sessions, or devices, group related rows so they do not leak across folds. Temporal joins need point-in-time correctness: the feature store must return what was available at the prediction timestamp. Keep training and serving consistent Package the same preprocessing for inference. Validate feature names, order, dtypes, and units at the boundary. Log aggregate input statistics and monitor drift. A model trained with meters will behave badly on centimeters even though both are valid floating-point numbers. Worked example from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression model = make_pipeline( SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000), ) # Fit only on training data; evaluate on a held-out split. What goes wrong Calling fit_transform on the full dataset before cross-validation leaks distribution information into every fold. A pipeline prevents this only if the split design is also correct. Check your understanding Should validation labels influence a feature selector? Reveal the explanation No. Feature selection is part of training and must be fit inside the training fold. An operating model for features, preprocessing & leakage Preprocessing is part of the model. A median imputer, category vocabulary, target encoder, and feature selector all encode information learned from data. Fitting them before a split lets validation influence training even if the final estimator never sees validation labels. The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test. Worked system: one transformation, two very different outcomes Suppose income has missing values. Filling them with the median seems harmless, but the median is learned from data. If it is calculated on the full dataset before the split, validation rows influence the training representation. The same issue appears with scaling, category vocabularies, feature selection, target encoding, and dimensionality reduction. A pipeline only protects you when its fitting step is restricted to the training fold. The operational version matters as much as evaluation. At serving time, the pipeline must accept an unseen category, a missing field, a reordered payload, and the units supplied by the real producer. Version the feature definitions with the model, then test a raw production-shaped record through the exact same object used during training. Training-serving skew is a contract failure A feature has a definition, timestamp, entity key, unit, missing-value rule, and availability boundary. Understand lexical search, embeddings, approximate indexes, and ranking before adding an LLM. How the pieces connect MENTAL MODEL Search, indexes vector retrieval — from question to evidence 01 Ingest Parse, normalize, version, and authorize documents. 02 Index Build lexical and vector representations. 03 Retrieve Generate a candidate set for the query. 04 Verify Rerank, cite, and abstain when evidence is absent. Ingest → Index → Retrieve → Verify. Each transition is a place where an assumption can be inspected before the next layer of the system compounds it. Lexical and semantic retrieval An inverted index maps terms to matching documents. BM25 uses term frequency, document length, and term rarity for lexical ranking. Dense retrieval maps queries and documents to embeddings and compares them with an appropriate similarity measure. Lexical search is strong for exact identifiers; dense search can recover paraphrases. Approximate nearest neighbors Exact vector search scans all candidates and can be expensive. HNSW navigates a graph; IVF partitions vector space; product quantization compresses representations. Index settings trade recall, latency, build cost, and memory. Evaluate retrieval recall against exact search on a representative sample. Chunking defines what can be retrieved A chunk should preserve enough context to answer a question while remaining focused. Respect headings, tables, code boundaries, and source metadata. Overlap can reduce boundary losses but duplicates content and increases index size. Track document versions and delete stale chunks. Rerank and authorize A reranker spends more computation on a small candidate set. Hybrid retrieval can merge lexical and semantic evidence. Enforce access permissions before exposing retrieved content and check them again if documents change. A citation must point to a source passage that actually supports the answer. Worked example For “error E1042 in firmware 2.7,” lexical matching preserves the exact code and version. For “why does the device restart after sleeping,” embeddings may find a differently worded power-management note. A hybrid candidate set plus a reranker can combine both strengths. What goes wrong Nearest in embedding space does not mean true, relevant, current, or authorized. An LLM cannot answer from a passage retrieval never found. Check your understanding What should you measure before answer quality in RAG? Reveal the explanation Whether the required evidence appears in the retrieved top-k results, then whether the generated answer is supported by that evidence. An operating model for search, indexes & vector retrieval Retrieval quality places a hard ceiling on grounded generation. If the source passage is absent from the candidate set, a later reranker or language model cannot reliably recover it. Treat retrieval recall, source freshness, and authorization as first-class product metrics before prompt polish. The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test. Worked system: the answer cannot outrun retrieval recall A maintenance assistant receives the question “Why does firmware 2.7 restart after sleep?” If the candidate set omits the power-management bulletin, a language model may write a plausible answer but it cannot ground it in the required evidence. Retrieval is therefore a two-stage problem: first find a set that contains the answer; then rank, quote, and synthesize it. Generation quality should be measured only after evidence recall is known. Construct a small benchmark where each question names the required passage or passages. Inspect exact-code queries separately from paraphrases, stale documents separately from current ones, and unauthorized documents separately from authorized ones. A nearest neighbor is merely a geometric neighbor; it is not automatically true, current, or permitted. Notebook: Make the split an explicit artifact Maintain a query set with required passages and unanswerable cases. Measure top-k evidence recall, citation entailment, latency, and access-control behavior separately. train_ids = set(train["record_id"]) assert not train_ids set(test["record_id"]) assert train["event_time"].max() = cutoff # Fit transformations only after this boundary exists. Verify: Rerank, cite, and abstain when evidence is absent. The gotcha. A small inspection script proves only the quantities it prints. Preserve units, shapes, versions, and the input fixture beside its output. A rigorous way to practice Ingest. Parse, normalize, version, and authorize documents. Index. Build lexical and vector representations. Retrieve. Generate a candidate set for the query. Verify. Rerank, cite, and abstain when evidence is absent. Maintain a query set with required passages and unanswerable cases. Measure top-k evidence recall, citation entailment, latency, and access-control behavior separately. Verification questions for search, indexes & vector retrieval Boundary Question Evidence Ingest What would show that this boundary failed? Parse, normalize, version, and authorize documents. Index What would show that this boundary failed? Build lexical and vector representations. Retrieve What would show that this boundary failed? Generate a candidate set for the query. Verify What would show that this boundary failed? Rerank, cite, and abstain when evidence is absent. The gotcha. Passing each component check separately does not prove the composed path preserves identity, units, ordering, or authority. Retrieval is a measured cascade Ingestion creates searchable units; candidate generation seeks recall; reranking spends more computation on a small set; answer construction cites or abstains. Chunking defines retrievable evidence. Chunks that are too small lose context; chunks that are too large dilute matching and consume context budget. Lexical and dense retrieval fail differently. Exact identifiers favor token matching; paraphrase favors learned geometry. Hybrid fusion needs score normalization or rank-based combination. Metadata filters enforce scope before ranking. Post-filtering can return too few authorized candidates or leak counts and snippets. Reranking cannot recover an absent passage. Learn a prediction function from labeled examples and test whether it generalizes. How the pieces connect MENTAL MODEL Supervised learning: regression classification — from question to evidence 01 Define target Specify label time, decision, and error costs. 02 Prepare split Protect future, grouped, and held-out data. 03 Fit baseline Use a simple interpretable model first. 04 Choose action Calibrate and set a threshold for deployment. Define target → Prepare split → Fit baseline → Choose action. Each transition is a place where an assumption can be inspected before the next layer of the system compounds it. Specify inputs, targets, and costs Regression predicts a numerical target; classification predicts a discrete label or probability. The target must match the decision you want to make. Predicting whether a customer cancels is different from predicting whether an intervention would prevent cancellation. Linear models are serious baselines Linear regression combines features through weighted sums and commonly minimizes squared error. Logistic regression maps a linear score through a sigmoid for binary probabilities. Feature transformations permit nonlinear boundaries while retaining a linear model in the transformed space. Regularization constrains coefficient magnitude. Bias, variance, and generalization A model can underfit by missing structure or overfit by learning noise and sample-specific details. Training performance measures fit; held-out performance estimates generalization under the split assumptions. Learning curves compare performance as training data increases and can reveal whether more data is likely to help. Thresholds implement decisions A predicted probability is not yet an action. A threshold determines false positives and false negatives. Choose it using validation data and application costs. Report calibration as well as discrimination when probabilities inform decisions. Worked example Suppose missing a true defect costs 20 units and inspecting a non-defective item costs 1. Under a simplified binary decision model with calibrated probabilities, inspecting is worthwhile when expected missed-defect cost exceeds inspection cost. The optimal threshold depends on the exact cost matrix, not on the default value 0.5. What goes wrong A high random-split score does not prove future performance. Changes in acquisition, population, or policy can invalidate the learned relationship. Check your understanding Is logistic regression a regression or classification method in typical use? Reveal the explanation It models probabilities for classification despite its name. The logistic link transforms a real-valued linear score. An operating model for supervised learning: regression & classification Supervised learning generalizes from a sample to a stated future population. The label is not the decision: a probability must still be converted into an action under asymmetric costs, capacity limits, and human review. Better classification ranking does not automatically improve intervention outcomes. The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test. Worked system: a probability needs a policy A fraud model gives a transaction a score of 0.62. That score is not an action. A review queue with capacity for one percent of transactions may require a high threshold; a low-friction extra verification step can be used more broadly; an irreversible decline may require a different threshold and a human appeal path. The same ranking model can support several policies, each with different costs for false positives and false negatives. Start with an interpretable baseline and a held-out decision table. Inspect examples around the selected threshold, then compare the observed error mix with the people and resources the policy affects. A model that improves area under a curve can still make a workflow worse if it moves the wrong cases across the operating threshold. A practical family of models for structured data, nonlinear interactions, and strong baselines. How the pieces connect MENTAL MODEL Decision trees, forests boosting — from question to evidence 01 Partition A tree selects feature conditions. 02 Regularize Depth, leaves, and sampling control capacity. 03 Combine Average or sequentially correct weak learners. 04 Inspect Test importances and errors against leakage and proxies. Partition → Regularize → Combine → Inspect. Each transition is a place where an assumption can be inspected before the next layer of the system compounds it. Trees partition feature space A decision tree chooses splits that make child nodes more homogeneous under an objective. Following splits routes a sample to a leaf with a prediction. Depth, minimum leaf size, and pruning limit complexity. Trees can model interactions without manually enumerating every feature combination. Random forests reduce variance A forest fits many trees using randomized samples and feature choices, then aggregates predictions. Diversity reduces correlated errors. More trees often stabilize predictions but increase memory and inference work. Out-of-bag estimates can be useful under their sampling assumptions; they do not replace an appropriate temporal or grouped holdout. Boosting corrects residual mistakes Gradient boosting adds weak learners sequentially to reduce an objective. Learning rate, tree count, leaf complexity, and subsampling control capacity. Early stopping uses a validation set. Modern implementations optimize histograms, missing-value handling, and hardware efficiency. Interpretation requires care Feature importance can favor high-cardinality variables or distribute credit unpredictably among correlated features. Permutation importance measures a change in predictive performance under a particular perturbation. Partial dependence can evaluate unrealistic combinations when features are correlated. Worked example Method How learners combine Main tradeoff Single tree One partition Readable when small; unstable when deep Random forest Average randomized trees Robust baseline; larger model Gradient boosting Sequential corrective additions Strong fit; careful tuning and leakage control What goes wrong Training deep trees until error vanishes invites overfitting. A feature that predicts well may be a leakage channel or a proxy, not a causal driver. Check your understanding Why does averaging identical trees give little benefit? Reveal the explanation Their errors are perfectly correlated. Ensembles gain from useful diversity, not just repeated copies. An operating model for decision trees, forests & boosting Trees are powerful because they create interactions and nonlinear regions without feature engineering, but every split is a chance to memorize an accident of the sample. Forests reduce variance through diverse trees; boosting reduces residual error through sequential trees. The choice depends on data size, noise, latency, and explainability needs. The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test. Worked system: a feature importance can be a proxy story A tree ensemble assigns high importance to “number of account logins.” It is tempting to infer that frequent logins cause retention. But the feature may be a proxy for a paid plan, a region, a customer-support intervention, or a post-outcome event that leaked into the data. Trees are excellent at exploiting predictive structure and do not distinguish a useful signal from a causal explanation. Probe importance by perturbing a feature, retraining on different splits, and comparing with a simpler model. Examine correlated features as a group: a tree may choose one arbitrary member of a correlated set and make it look uniquely decisive. Use the model to prioritize investigation, then return to the underlying process before making a policy claim. Explore structure without labels, while keeping the meaning of a discovered pattern separate from its existence. How the pieces connect MENTAL MODEL Clustering, PCA anomaly detection — from question to evidence 01 Choose geometry Decide distance, scaling, and neighborhood 02 Fit structure Cluster, reduce dimensions, or score outliers. 03 Stabilize Repeat across seeds, samples, and settings. 04 Interpret Return to original variables and external evidence. Choose geometry → Fit structure → Stabilize → Interpret. Each transition is a place where an assumption can be inspected before the next layer of the system compounds it. Clustering encodes a similarity choice K-means minimizes within-cluster squared Euclidean distance to centroids. It favors roughly compact groups and needs a chosen k. Density-based methods can find irregular shapes and label noise but depend on scale and density parameters. Standardize meaningful units before distance-based modeling. PCA finds variance directions Principal component analysis projects centered data onto orthogonal directions of large variance. It can denoise or compress features. Large variance is not necessarily predictive: rare but decisive signals may lie in low-variance directions. Fit PCA only on training data when used in a supervised pipeline. Visual embeddings are not proof Two-dimensional projections can reveal local neighborhoods but distort global geometry. Apparent islands depend on method and settings. Confirm a proposed cluster using original features and external evidence rather than treating a plot’s spacing as a measurement. Anomalies need an operational definition An isolation score, density score, or reconstruction error ranks unusual examples. Unusual does not mean fraudulent or faulty. Evaluate with known incidents, synthetic perturbations where appropriate, and investigation outcomes. Set an alert budget to avoid overwhelming reviewers. Worked example A machine has temperature in degrees and vibration in micrometers. Without scaling, the numerically larger unit can dominate Euclidean distance. Standardization changes the clustering question to deviations relative to typical variability; that may be useful, but it must match the physical objective. What goes wrong Choosing clusters until they match a desired narrative turns exploration into confirmation bias. Report stability across seeds and samples. Check your understanding Does PCA preserve the features most useful for a label? Reveal the explanation Not necessarily. It preserves variance without using the label, so low-variance predictive information may be discarded. An operating model for clustering, pca & anomaly detection Unsupervised methods discover structure relative to the representation you selected. K-means sees Euclidean compactness; PCA sees variance; density methods see local concentration. None discovers a natural category independent of measurement, scaling, and modeling assumptions. The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test. Worked system: a cluster is a hypothesis, not a discovered tribe A team projects customer behavior into two dimensions and sees three colored islands. Changing scaling, distance metric, random seed, or the dimensionality-reduction setting may produce two islands, five islands, or a different boundary. The visualization is still useful: it suggests questions, outliers, and candidate segments. It is not evidence that nature contains exactly three customer types. Return to original records. Read examples near each cluster center, compare outcomes that were not used to fit the model, and check whether the structure is stable under reasonable preprocessing choices. Unsupervised methods expose regularities relative to a representation. The representation is where the most consequential assumptions live. Structure appears relative to a representation Clustering, dimensionality reduction, and anomaly detection optimize a geometry selected through features, scaling, distance, neighborhood, and density assumptions. K-means assumes Euclidean compactness. It prefers roughly spherical groups and its mean is sensitive to scale and outliers. PCA preserves variance, not task relevance. High-variance directions can be nuisance; rare low-variance directions can carry the decision. Density methods define local normality. Neighborhood size changes whether a point looks isolated. Make model comparisons that survive contact with real data and actual decisions. How the pieces connect MENTAL MODEL Evaluation, calibration experimental design — from question to evidence 01 Specify outcome Name the user decision and target population. 02 Design split Protect held-out data from all selection steps. 03 Measure Use metrics, uncertainty, and slices. 04 Decide Compare against baseline and operational Specify outcome → Design split → Measure → Decide. Each transition is a place where an assumption can be inspected before the next layer of the system compounds it. Separate fitting from selection Use training data to fit parameters, validation data to choose models and thresholds, and a held-out test for the final comparison. Repeatedly optimizing against a test set effectively turns it into validation data. Cross-validation helps estimate variability, provided folds respect groups and time. Metrics answer different questions Precision asks how many predicted positives were positive. Recall asks how many actual positives were found. PR curves are often informative for rare events. AUROC evaluates ranking across thresholds but can look strong while precision is poor. For regression, MAE and RMSE penalize errors differently. Calibrated confidence Among predictions near 0.8, calibration asks whether roughly 80% are correct under the specified event definition. Reliability diagrams, Brier score, and log loss help assess probability quality. Recalibration uses held-out data and can fail under distribution shift. Measure the system and its slices Report sample counts, uncertainty, baselines, and important subgroups. Paired comparisons on the same examples can reduce variance. Online experiments need assignment units that avoid interference. Evaluate fallback behavior, cost, response time, and human correction work alongside model quality. Worked example A classifier yields 80 true positives, 20 false positives, and 40 false negatives. Precision=80/100=0.80; recall=80/120≈0.667; F1≈0.727. Neither metric alone says whether the system is acceptable without error costs and population context. What goes wrong An improvement smaller than run-to-run variation may be noise. Selecting the best of many trials without accounting for selection makes gains look more reliable than they are. Check your understanding Why is a customer-grouped split sometimes better than a random row split? Reveal the explanation It tests generalization to new customers rather than recognition of repeated patterns from customers already seen in training. An operating model for evaluation, calibration & experimental design Evaluation is an experiment design problem. The test set estimates behavior under the world your split represents. If deployment is temporal, grouped, adversarial, multilingual, or costly, a random aggregate score cannot answer the whole question. Measurement needs to follow the actual decision path. The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test. Worked system: the aggregate score that conceals a release failure An assistant scores 92% on a mixed evaluation set. Broken down by language, document age, and question type, it may be 98% on common English requests, 71% on a supported language, and near zero on requests requiring a current internal policy. The aggregate is mathematically correct but operationally incomplete. A user experiences a slice, a task, and a consequence—not the weighted average. Define a release scorecard before tuning: baseline, split rule, sample counts, confidence interval or repeated-run variance, important slices, latency, cost, abstention behavior, and known exclusions. Keep the test set separate from the examples used to select prompts or thresholds. Evaluation becomes useful when it can veto a release for a reason a user would recognize. Build the conceptual bridge from linear models to learned representations. How the pieces connect MENTAL MODEL Neural networks, activations backpropagation — from question to evidence 01 Encode Map raw input to tensors and representations. 02 Transform Apply learned linear maps and nonlinearities. 03 Score Compare outputs with an objective. 04 Learn Backpropagate, update, validate, and repeat. Encode → Transform → Score → Learn. Each transition is a place where an assumption can be inspected before the next layer of the system compounds it. A layer transforms a representation A dense layer computes a weighted sum and bias, then usually applies a nonlinear activation. Stacking only linear layers collapses into one linear map. Nonlinearities such as ReLU or GELU let a network express more complicated functions. Width and depth shape capacity and computational cost. Learning uses a computation graph The forward pass produces predictions and a loss. The backward pass computes gradients for trainable values. An optimizer updates weights. Clear or accumulate gradients deliberately; accidental accumulation changes the effective update. Validation runs should use the intended inference behavior and avoid gradient storage. Initialization and normalization Poor initialization can make activations or gradients shrink or explode with depth. Normalization changes the scale and statistics passed between operations. Residual connections let a block add a correction to an existing representation and improve gradient flow, although they do not guarantee successful training. Diagnose before scaling Start with a tiny dataset and confirm the model can overfit it. Check shapes, labels, loss conventions, and gradient magnitudes. Compare against a simple baseline. Track training and validation curves; a large gap can indicate overfitting, leakage differences, or mismatched processing. Worked example A dense layer mapping 128 inputs to 64 outputs has 128×64 weights and 64 biases, or 8,256 parameters. With a batch of 32 examples, its output shape is (32,64). Parameters are shared across all examples in the batch. What goes wrong A large network does not repair incorrect labels or an impossible target. Zero loss on training data does not demonstrate generalization. Check your understanding Why do networks need nonlinear activations? Reveal the explanation Without nonlinearities, a composition of affine layers is still affine, so depth does not add nonlinear representational power. An operating model for neural networks, activations & backpropagation A neural network is a compositional function with learned parameters, not a lookup table of answers. Its useful behavior depends on representation, architecture, objective, optimizer, and data together. More parameters increase capacity, but optimization, data coverage, and regularization determine whether that capacity becomes generalizable structure. The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test. Worked system: fitting eight examples before buying more compute Before launching a large training job, take eight labeled examples and try to overfit them. A small network should drive their loss near zero if the input path, labels, loss, gradient flow, and optimizer update are wired correctly. If it cannot, a thousand GPUs will only produce a more expensive failure. This check catches swapped labels, detached tensors, an incorrect reduction, frozen parameters, and shape mistakes that are otherwise easy to miss. Once the tiny case works, scale one axis at a time: data size, model width, learning rate, precision, or batch size. Neural networks have enough capacity to hide mistakes temporarily. The fastest path to understanding is a run small enough that every input, activation, loss, and parameter update can be inspected. Capacity comes from composition A neural network alternates learned affine maps with nonlinear operations. The nonlinearities prevent the entire stack from collapsing into one matrix and let depth reuse intermediate features. Initialization controls signal scale. Poor variance propagation saturates activations or makes gradients vanish and explode. Residual paths create short gradient routes. Understand the architectural ideas that preceded and still complement transformers. How the pieces connect MENTAL MODEL Convolutions, recurrence representation learning — from question to evidence 01 Choose inductive bias Locality, recurrence, global attention, or state-space structure. 02 Share computation Reuse weights across positions or time. 03 Build representation Train with task labels or a self-supervised objective. 04 Transfer Adapt and evaluate under the target domain shift. Choose inductive bias → Share computation → Build representation → Transfer. Each transition is a place where an assumption can be inspected before the next layer of the system compounds it. Convolution shares local computation A convolution applies the same small filter across spatial positions. Weight sharing reduces parameter count and encodes a locality bias. Stride reduces spatial resolution; padding controls boundaries; dilation expands receptive fields. Translation equivariance can be affected by padding, stride, and subsequent operations. Recurrence carries state An RNN updates a hidden state from the current input and previous state. LSTMs and GRUs use gates to regulate information flow. Recurrence is natural for streaming, but sequential dependencies limit training parallelism and long gradient paths can be difficult. State-space models revisit efficient recurrent representations with different parameterizations. Learn from unlabeled structure Autoencoders reconstruct inputs through a bottleneck. Contrastive learning draws related representations together and separates selected alternatives. Masked prediction learns to infer hidden parts. Each pretext task builds an inductive bias and can exploit shortcuts unrelated to the downstream objective. Transfer and domain shift A pretrained representation may support many tasks through a linear probe or fine-tuning. Match preprocessing and investigate the pretraining domain. A representation useful for natural photos may fail on microscopy or manufacturing images with different textures and acquisition processes. Worked example A 3×3 convolution with 3 input channels and 32 output channels has 3×3×3×32=864 weights, plus 32 biases if enabled. These weights are reused across the image rather than learned separately for every pixel location. What goes wrong A visually impressive embedding plot is not a downstream evaluation. Augmentations that preserve labels in one domain may destroy them in another. Check your understanding Does enlarging an input image necessarily increase convolution parameter count? Reveal the explanation No. Shared filter parameters stay the same. The number of spatial operations and activation memory generally increase. An operating model for convolutions, recurrence & representation learning Architectures encode assumptions about how information is organized. Convolution assumes nearby pixels share patterns; recurrence assumes a useful state can summarize the past; attention enables content-based interaction across positions. These are not interchangeable slogans: they change memory, parallelism, data needs, and failure modes. The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test. Worked system: the architecture encodes a bet about the data A convolutional layer shares one filter across image positions. That is a bet that a useful edge or texture should be recognized wherever it appears. A recurrent layer carries a compact state forward through time; that is a bet that the past can be summarized. Attention lets every position consult every other position, trading that flexibility for quadratic interaction cost. These are engineering commitments about locality, memory, and parallelism, not interchangeable brand names. State the invariances you want before selecting a model. If translating an image a few pixels should not change a label, test it. If timing should matter in an audio task, perturb timing. A good inductive bias reduces the data required to learn a pattern; a mismatched one can make a larger model look capable while remaining brittle under the shift users actually encounter. Understand accelerator families by their execution and memory models, not just their product names. How the pieces connect MENTAL MODEL CPUs, GPUs, TPUs Apple silicon — from question to evidence 01 Characterize workload Measure shape, precision, batch, memory, and latency 02 Match hardware Compare supported operations and memory model. 03 Map software Validate framework, compiler, kernels, and libraries. 04 Benchmark system Measure useful end-to-end throughput and tail latency. Characterize workload → Match hardware → Map software → Benchmark system. Each transition is a place where an assumption can be inspected before the next layer of the system compounds it. CPU: flexible control and low latency A CPU is good at irregular control flow, modest parallelism, orchestration, and many general-purpose tasks. Vector instructions accelerate arrays, while caches reduce repeated memory access. Small models or tiny batches may run efficiently on CPUs because accelerator launch and transfer overheads can dominate. GPU: programmable parallel throughput GPUs organize many lightweight threads around shared execution resources. NVIDIA exposes CUDA; AMD provides ROCm and HIP on supported devices; other platforms expose their own runtimes. Similar source syntax does not guarantee identical scheduling, numerical behavior, or kernel availability. Check the particular device and framework build. TPU: matrix-centric execution TPUs emphasize matrix multiplication and compiler-managed execution. Tensor layout, sharding, and compiler decisions matter greatly. Tensor programs must map to available operations and topology. A comparison with GPUs needs equal model quality, batch size, precision, memory fit, and software optimization effort. Unified memory systems Apple silicon integrates CPU and GPU with shared physical memory. This can avoid some explicit copies but does not eliminate synchronization or bandwidth limits. Metal provides GPU programming; frameworks such as MLX expose array operations on this architecture. Unified memory capacity is shared with the rest of the system. Worked example Workload First question Interactive tiny model Does transfer or launch overhead dominate? Large batched training Can matrix operations feed the accelerator efficiently? Local LLM Do weights plus KV cache fit available memory? Multi-device model What is the interconnect and collective cost? What goes wrong A CUDA example does not run on Apple’s GPU simply because both devices are called GPUs. Portability is a software and kernel question as well as a hardware question. Check your understanding Does unified memory mean unlimited GPU memory? Reveal the explanation No. Physical capacity is finite and shared. The operating system and other applications also consume it. An operating model for cpus, gpus, tpus & apple silicon Accelerator choice is a workload and software decision. A theoretical peak describes a particular numerical operation under favorable conditions; it does not guarantee a specific model, framework, sequence length, or service will approach that peak. Memory capacity and a reliable kernel stack often matter more than the headline number. The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test. Worked system: peak throughput is not a deployment plan Two accelerators may advertise dramatically different FLOPS, yet the smaller one can serve a particular model more effectively if the model fits its memory, its framework has mature kernels, and the service is limited by latency rather than matrix throughput. A headline peak assumes a particular operation, precision, and favorable arithmetic intensity. It says little about tokenization, retrieval, host-device transfers, unsupported operations, or long-context memory. Benchmark the exact model, sequence lengths, numerical format, and batch policy you intend to ship. Record time to first token, decode speed, memory peak, error rate, power or cost assumptions, and tail latency. Hardware choice is a system decision made at the workload boundary, not a contest between marketing tables.
