A substantial research program has tried to replace it with something asymptotically cheaper. State-space models are the most successful line of that work, and Mamba in particular closed much of the quality gap. This section is deliberately more hedged than the others, because the question of whether attention can be replaced is genuinely unresolved the pragmatic answer the field has converged on so far is a hybrid, not a replacement. The problem: quadratic compute and unbounded cache Two distinct costs motivate this entire literature, and they bite at different times. Training cost Inference cost Attention O(n sup 2 /sup ) compute in sequence length KV cache grows linearly and forever; O(n) work per new token RNN / SSM O(n) compute Fixed-size state; O(1) work per new token The training-side cost is the n n attention matrix. Every position attends to every other, so doubling the sequence length quadruples attention's compute. At short context this is a minority of total FLOPs the FFN dominates (section 1.6) but the quadratic term eventually wins, and past the tens of thousands of tokens it becomes the dominant cost. The inference-side cost is the KV cache and it is arguably worse. Generating each new token requires attending over every previous token, so the keys and values for the entire context must be retained in memory. That cache grows linearly with context length and is charged per concurrent request, so it directly caps how many users a GPU can serve. Section 6.3 works through the arithmetic. The RNN's asymptotics are exactly what one would want which is why this line of research exists at all. A recurrent model compresses history into a fixed-size state, so per-token cost is constant and memory does not grow with context. Section 1.1 explained why that was abandoned: the sequential recurrence cannot be parallelized across positions during training. The prize the SSM literature is chasing is precise recover the RNN's inference profile without giving up parallel training. Attention at inference: generating token 5 must attend over every previous token; KV cache holds all of them k,v 1 k,v 2 k,v 3 k,v 4 KV cache k,v 5 cache keeps growing: memory N, per request token 5 out O(N) work per token 4 dot products now, N at step N SSM at inference: generating token 5 history is compressed into one fixed-size state; past tokens are not revisited tok 1 tok 2 tok 3 tok 4 already absorbed discarded, never re-read state h fixed size d, constant h Ah + Bx y = Ch token 5 out same state slot overwritten each step nothing accumulates O(1) work per token, O(1) memory independent of how long the context already is Attention must re-read a KV cache that grows with every token generated, costing O(N) work and O(N) memory per step, whereas an SSM folds all history into one fixed-size state that is overwritten each step, giving constant work and constant memory regardless of context length. The classical state-space formulation A state-space model comes from control theory and describes a continuous-time linear system: a hidden state h(t) evolves under its own dynamics while being driven by an input x(t) , and an output y(t) is read off from it. h'(t) = A @ h(t) + B @ x(t) # state evolution y(t) = C @ h(t) + D @ x(t) # output readout The intuition is a leaky accumulator with structure. A governs how the existing state decays and mixes as time passes, B governs how new input is written into the state, and C governs what is read out. Because A is applied repeatedly, its eigenvalues determine how long information persists: eigenvalues near the unit circle retain information over long horizons, smaller ones forget quickly. Long-range memory is thus a property of the spectrum of A . Discretization converts this to something a computer can run. Sequences are discrete, so the continuous system is discretized with a step size Delta , producing discrete matrices A_bar and B_bar (via a zero-order hold or bilinear transform). The result is a linear recurrence: h_t = A_bar @ h_{t-1} + B_bar @ x_t y_t = C @ h_t The key property the one this entire field is built on is that this recurrence has two equivalent computational forms. Because it is linear with time-invariant matrices, unrolling it gives a closed form with no sequential dependency: h_t = sum over j of (A_bar ** j) @ B_bar @ x_{t-j} # so the output is a convolution with a fixed kernel K: K = (C @ B_bar, C @ A_bar @ B_bar, C @ A_bar**2 @ B_bar, ...) y = K * x # * = convolution This dual form is the whole trick. Training uses the convolutional form, computed in parallel across the entire sequence (efficiently via FFT), so there is no sequential bottleneck. Inference uses the recurrent form, carrying a fixed-size state forward at O(1) cost per token with no growing cache. The same model, two execution modes, each chosen for the regime it suits. Note precisely why this works and an LSTM cannot do it: linearity. The moment a nonlinearity sits inside the recurrence, it cannot be unrolled into a convolution. S4 and the HiPPO initialization Naive SSMs did not work, and understanding why is instructive. With a randomly initialized A , the powers A**j either vanish or explode as j grows the same vanishing/exploding-gradient pathology as the RNN, reappearing in the convolution kernel. Early SSMs performed poorly on long-range tasks for exactly this reason. HiPPO supplied the fix by deriving A rather than initializing it randomly. The HiPPO framework (Gu et al., 2020) asks a specific mathematical question: what state-update matrix causes the hidden state to maintain an optimal compression of the entire input history, in the sense of best approximating it by a projection onto a basis of orthogonal polynomials? That question has a closed-form answer, and it yields a specific structured matrix. Initializing A to it means the model starts out as a principled online compressor of history rather than something that must discover long-range memory from scratch. S4 (Gu et al., 2021), Efficiently Modeling Long Sequences with Structured State Spaces , made this computationally tractable. Computing the convolution kernel naively requires repeated powers of A , which is prohibitive for a large state. S4's contribution was a parameterization a normal-plus-low-rank structure permitting the kernel to be computed efficiently. The empirical result that got attention was on the Long Range Arena benchmark, where S4 dramatically outperformed transformers on tasks requiring very long-range dependencies, including the Path-X task that transformers had failed entirely. The caveat that mattered: LRA is not language modeling. S4's dominance on synthetic long-range tasks did not transfer to competitive language modeling, and the reason turned out to be structural rather than incidental which is what Mamba addressed. Mamba: selectivity and the hardware-aware scan The limitation of S4 is that it is linear time-invariant. The matrices A_bar , B_bar and C are fixed the same for every position and every input. This is exactly the property that permits the convolutional form, and it is also a hard ceiling on expressiveness: the model processes every token identically and cannot decide that a particular token deserves to be written into state while another should be ignored. Attention does this natively, since its weights are computed from content. An LTI system cannot do it at all. Mamba (Gu Dao, 2023) makes the SSM parameters functions of the input. In the selective SSM, B , C and the step size Delta are produced by linear projections of the current token, so state updates become content-dependent: Delta_t = softplus(x_t @ W_delta) # per-token step size B_t = x_t @ W_B C_t = x_t @ W_C h_t = A_bar(Delta_t) @ h_{t-1} + B_bar(Delta_t) @ x_t The Delta parameter is the most intuitive lever. It acts as a learned gate on time: a large Delta means "this input matters write it firmly into the state," while a small Delta means "ignore this, carry the existing state forward." The model can therefore skip filler and attend to salient tokens, which is precisely the selectivity S4 lacked. Mamba showed this fixes tasks that LTI models provably fail, such as selective copying, where the model must copy specific tokens while ignoring interspersed noise. The cost is that the convolutional form is destroyed. Time-varying matrices mean no fixed kernel and no FFT-based parallel training. This is the exact trade that made selectivity look unaffordable before Mamba and Mamba's second contribution was a systems answer rather than a mathematical one. The hardware-aware parallel scan. Although the recurrence is time-varying, it remains associative , and associative operations can be computed by a parallel scan (a prefix-sum-style algorithm) in O(log n) depth rather than O(n) sequential steps. Mamba implements this scan in a fused kernel using the same IO-aware philosophy as FlashAttention (section 6.2): keep the large hidden state in fast SRAM, perform discretization and the scan without writing intermediates to slower HBM, and recompute rather than store activations for the backward pass. The parallelism is recovered by an algorithm-plus-kernel co-design, not by restoring linearity. The reported results were strong matching or exceeding transformers of comparable size on language modeling, with linear scaling in sequence length and substantially faster inference throughput given the absence of a KV cache. Linear attention and the kernel reformulation A parallel line of work attacks the same problem from the attention side. Write standard attention for one query position without the softmax normalizer: out_i = sum over j =i of sim(q_i, k_j) * v_j # standard attention: sim(q,k) = exp(q . k / sqrt(d)) The quadratic cost comes entirely from the exponential's non-separability. Because exp(q . k) cannot be factored into a product of a function of q and a function of k , every pair must be computed explicitly. Linear attention (Katharopoulos et al., 2020) replaces the similarity with a separable feature map, sim(q,k) = phi(q) . phi(k) . Then associativity can be exploited: # quadratic order: (Q @ K.T) @ V - n x n intermediate # linear order: Q @ (K.T @ V) - d x d intermediate Reassociating the matrix product is the entire trick. K.T @ V is a d d matrix independent of sequence length, so the cost becomes linear in n . In the causal setting this state can be accumulated incrementally, which makes the connection explicit: linear attention is a linear RNN with a matrix-valued hidden state. The d d running sum is the recurrent state. This is why SSMs and linear attention converged they are two derivations of nearly the same object, one from control theory and one from attention. The consistent finding is that linear attention underperforms softmax attention at matched size. The softmax is not incidental; its sharpness lets a query concentrate on a few positions, whereas a fixed-size state summed over all positions is a lossy summary that cannot support precise retrieval. Performer (Choromanski et al., 2020) approximated the softmax kernel with random features to recover some of this, and later work added decay and gating mechanisms, but the fundamental compression limit stands. The wider family Model Core idea Distinctive property S4 (Gu et al., 2021) Structured LTI SSM with HiPPO init Excellent long-range; not competitive on language Mamba (Gu Dao, 2023) Input-dependent selective SSM + parallel scan First SSM broadly competitive with transformers on language RWKV (Peng et al., 2023) RNN with a transformer-like block; parallelizable training Community-driven; multiple generations released RetNet (Sun et al., 2023) Retention with explicit decay Parallel, recurrent and chunkwise-recurrent forms Hyena (Poli et al., 2023) Long implicit convolutions plus gating Subquadratic without a recurrence The unifying pattern is worth stating explicitly: every one of these replaces content-based all-pairs comparison with a fixed-size state that history is compressed into, and each offers a parallel training form alongside a recurrent inference form. They differ in how the state decays, whether the dynamics depend on the input, and how the parallel form is computed but the underlying bet is the same, and so is the underlying limitation. The honest empirical picture SSMs win on efficiency and on genuinely long sequences; they lose on precise recall. The weakness is specific and well-characterized, and it follows directly from the architecture rather than being an incidental bug. Task type Transformer SSM Language modeling perplexity, matched size Strong Comparable (Mamba-class) Throughput at long sequence length Degrades quadratically Linear clear win Inference memory KV cache grows with context Fixed state clear win Associative recall / copying from context Strong Notably weaker In-context learning from many examples Strong Weaker The associative-recall weakness is structural. Consider retrieving a specific value seen 10,000 tokens earlier. A transformer can attend directly to that position the information is still verbatim in the KV cache, and attention is content-addressed lookup. An SSM must have retained it in a fixed-size state that has since absorbed 10,000 more tokens. Since the state has bounded capacity, this is lossy compression, and exact retrieval of arbitrary detail is not something a bounded state can guarantee. The tradeoff is not an implementation deficiency to be engineered away; a fixed-size state is precisely what buys the O(1) inference cost, and precise unbounded recall is what it costs. Work on this failure mode including the Based line of research (Arora et al., 2024) analyzing the recall-versus-memory tradeoff has characterized it as a genuine frontier rather than a bug. This weakness is disproportionately damaging in practice , because retrieval from context is what long context is mostly for : RAG pipelines, reading long documents, in-context learning from many examples, and agent trajectories that must recall an earlier tool result. A model with efficient long context that cannot reliably retrieve from it has solved the cheaper half of the problem. Hybrids as the pragmatic resolution If attention provides precise retrieval at high cost and SSM layers provide cheap sequence mixing with lossy memory, the obvious move is to use both. Hybrid architectures interleave a minority of attention layers among a majority of SSM layers and the empirical finding that makes this attractive is that the attention proportion can be surprisingly small, on the order of one attention layer in every six to eight, while recovering most of the recall capability. Jamba (AI21, 2024) was a prominent published example, interleaving Mamba and attention layers with MoE and reporting a substantially smaller KV cache at long context than a comparable pure transformer. Samba (Ren et al., 2024) combined Mamba with sliding-window attention, the SSM carrying long-range compressed context while local windowed attention handles precise nearby retrieval. Several subsequent model families have adopted broadly similar hybrid designs. The division of labor is intuitive. The SSM layers maintain a running compressed summary at linear cost; the sparse attention layers provide the exact lookups that a compressed state cannot. Since KV cache is only maintained for the attention layers, memory falls roughly in proportion to how few of them there are. Where this stands, stated honestly. As of the early-2025 literature, pure SSM models have not displaced transformers for frontier general-purpose language models, and hybrids look like the most credible path for efficient long context. But the picture is actively moving, comparisons are confounded by unequal engineering investment transformers have received vastly more optimization effort, so like-for-like efficiency comparisons systematically flatter the incumbent and evaluation of long-context quality is itself unreliable (section 6.8). Anyone claiming this question is settled in either direction is overstating what the evidence supports. Gotcha The tempting summary is "SSMs are linear-time attention replacements, so they win once sequences get long enough." That is wrong in a way that matters. The linear scaling is real, but it is purchased with a fixed-size state , and a fixed-size state is a lossy compression of unbounded history which is exactly why SSMs underperform on associative recall and copying from context. This is not an engineering gap awaiting a better kernel; it is the price of the asymptotic improvement, and the two cannot be decoupled. The practical trap is benchmark-shaped: perplexity and Long Range Arena scores can look excellent while retrieval-from-context quietly fails, because averaged next-token loss barely penalizes rare retrieval failures that nonetheless break a RAG pipeline or an agent. Evaluate long-context claims on recall-heavy tasks specifically, never on perplexity alone and note that the field's own convergence on hybrid architectures is a tacit admission that a few real attention layers remain necessary.

Context windows went from 2k tokens in 2020 to hundreds of thousands within a few years, and that progress came from several unrelated techniques solving several unrelated bottlenecks. The single most useful thing to get straight here is that "long context is expensive" conflates two distinct problems with different causes, different solutions, and different regimes in which they bite. Section 6.1 separates them; everything after follows from that split. Two distinct bottlenecks Quadratic attention compute KV cache memory When it bites Training, and prefill at inference Decoding at inference Scales as O(n sup 2 /sup ) in sequence length O(n) per sequence, batch size Resource exhausted FLOPs and, naively, memory for the n n matrix Accelerator memory and memory bandwidth Fixed by FlashAttention, sparse patterns, SSM layers MQA/GQA/MLA, PagedAttention, quantized cache The quadratic-compute problem is about the attention matrix. Each of n positions attends to up to n others, so the score matrix has n sup 2 /sup entries. At 32k tokens that is over a billion entries per head per layer and materializing it in memory, which is what a naive implementation does, is what actually breaks first. The KV cache problem is about memory during generation, and it is independent of the above. Even with attention compute made perfectly efficient, generating token n+1 requires the keys and values of all n prior tokens. That cache grows linearly with context and is charged per concurrent request , so it caps serving throughput rather than latency. Why the conflation matters practically: FlashAttention does essentially nothing for KV cache memory, and GQA does essentially nothing for training-time attention compute. Deploying the wrong one for your bottleneck yields no improvement, and the two bottlenecks dominate in different phases prefill is compute-bound, decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound. FlashAttention FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022) is an exact algorithm, not an approximation. It computes bit-for-bit the same attention output as the standard implementation, up to floating-point reassociation. It is faster because it is IO-aware it optimizes memory movement rather than arithmetic. The insight is that attention is memory-bound, not compute-bound. A GPU has a small, extremely fast on-chip SRAM (on the order of tens of MB, tens of TB/s) and a large, much slower HBM (tens of GB, roughly an order of magnitude less bandwidth). A standard implementation does this: S = Q @ K.T # write n x n to HBM P = softmax(S) # read n x n, write n x n O = P @ V # read n x n The arithmetic is a small fraction of the time. The bottleneck is shuttling an n n matrix to and from HBM three times and it is also why memory blows up, since that matrix must exist in full. The fix is tiling plus online softmax. FlashAttention splits Q , K and V into blocks sized to fit in SRAM and computes attention block by block, keeping intermediates on-chip and never writing the full attention matrix anywhere. The obstacle is that softmax needs a normalizer over the whole row, which a single block does not have. The solution is the online-softmax trick: maintain a running maximum and running sum per row, and rescale the accumulated output as each new block arrives: for each block of K, V: S_block = Q_block @ K_block.T m_new = max(m_old, rowmax(S_block)) # running max P_block = exp(S_block - m_new) l_new = exp(m_old - m_new)*l_old + rowsum(P_block) O = (exp(m_old - m_new)*l_old*O + P_block @ V_block) / l_new m_old, l_old = m_new, l_new Each block's contribution is folded in with a correction factor for the updated maximum, so the final result equals the full softmax exactly. The running maximum also provides the standard numerical-stability subtraction for free. The results: attention memory drops from O(n sup 2 /sup ) to O(n) , with substantial wall-clock speedups. Compute remains O(n sup 2 /sup ) the same FLOPs, moved far less. The memory reduction is what actually unlocked long-context training, since materializing the attention matrix was the binding constraint. The backward pass recomputes attention blocks on the fly rather than storing them, trading extra FLOPs for memory a good trade precisely because the operation is memory-bound. FlashAttention-2 (Dao, 2023) improved work partitioning and reduced non-matmul operations, roughly doubling throughput. FlashAttention-3 (Shah et al., 2024) targeted Hopper-generation hardware specifically, exploiting asynchrony and low-precision support. The progression is worth noting for what it says about the field: successive versions are largely hardware-specific engineering, and the algorithm is now standard in every major training and serving framework. KV cache mechanics Why the cache exists. Under causal masking, a token's key and value vectors never change once computed later tokens cannot affect earlier ones. Recomputing them at every generation step would be pure waste, so they are cached. This is what makes decoding O(n) per token rather than O(n sup 2 /sup ) . kv_bytes = batch * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * seq_len * 2 * bytes_per_element # ^ the 2 is for K and V A worked example makes the scale concrete. Take a 70B-class model: 80 layers, 64 heads, head_dim 128, bf16 (2 bytes), one sequence of 32k tokens with standard multi-head attention: 1 * 80 * 64 * 128 * 32768 * 2 * 2 = ~85.9 GB That is for a single request, and it exceeds the memory of an 80GB accelerator before counting the ~140GB of model weights. Batch 16 requests and the cache alone would need over a terabyte. This is the constraint that made KV cache reduction one of the highest-priority problems in inference, and it is why the techniques below exist. MQA, GQA, and MLA Every term in the cache equation is fixed by the model or the workload except one: kv_heads . The insight behind this whole family is that queries and keys/values need not have the same number of heads. Scheme Query heads KV heads Cache size Quality MHA h h Baseline Baseline MQA h 1 Baseline / h Measurable degradation GQA h g (e.g. 8) Baseline g/h Near-MHA the sweet spot MLA h compressed latent Large reduction Reported comparable or better Multi-Query Attention (Shazeer, 2019) takes the extreme position: all query heads share a single key head and a single value head. With 64 heads this cuts the cache 64-fold the 85.9GB example drops to about 1.3GB. The cost is real quality degradation and reported training instability, since the shared KV projection is a genuine bottleneck on what attention can express. Grouped-Query Attention (Ainslie et al., 2023) interpolates: query heads are partitioned into g groups, each sharing one KV head. With 64 query heads and 8 KV heads the cache shrinks 8 while quality stays close to full MHA. GQA also has a practical virtue that aided adoption an existing MHA checkpoint can be converted by mean-pooling the KV projections within each group and briefly continuing training, rather than retraining from scratch. GQA is now the default in most modern open-weight models, including the Llama 3 family. Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) , introduced in the DeepSeek-V2 work (2024), takes a different route: rather than reducing the number of KV heads, it compresses keys and values into a low-rank latent vector that is what actually gets cached, then projects back up at use time. The reported result was a large cache reduction with quality comparable to or better than MHA. The trade is that the up-projection costs extra compute at inference and the implementation is more intricate and since decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound, spending compute to save memory traffic is usually the right direction. PagedAttention and cache fragmentation A second, purely systems-level source of waste : even with a small per-token cache, naive allocation wastes most of the memory it reserves. Because the cache must grow as generation proceeds, the straightforward approach reserves a contiguous block sized for the maximum possible length of each request. A request that could produce 2048 tokens but stops after 100 leaves the rest reserved and unusable. PagedAttention (Kwon et al., 2023), the technique underlying vLLM, applies operating-system virtual memory to the KV cache. The cache for a sequence is split into fixed-size blocks that need not be contiguous in physical memory, with a block table mapping logical positions to physical blocks exactly the paging structure an OS uses: Problem OS analogue PagedAttention solution Over-reservation for max length Internal fragmentation Allocate blocks on demand as generation proceeds Unusable gaps between allocations External fragmentation Uniform blocks, no contiguity requirement Duplicate prefixes across requests Shared memory pages Share blocks; copy-on-write when they diverge The reported effect was near-elimination of cache waste and a large throughput gain , because the memory recovered translates directly into a bigger batch and bigger batches are what amortize the weight-loading cost that dominates memory-bandwidth-bound decoding. The prefix-sharing property is a substantial secondary win: a long system prompt shared across many requests, or the common prefix of a beam search, can occupy one physical copy. Extending context after training Training natively at very long context is expensive, so the standard practice is to train at moderate length and extend afterwards. With RoPE (section 1.4), position enters as a rotation angle, which gives a handle on the problem a model asked to handle unseen positions encounters out-of-distribution rotation angles and degrades sharply. Method Mechanism Note Position Interpolation Scale positions down so they fall inside the trained range Chen et al., 2023; needs brief fine-tuning NTK-aware scaling Scale frequencies unevenly high frequencies less Community-originated; works with little or no tuning YaRN Frequency-band-dependent scaling plus attention temperature Peng et al., 2023; strong results, needs some tuning Continued pretraining Keep training on genuinely long documents Most reliable; most expensive; complements the above Position Interpolation is the simplest idea: instead of extrapolating to unseen positions, squeeze the new longer range into the trained one by dividing position indices by a scale factor. Position 8000 in a model trained to 2048 becomes an effective position of 2000. The rotations stay in-distribution, and a short fine-tune adapts the model. The cost is reduced positional resolution adjacent tokens now differ by a smaller angle, so fine-grained position distinctions blur. NTK-aware scaling refines this by observing that RoPE's dimension pairs rotate at geometrically spaced frequencies encoding different scales, and interpolating all of them uniformly needlessly damages the high-frequency pairs carrying local position information. Instead it scales low-frequency (long-range) components more and high-frequency (local) components less, preserving local resolution while extending global range. YaRN systematizes this into explicit frequency bands and adds a temperature adjustment to attention, reporting strong extension with less fine-tuning data. The blunt caveat is that context length is not context competence . These methods make a model accept longer inputs without producing garbage. Genuinely using distant information generally requires continued pretraining on long documents and the scarcity of naturally-occurring high-quality long documents is itself a real constraint. An advertised context window is an upper bound on input length, not a claim about usable comprehension across it. Sparse and structured attention patterns An orthogonal approach: have each token attend to a structured subset of positions rather than all of them, trading exactness for asymptotics. Sliding-window attention restricts each token to the previous w positions, making cost linear in sequence length. Longformer (Beltagy et al., 2020) combined a local window with a few global tokens attending everywhere; Mistral 7B (2023) used sliding-window attention in a decoder-only LLM. The property that makes windowing more powerful than it first appears is receptive field stacking : with a window of w across L layers, information propagates up to w L positions, since each layer's output at a position already summarizes its own window. Information travels far, but indirectly and lossily which is a different thing from attending directly, and precise retrieval suffers accordingly. rows = query position i (newest at bottom), columns = key position j; filled = attended, faint = masked out Dense causal every j i O(n ) pairs, exact Sliding window (w = 3) only the last 3 positions O(n w), reach grows w L over layers Strided / sink local band + every 3rd column O(n w) with global columns kept i=0 i=7 upper triangle is the causal mask a token may never attend to its own future The same 8 8 causal attention mask under three patterns: dense attention fills the whole lower triangle, sliding-window keeps only a narrow band of recent positions, and a strided pattern adds back a few globally-visible columns so distant information still has a direct path. Attention sinks are the most surprising result in this area. StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2023) investigated why sliding-window attention on a pretrained model catastrophically fails when the window slides past the beginning of the sequence. Naively, evicting the oldest tokens should cost little they are far away and presumably irrelevant. Instead, perplexity explodes. The cause is that models dedicate a large share of attention to the first few tokens regardless of their content , and the explanation is mechanical rather than semantic. Softmax forces every attention row to sum to 1: a head must distribute its full attention budget somewhere even when nothing in the context is relevant to it. Models learn to dump this excess onto the earliest tokens, which are visible to every position under causal masking. Those tokens function as a no-op sink for unneeded attention mass. Evict them and the mass is forcibly redistributed onto tokens that are actually being used, corrupting every attention distribution in the model. # StreamingLLM: keep a few initial "sink" tokens permanently, # plus a sliding window of recent tokens. [ t0 t1 t2 t3 ] ... [ ...... recent window ...... ] sinks (kept) slides forward Retaining as few as four initial tokens alongside the sliding window restores stable perplexity over inputs far longer than the trained context. Note carefully what this does and does not deliver: it enables indefinite streaming with bounded memory, not comprehension of unbounded context the evicted middle is genuinely gone. Evaluating long context Needle-in-a-haystack is the standard test and it is far too easy. A random fact is inserted at a controlled depth in a long filler context and the model is asked to retrieve it. Passing demonstrates that a specific string is retrievable but the needle is typically semantically unrelated to the filler, making it trivially distinctive. Models can score near-perfectly while failing at tasks requiring aggregation over many positions, multi-hop reasoning across distant sections, or noticing that something is absent . Harder variants exist multiple needles, needles requiring reasoning rather than copying, and benchmarks such as RULER (Hsieh et al., 2024) designed with tasks of graded difficulty and models that saturate the simple version routinely degrade badly on them. Lost in the middle (Liu et al., 2023) is the key empirical finding. Measuring retrieval accuracy as a function of where the relevant information sits, they found a pronounced U-shape: models use information at the beginning and end of a long context reliably, and information in the middle much less so. Performance on a document-QA task could vary substantially based on position alone, with the same information present in every case. The finding has held up across models and is directly practical put the most important material at the start or end of a long prompt, and be skeptical of RAG pipelines that bury the retrieved passage among many others. The plausible cause is a training-data artifact. Attention sinks bias toward the beginning, recency effects toward the end, and natural documents concentrate salient content in openings and conclusions. Long-context continued pretraining with information deliberately placed in the middle appears to mitigate the effect, which supports the artifact explanation over an architectural one. Gotcha FlashAttention is exact, not approximate and the near-universal assumption otherwise leads to real mistakes. Because it is filed mentally alongside sparse and linear attention, people assume it trades quality for speed, and then either avoid it in quality-sensitive settings or wrongly blame it when results shift. It computes precisely the same function as standard attention; the only differences are floating-point reassociation, of the same magnitude as changing any kernel or batch size. It is faster purely because it moves less data between HBM and SRAM. Two corollaries follow. First, there is no accuracy reason to disable it if a result changed, the cause is elsewhere. Second, and more subtly, FlashAttention does not change attention's O(n sup 2 /sup ) compute and does not shrink the KV cache. It makes attention memory linear during the forward and backward pass, which is what unlocked long-context training , but a serving system running out of memory while decoding needs GQA, MLA or PagedAttention instead. Reaching for FlashAttention against a KV-cache bottleneck is fixing the wrong one of the two problems in section 6.1.

Sections 1 and 4 6 covered the transformer and the major architectural families in their canonical forms. This section covers what frontier open-weight models actually ship in 2025 2026, which is a specific and somewhat surprising answer: the macro-architecture has barely moved since GPT-2, while nearly every component inside it has been replaced. A 2026 model is still a stack of pre-normalized attention-plus-feedforward blocks with residual connections. But the attention is grouped or latent rather than multi-head, the normalization is RMSNorm applied in more places, the positional encoding is rotary or absent, the feedforward is gated and frequently sparse, and the KV cache is compressed or shared across layers. This section is organized as a component-by-component survey of those substitutions, because that is how practitioners actually reason about new releases: not "what is this architecture" but "which of the known choices did they make at each slot, and why." The attention slot Attention is where the most consequential divergence has happened, driven almost entirely by the KV-cache pressure described in section 22. Five distinct designs are in current production use. Variant Mechanism Used by Tradeoff MHA Every head has its own K and V projections OLMo 2 (7B), SmolLM3 Best modeling quality per head; largest KV cache GQA Groups of query heads share one K/V head Gemma 3, Llama 4, Qwen3, gpt-oss, Mistral Small 3.1 The current default: most of MHA's quality at a fraction of the cache MQA All query heads share a single K/V head Older models; largely superseded by GQA Smallest cache, measurable quality cost MLA K and V compressed into a low-rank latent space; the latent is cached, decompressed on use DeepSeek V3/R1, Kimi K2 Extra matmul at inference; DeepSeek's ablations report it beating GQA on quality Sliding window Attention restricted to a local window, usually interleaved with occasional global layers Gemma 2/3, gpt-oss (alternating), Olmo 3 Cache bounded by window rather than context; minimal reported quality impact MHA cache 4 K/V pairs kv kv kv kv one K/V per head largest cache GQA cache 2 K/V pairs kv kv head groups share K/V quality cost MLA cache 1 latent latent c full head count preserved MLA at attention time K, V (full) down-proj latent c cached up-proj K, V restored attention, all heads Only the small latent occupies the KV cache; the full K/V are reconstructed per step. Trades compute (abundant at decode) for memory bandwidth (scarce) see section 22. MHA, GQA and MLA differ in what actually sits in the KV cache: one entry per head, one per group, or a single compressed latent that is decompressed on use. Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) deserves emphasis because it inverts the usual assumption that cache savings cost quality. Rather than reducing the number of K/V heads as GQA does, MLA keeps full head count but projects keys and values down into a shared low-rank latent vector, caches only that latent, and projects back up when attention is computed. The cache shrinks because the latent is small; quality holds because no head is forced to share another head's keys. The cost is an additional projection on every attention call trading compute, which is abundant at decode time, for memory bandwidth, which is not. Linear and hybrid attention is the most active area. Gated DeltaNet (Qwen3-Next) and Kimi Delta Attention (Kimi Linear) replace quadratic attention with linear-complexity recurrent-style updates, but critically they are not used alone: both interleave linear layers with full-attention layers at roughly a 3:1 ratio. The empirical finding driving this pattern is that linear attention degrades content-based retrieval the needle-in-a-haystack capability and periodic full-attention layers restore it. This is the same hybrid conclusion section 5 reaches about state-space models, arrived at independently. Gotcha Reading "linear attention" as "attention, but faster" misses the actual engineering position. Every shipped linear-attention model is a hybrid, and the full-attention layers are not a transitional compromise being engineered away they are load-bearing for retrieval. When a release advertises linear complexity, the questions to ask are what fraction of layers are actually linear, and what the long-context retrieval benchmarks look like relative to a full-attention baseline of matched size. A model can be linear in the asymptotic sense and still carry most of a transformer's cache cost. The normalization slot Nearly universal agreement exists on RMSNorm over LayerNorm it drops the mean-centering and the learned bias, costs less, and performs equivalently. The live disagreement is about placement . Pre-Norm (normalize before the sublayer, GPT-2 onward, Llama 3) remains the default. Gradients are well-behaved and learning-rate warmup is less critical. Post-Norm (normalize after, inside the residual path) was abandoned years ago for instability, then revived by OLMo 2 and Olmo 3, which report it improving training stability in their setup a genuine reversal worth noticing. Dual normalization (Gemma 2/3) applies RMSNorm both before and after each sublayer, taking both effects at negligible cost. QK-Norm applies RMSNorm to queries and keys before RoPE is applied. Adopted by OLMo 2, Gemma 2/3, and MiniMax-M2, it stabilizes attention logits and, combined with Post-Norm, stabilizes the loss curve. MiniMax-M2 extends this to per-layer QK-Norm with distinct scale parameters per head. The MoE slot Section 4 covered mixture-of-experts mechanics. The 2026 design consensus has converged on several specifics that were open questions two years earlier. Choice Current consensus Evidence Expert count vs size Many small experts beat few large ones at fixed budget DeepSeek V3: 256 experts, 9 active. Qwen3 235B: 128 experts, 8 active. gpt-oss: 32 experts, 4 active Shared expert One always-active expert alongside routed ones helps DeepSeek V3/R1, Grok 2.5, GLM-4.5, Qwen3-Next use it; Qwen3 and MiniMax-M2 do not not fully settled First layers dense Keep the first few layers dense before switching to MoE DeepSeek V3 and GLM-4.5 (first 3 layers); improves convergence stability Active fraction Trending lower sparser activation at larger totals DeepSeek V3: 37B of 671B (5.5%). MiniMax-M2: 10B active (4.4%) The rationale for a shared expert is that common, universally-useful patterns otherwise have to be redundantly relearned inside many routed experts, wasting capacity. Keeping early layers dense reflects that the first layers do broad syntactic and lexical work where routing has little to specialize on, and premature routing destabilizes training. The positional encoding slot RoPE is standard, with YaRN rescaling (Qwen3, Olmo 3) the usual mechanism for extending a trained context window. Two departures are worth knowing: Partial RoPE (MiniMax-M1/M2) applies rotation to only a subset of head dimensions, leaving the rest unrotated, which improves length extrapolation without the degradation full-RoPE extension can cause. NoPE no positional embedding at all relies on the causal mask alone to convey order, since a causally-masked token can only see its predecessors and that asymmetry is itself positional information. SmolLM3 uses it on every fourth layer; Kimi Linear uses it in MLA layers. It shows better length generalization, though whether it scales to the largest models is unresolved. Attention sinks also belong here. The classical version prepends a dummy token that attention heads can dump probability mass onto when no real token is relevant. gpt-oss instead implements sinks as learned per-head bias logits added directly to the attention scores the same stabilizing function with no input-sequence change. The 2026 frontier: KV sharing, compressed attention, and hyper-connections Three developments from 2026 releases go beyond component substitution and change the block structure itself. Cross-layer KV sharing (Gemma 4 E2B/E4B) has later layers reuse the key-value projections computed by earlier layers, while still computing their own queries. Since queries are what differentiate a layer's attention pattern and K/V are relatively redundant across depth, this halves KV cache memory a reported 2.7 GB saving at 128K context for the E2B model with minimal measured quality cost at the tested scales. Compressed attention (DeepSeek V4) compresses along the sequence dimension rather than the per-token representation dimension that MLA targets. Two variants are interleaved: CSA applies mild compression with sparse top-k selection, while HCA compresses aggressively on the order of 128 tokens into a single entry and attends densely over the compressed entries. At 1M-token context, DeepSeek V4-Pro is reported at roughly 27% of the single-token inference FLOPs and 10% of the KV cache of DeepSeek V3.2. The cost is genuine loss of token-level detail in the heavily compressed regions. Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) , also from DeepSeek V4, replaces the single residual stream with several parallel residual streams that exchange information through learned mappings. The "manifold-constrained" part keeps those mappings non-negative with rows and columns summing to one, which prevents the signal from being amplified or attenuated as it propagates the stability problem that makes naive multi-stream residuals fail. Reported cost is about 6.7% training overhead for modest quality gains and better stability at depth. This is the most structurally significant departure from the standard block in years: the residual stream, essentially unchanged since 2015, becomes plural. Width, depth, and the other slots SwiGLU has displaced GELU as the feedforward activation nearly universally, and output gating a sigmoid gate scaling attention output before the residual add appears in Qwen3-Next, Kimi Linear, and Grok 2.5 for stability. Width versus depth at fixed parameters is a real and unsettled tradeoff. Gemma 2's ablation found a wider variant scoring 52.0 against 50.8 for a deeper one at equal size; wider models also throughput better. Deeper models offer more compositional flexibility but train less stably. Qwen3 0.6B goes deep, gpt-oss goes wide. Attention bias units persist in gpt-oss as a GPT-2 inheritance, but recent analysis finds them redundant with negligible effect. Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) (DeepSeek V3, GLM-4.5, Qwen3-Next) trains the model to predict several future tokens at once. It accelerates training and, importantly for section 22, yields a model that can serve as its own speculative-decoding draft head. Per-Layer Embeddings (PLE) and MatFormer (Gemma 3n, Gemma 4) target on-device deployment: PLE streams a subset of parameters from CPU or SSD on demand to cut GPU memory, while MatFormer trains one model whose nested slices each function as an independently usable smaller model. Gotcha The single most useful corrective when reading a new model release: the headline is almost never where the gain came from. Releases foreground whatever is novel, but ablations across this literature repeatedly show the measured improvement dominated by data quality, data mixture, and post-training rather than the architectural change being announced. Two models with near-identical component choices routinely differ by large margins on benchmarks, and two models with very different attention designs routinely land within noise of each other. Architecture determines the cost curve memory, throughput, context ceiling far more reliably than it determines capability. When comparing releases, read the architecture section to understand what the model will cost to serve, and look to the data and post-training sections to understand how good it will be.

Learn actions from interaction, delayed rewards, and the consequences of exploration. How the pieces connect MENTAL MODEL Reinforcement learning decision-making — from question to evidence 01 Observe Define state, partial observation, and reset conditions. 02 Act Select actions through a policy with exploration. 03 Learn Assign delayed reward through returns and value estimates. 04 Evaluate Test across seeds, scenarios, and real constraints. Observe → Act → Learn → Evaluate. Each transition is a place where an assumption can be inspected before the next layer of the system compounds it. The interaction loop An agent observes a state or partial observation, chooses an action through a policy, receives reward, and transitions. The objective usually maximizes expected discounted return. A Markov state contains the information needed to model the next transition; real observations may not satisfy this assumption. Value functions and credit assignment A value function estimates future return from a state; an action-value function includes the selected action. Bellman equations connect present value to immediate reward and next value. Temporal-difference learning bootstraps from estimates, while Monte Carlo methods use sampled returns. Families of algorithms Value-based methods learn action values. Policy gradients directly adjust policy parameters using estimates of return. Actor-critic methods combine both. Model-based methods learn or use environment dynamics for planning. Off-policy methods can reuse experience collected by a different policy, subject to their assumptions. Rewards and evaluation Reward is a proxy. A policy can exploit loopholes while scoring well. Evaluate across seeds, initial states, and held-out environments. Exploration in a simulator is different from exploration in a real system where actions can be costly or irreversible. Demonstrations and offline datasets change the learning problem. Worked example With immediate rewards [2,0,4] and discount γ=0.5, return from the first step is 2 + 0.5×0 + 0.25×4 = 3. A greedy policy that only considers immediate reward can miss a lower-reward action leading to a much better future state. What goes wrong A high training return can reflect memorized environments or reward hacking. Off-policy evaluation is difficult when logged data rarely contains actions the new policy prefers. Check your understanding How is supervised learning different from RL? Reveal the explanation Supervised learning receives target examples. RL chooses actions that influence future observations and feedback, introducing exploration and delayed credit assignment. An operating model for reinforcement learning & decision-making Reinforcement learning changes the data distribution as the policy changes it. This makes offline performance fragile: a model can prefer actions never well represented in its logged experience. Reward design is equally central, because the learner will exploit whatever proxy is easiest to optimize. The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test. Worked system: the reward that teaches the wrong behavior A warehouse robot receives a reward for moving packages quickly. It discovers that nudging a package off a sensor resets the task and produces favorable timing metrics. The reward was a proxy for the desired outcome, and the agent optimized the proxy exactly. This is not a bizarre edge case: any omission in a reward function becomes an invitation for a sufficiently capable policy to exploit the measurement. Start with a small environment where trajectories can be replayed. Log states, actions, reward components, interventions, and termination reasons, not only total return. Evaluate across different seeds and scenarios, then inspect the highest-scoring trajectories for behavior a human would reject. The reward is part of the specification, not merely a training signal. Notebook: Log the update, not only the loss Build a small environment with transparent rewards before adding a neural policy. Log trajectories, not only return, and inspect the policies that score best for unsafe or unintended strategies. metrics = { "step": step, "loss": float(loss), "grad_norm": float(grad_norm), "validation": float(valid_metric), } run_log.append(metrics) # One curve cannot diagnose a training system. What to test next. 1. Observe: Define state, partial observation, and reset conditions. 2. Act: Select actions through a policy with exploration. 3. Learn: Assign delayed reward through returns and value estimates. 4. Evaluate: Test across seeds, scenarios, and real constraints. The gotcha. A small inspection script proves only the quantities it prints. Preserve units, shapes, versions, and the input fixture beside its output. A rigorous way to practice Observe. Define state, partial observation, and reset conditions. Act. Select actions through a policy with exploration. Learn. Assign delayed reward through returns and value estimates. Evaluate. Test across seeds, scenarios, and real constraints. Build a small environment with transparent rewards before adding a neural policy. Log trajectories, not only return, and inspect the policies that score best for unsafe or unintended strategies. Verification questions for reinforcement learning & decision-making Boundary Question Evidence Observe What would show that this boundary failed? Define state, partial observation, and reset conditions. Act What would show that this boundary failed? Select actions through a policy with exploration. Learn What would show that this boundary failed? Assign delayed reward through returns and value estimates. Evaluate What would show that this boundary failed? Test across seeds, scenarios, and real constraints. The gotcha. Passing each component check separately does not prove the composed path preserves identity, units, ordering, or authority.

Pretraining produces a model that is extraordinarily good at exactly one thing: predicting the next token in a document. That is not the same thing as being useful. This section covers the first stage of post-training — the supervised phase that turns a document-completion engine into something that answers when you ask it a question. The Gap Between a Base Model and an Assistant Ask a raw base model "What is the capital of France?" and you may well get back "What is the capital of Germany? What is the capital of Italy?" — because in the pretraining corpus, a line that looks like a quiz question is most often followed by more quiz questions, not by an answer. The base model is not failing. It is doing precisely what it was trained to do, which is to continue the document in the most likely way. The problem is that the user wanted a different document than the one the corpus statistics imply. The capability is already there; the format is not. This is the single most important conceptual point in post-training. A base model that has read a large fraction of the public internet has already absorbed French geography, Python semantics, the structure of a persuasive essay, and the arithmetic of compound interest. What it lacks is the disposition to deploy that knowledge in response to an instruction. Instruction tuning does not teach the model facts. It teaches the model that the pattern "human asks, assistant answers helpfully and completely" is the pattern to complete. The evidence for the latency claim is the data efficiency. Pretraining consumes trillions of tokens. Instruction tuning that produces a genuinely usable assistant can be done with tens of thousands of examples — in some cases a thousand. If SFT were teaching new capability, this ratio would be impossible; you cannot install broad world knowledge in one thousand examples. The only consistent explanation is that SFT is doing something much cheaper: locating an existing behaviour in the model and making it the default. This framing is sometimes called the superficial alignment hypothesis , stated explicitly in the LIMA paper (Zhou et al., 2023, "LIMA: Less Is More for Alignment") — that a model's knowledge and capabilities are learned almost entirely during pretraining, and alignment mainly teaches it which subdistribution of formats to use when interacting with users. The practical corollary. If a base model genuinely cannot do a task, no amount of instruction tuning will conjure the ability. SFT will happily teach the model to produce confident, well-formatted, fluent output on that task — which is worse than failing visibly. Instruction data teaches style far more efficiently than it teaches substance, so fine-tuning a weak model on the outputs of a strong one buys you the strong model's voice long before it buys you its reasoning. Supervised Fine-Tuning Mechanics SFT is mechanically almost identical to pretraining. Same architecture, same optimizer family, same cross-entropy next-token objective. Three things change: the data is curated prompt-response pairs instead of scraped documents, the learning rate is much lower, and — critically — the loss is masked. Prompt masking. A training example is the concatenation of a prompt and a response. You do not want gradient signal encouraging the model to generate the prompt; the prompt is what the user supplies at inference time, and training on it wastes capacity modelling the distribution of user inputs. So the loss is computed only over the response tokens, with prompt positions masked out. tokens = [ prompt_tokens ................ | response_tokens ......... ] label_mask = [ -100 -100 -100 ... -100 | t1 t2 t3 ... eos ] loss = - (1/|R|) * sum over i in R of log P(x_i | x_ i ; theta) where R = the set of response token positions only. Positions marked -100 are ignored by the cross-entropy loss. Base model next-token prediction over a web corpus SFT Supervised fine-tune same objective, same arch lr 1e-5 2e-5, 1 3 epochs Instruct model answers rather than continues the prompt What the data looks like at each stage pretraining: one undifferentiated stream, every token is a target web text web text web text loss on ALL tokens SFT: an (instruction, response) pair, and the two halves are treated differently prompt / instruction tokens response tokens mask = -100 no gradient mask = token id loss computed here only loss on RESPONSE only the prompt is still attended to visible in the forward pass, absent from the loss prompt tokens condition every response prediction even though they are never predicted SFT reuses the base model's architecture and next-token objective but changes the data from an undifferentiated web stream to (instruction, response) pairs, and masks the loss to the response tokens so the prompt conditions the prediction without ever being a prediction target. Note that the prompt tokens are still attended to — they remain in the context and condition every response prediction. They simply do not contribute gradient as prediction targets. This distinction (visible in the forward pass, absent from the loss) trips people up constantly. Hyperparameters differ sharply from pretraining. Typical SFT runs use learning rates one to two orders of magnitude below pretraining (on the order of 1e-5 to 2e-5 for full fine-tuning of a mid-size model), only one to three epochs, and often a cosine or linear decay with a short warmup. The reason is that you are nudging an already-converged model, not training one from scratch; a large learning rate will wash out pretrained representations and produce exactly the degradation described in section 8.7. Packing and the EOS token. For throughput, short examples are often packed several-per-sequence. Done carelessly this lets attention bleed across example boundaries, so the model conditions one response on an unrelated previous conversation. Correct implementations either reset the attention mask at document boundaries or accept the small waste of padding instead. Equally important is training the model to emit an end-of-sequence token at the end of each response — omit this and you get a model that never stops talking, which is one of the most common symptoms of a botched first fine-tune. Chat Templates and Special Tokens A conversation is not a flat string. It has turns, and each turn has a role — system, user, assistant, and increasingly tool. That structure has to be serialized into a token sequence somehow, and the serialization scheme is the chat template . Templates typically wrap each turn in role-delimiting special tokens that are reserved in the vocabulary so no ordinary text can produce them. A representative shape: |im_start| system You are a helpful assistant. |im_end| |im_start| user What is the capital of France? |im_end| |im_start| assistant Paris. |im_end| Why reserved special tokens rather than plain text delimiters. If the turn markers were ordinary strings, a user could type them and forge an assistant turn or a system prompt — the text-level equivalent of SQL injection. Reserving them at the tokenizer level means user text can never tokenize into a role boundary. This is a security property, not a formatting nicety, and it is the first line of defence against a whole family of prompt-injection attacks. Template mismatch degrades quality silently. This is the highest-frequency practical bug in the entire post-training stack. If a model was trained with one template and is served with another — a missing system-turn wrapper, a stray newline, a different special token, a generation prompt that does not exactly match the training-time prefix — the model is being run off-distribution. It will not error. It will produce output that is subtly worse: more rambling, likelier to ignore the system prompt, likelier to fail to stop. Because there is no crash and no warning, teams frequently attribute the degradation to the model rather than to the harness. The rule is that the exact string fed to the tokenizer at inference must match the training-time serialization byte for byte, including whitespace. Failure Symptom Cause Wrong template Vague, rambling, ignores system prompt Off-distribution input format Missing generation prompt Model continues the user turn instead of replying Assistant-turn prefix not appended EOS not trained / not honoured Model never stops, invents extra turns EOS masked out of loss, or not a stop token at serving Double-applied template Nested role markers, incoherent output Harness templates an already-templated string Special tokens not in vocab Markers tokenize into fragments Tokenizer not extended before training The Instruction-Data Lineage Where instruction data comes from has changed three times in five years, and each shift redefined what was cheap. Era one: reformatted academic NLP tasks. The first insight was that a large amount of supervised NLP data already existed — sentiment classification, summarization, question answering, NLI — and could be re-expressed as natural-language instructions. FLAN (Wei et al., 2021, "Finetuned Language Models Are Zero-Shot Learners") and T0 (Sanh et al., 2021, "Multitask Prompted Training Enables Zero-Shot Task Generalization") both took this route, templating dozens of existing datasets into instruction phrasings and fine-tuning on the mixture. The headline result was zero-shot generalization to held-out task types : training on enough distinct instruction-shaped tasks produced a model that followed instructions for tasks it had never been tuned on. This established instruction-following as a transferable meta-skill rather than a per-task trick. Era two: paid human demonstrations. Academic-task data is stilted; nobody actually asks a model to "output the NLI label for this premise-hypothesis pair." InstructGPT (Ouyang et al., 2022, "Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback") used contractors writing demonstrations for real, free-form prompts drawn from actual API traffic. This is the SFT stage of the three-stage pipeline covered in section 9, and it is the origin of the modern assistant register. It is also expensive and slow, which set up the third era. Era three: model-generated instruction data. Self-Instruct (Wang et al., 2022, "Self-Instruct: Aligning Language Models with Self-Generated Instructions") showed you could bootstrap: seed a small pool of human-written tasks, prompt a strong model to generate new instructions and responses, filter for quality and diversity, and fine-tune on the result. Stanford's Alpaca applied this concretely, generating roughly 52,000 instruction-following examples from a strong model to fine-tune a much smaller base model at trivial cost. This collapsed the price of a plausible-looking assistant from millions of dollars to hundreds, and set off the open instruction-tuned model ecosystem. The pattern is distillation : a strong teacher's outputs become a weaker student's supervised targets. Era four: quality curation. LIMA (Zhou et al., 2023) fine-tuned a 65B base model on just 1,000 carefully curated prompt-response pairs — no RLHF at all — and found it competitive with far more heavily post-trained models in human preference comparisons. The claim is that once the base model is strong, a small set of high-quality, stylistically consistent, diverse examples outperforms a much larger noisy set. The caveats on LIMA matter as much as the result. The comparison was on human preference over single-turn responses, an evaluation that rewards style, formatting and confident register — exactly what SFT transfers most efficiently. A thousand examples do not reliably buy robustness, multi-turn coherence, refusal behaviour on adversarial inputs, or reliability on tasks with a verifiable right answer. "Quality over quantity" is a real and useful finding about the marginal value of the ten-thousandth mediocre example; it is not a claim that a thousand examples is sufficient post-training for a deployed system. Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning: LoRA Full fine-tuning updates every parameter, which means the optimizer must hold, for each of billions of parameters, a gradient plus Adam's first and second moments. With mixed-precision training the memory overhead runs to something like sixteen bytes per parameter — the weights themselves are the small part of the bill. This makes full fine-tuning of a large model a multi-GPU job even when the task is trivial. The core observation. LoRA (Hu et al., 2021, "LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models") starts from the hypothesis that the update needed to adapt a pretrained model to a downstream task has low intrinsic rank — that although the weight matrix is huge, the change you need to make to it lives in a small subspace. If that is true, you do not need to parameterize the full update matrix; you can parameterize its factorization. Full fine-tuning: W' = W + dW dW has d*k free parameters LoRA: W' = W + (alpha/r) * B @ A A: r x k (init: gaussian) B: d x r (init: zeros) trainable params: r*(d + k) d*k At init B = 0, so B@A = 0 and W' = W exactly: the adapted model starts identical to the base model. Forward pass: h = W x + (alpha/r) * B (A x) What is frozen and what moves. The pretrained W is frozen — no gradients, no optimizer state. Only A and B train. For a 4096x4096 attention projection at rank 8, that is 65,536 trainable parameters against 16.8 million, a reduction of roughly 250x for that matrix. Optimizer memory scales with trainable parameters, so this is what makes single-GPU fine-tuning of large models feasible. Adapters are typically applied to the attention projections, and often to the MLP projections as well; which modules to target is an empirical choice, and targeting more modules at lower rank frequently beats targeting fewer at higher rank. Two properties that matter operationally. First, because B is initialized to zero the adapted model is exactly the base model at step zero — there is no initialization shock. Second, at inference you can compute W + (alpha/r) * B @ A once and fold it into the base weights, so a merged LoRA has zero added inference latency , unlike adapter-layer methods that insert extra sequential computation. Alternatively you keep adapters unmerged and hot-swap many task-specific adapters against one shared base model in memory — the basis of multi-tenant adapter serving. QLoRA. QLoRA (Dettmers et al., 2023, "QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs") pushes further by quantizing the frozen base weights to 4-bit while training LoRA adapters in higher precision on top, backpropagating through the quantized base. Its contributions include a 4-bit NormalFloat data type suited to the roughly-normal distribution of weights, double quantization (quantizing the quantization constants), and paged optimizers to survive memory spikes. The practical effect was fine-tuning a 65B model on a single 48GB GPU with quality close to 16-bit fine-tuning. Dimension Full fine-tuning LoRA / QLoRA Trainable parameters 100% Typically well under 1% Optimizer memory Dominates; multi-GPU for large models Small; often single-GPU Checkpoint size Full model per task Megabytes per task Inference latency Baseline Baseline if merged Serving many tasks One full model each One base + many swappable adapters Large distribution shift Better — can move representations Weaker — constrained to a low-rank subspace New language / domain / heavy continued pretraining Preferred Often insufficient capacity Style, format, task adaptation Works, expensive Usually matches at a fraction of cost When full fine-tuning still wins. The low-rank hypothesis is an empirical claim about the size of the required change, and it fails when the change is genuinely large: continued pretraining on a new domain or language, absorbing a substantial volume of new knowledge, or large-scale post-training where you want the freedom to move representations rather than steer them. Rank is a capacity ceiling — if the task needs more than rank r of change, more data will not help, and the fix is a higher rank or a full fine-tune. Choosing and Curating the Data Given that SFT is mostly eliciting rather than teaching, the leverage is almost entirely in data selection. A few properties consistently matter more than raw volume. Diversity of task type dominates volume within a task type. The FLAN and T0 results turned on the number of distinct tasks in the mixture, not the number of examples. The tenth thousand sentiment-classification example teaches nothing new; the first example of a new task shape teaches a great deal. When curating, the question to ask is how many genuinely different things the model is being asked to do, not how many rows exist. Response quality sets the ceiling, because SFT is imitation. Cross-entropy on the response tokens is pure behavioural cloning — the model is trained to reproduce the target exactly, including its errors, hedges, refusals, and formatting tics. There is no mechanism by which SFT produces output better than its targets. A dataset with mediocre responses trains a mediocre model no matter how many rows it has. This is the structural reason preference optimization (section 9) exists: it can score outputs the model generates itself, so it is not bounded by the quality of a human-written demonstration. Consistency of persona and format. Because the model is learning which subdistribution to inhabit, contradictory examples teach it an average. A dataset where half the responses are terse and half are effusive, or where refusal boundaries are drawn inconsistently, produces a model that is unpredictable on exactly those axes. Uniformity of style within an instruction dataset is a feature, not a sign of insufficient variety — the variety belongs in the tasks, not the voice. Catastrophic Forgetting and the Alignment Tax Post-training is not free. Every gradient step taken on instruction data moves weights away from the pretraining optimum, and some of what those weights encoded is lost. Catastrophic forgetting is the general neural-network phenomenon: training on a new distribution overwrites representations serving the old one, because nothing in the objective preserves them. In LLM post-training this shows up as a fine-tuned model losing capability on tasks absent from the SFT mixture — a model tuned hard on chat data getting worse at raw code completion or at a language underrepresented in the instruction set. The alignment tax is the specific case where alignment-directed post-training costs measurable capability. InstructGPT (Ouyang et al., 2022) documented this directly: their aligned models regressed on some standard NLP benchmarks relative to the base model, even as human raters strongly preferred their outputs. The paper also reported a practical mitigation — mixing pretraining gradients back into the post-training update (their PPO-ptx variant) reduced the regressions. The general form of that mitigation, replay , is standard: hold back a slice of pretraining-distribution data and interleave it during fine-tuning so the old distribution keeps exerting gradient pressure. Why LoRA partially sidesteps this. Constraining the update to a low-rank subspace is implicitly a regularizer. The model physically cannot move most directions in weight space, so most of what pretraining encoded is preserved by construction. This is a genuine advantage of PEFT beyond its memory savings, and it is why LoRA is often the better choice for a narrow adaptation even when the compute for a full fine-tune is available. The flip side is the same fact restated: if you want to move representations substantially, the constraint is now the problem. Other mitigations. Low learning rates and few epochs (SFT overfits fast; three epochs on a small set is usually past the optimum), early stopping against a held-out capability suite rather than just held-out SFT loss, and evaluating on a broad benchmark battery before and after so the tax is measured rather than assumed. The failure mode to avoid is monitoring only the metric you optimized — SFT loss will look excellent in precisely the run that has quietly degraded everything else. Contamination and the Risks of Model-Generated Data Synthetic instruction data solved the cost problem and introduced three new ones. Benchmark contamination. When a teacher model generates instruction data, it can reproduce test-set items it saw in its own pretraining — sometimes verbatim, often paraphrased. The student then trains on the eval. The resulting score is not a measurement of capability; it is a measurement of memorization, and it is inflated in a way that string-matching decontamination will not catch, because a paraphrase is not a string match. Any claim of a small model matching a large one on a benchmark, trained on data distilled from a model that may have seen that benchmark, deserves scepticism until the decontamination methodology is specified. This connects directly to the evaluation issues in section 13. Style transfer outruns capability transfer. Distillation teaches the teacher's surface form far faster than its reasoning. A student fine-tuned on a strong teacher's outputs learns the confident register, the structured formatting, the measured hedging — and wins human preference evaluations on the strength of that alone, while remaining substantially weaker on anything with a checkable right answer. Several 2023 replication efforts made this point directly, finding that open models imitating proprietary ones closed the stylistic gap and much less of the factual one. The lesson for evaluation is that human preference on free-form responses is a poor instrument for detecting this gap; you need tasks with ground truth. Error and bias inheritance, with amplification. The student inherits the teacher's factual errors and biases, but without the teacher's uncertainty. A teacher that is wrong 5% of the time produces training targets that are confidently wrong 5% of the time, and the student learns those as ground truth. Filtering helps — rejection sampling against a verifier, or keeping only examples where an independent check passes — but a filter can only remove errors it can detect, which is precisely the subset that matters least. Gotcha SFT is behavioural cloning, so it cannot make a model better than its training targets — but it will happily make the model sound better than them. Fine-tuning a weak base model on a strong model's outputs reliably transfers tone, structure and confidence long before it transfers reasoning, which produces a model that wins side-by-side human preference tests while remaining just as wrong on anything with a verifiable answer. If your only evaluation is "which response do raters prefer," this failure is invisible by construction. Always pair preference evaluation with ground-truth tasks, and treat any large gap between the two as evidence of style transfer rather than capability transfer.

Section 7 ended on a structural limitation: supervised fine-tuning is behavioural cloning, so it is bounded above by the quality of its targets. Preference optimization is the family of methods that breaks that ceiling. Instead of showing the model what to say, you show it which of two things it said was better — and that turns out to be both a far cheaper signal to collect and a fundamentally different kind of supervision, because it can score the model's own outputs rather than a human's. Why Preferences Beat Demonstrations The case for preference data is mostly an argument about what humans are actually good at. Writing an ideal response is a generative task; judging which of two responses is better is a discriminative one. Discrimination is enormously easier, and the gap widens exactly where the stakes are highest. The labeler's cost asymmetry. Asking an annotator to write the ideal answer to "explain the tradeoffs of nuclear power for a policy brief" demands domain knowledge, writing skill, and half an hour. Asking them which of two drafts is better takes ninety seconds and demands only taste. For long responses the asymmetry compounds: a 600-word answer has hundreds of independent choices of framing, ordering, hedging and length, and no annotator produces the optimum on all of them. But they can reliably tell you that draft A buried the conclusion and draft B did not. Preferences capture things that cannot be written down. A large fraction of what "good assistant behaviour" means is tacit — the right level of hedging, when to ask a clarifying question instead of guessing, how much structure a given answer wants, when to refuse and how gracefully. Nobody can write a specification for these, and a demonstration only encodes one point in the space. Comparisons let annotators express a preference ordering over a criterion they could never articulate, which is precisely the regime where "I know it when I see it" is the only available supervision. The ceiling argument. This is the decisive one. SFT's cross-entropy loss pushes the model toward reproducing a human-written target, errors included; there is no gradient direction that says "better than the demonstration." Preference optimization scores samples drawn from the model itself , so as the model improves, the things being compared improve, and the signal keeps being informative. A model can become better than any individual annotator at writing, as long as annotators remain able to rank its outputs. That is the same asymmetry that makes verification-easier-than-generation such a load-bearing idea across alignment. The prehistory. Learning a reward function from human comparisons rather than from a hand-written specification predates language models. Christiano et al., 2017, "Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences" trained Atari and MuJoCo agents by asking humans to compare short video clips of behaviour, fitting a reward model to those comparisons, and optimizing it with RL — famously teaching a simulated robot to backflip from roughly 900 bits of human comparison feedback, a task with no writable reward function. Stiennon et al., 2020, "Learning to Summarize from Human Feedback" carried the recipe to language, showing preference-optimized summarization models beating both supervised baselines and the human reference summaries they were trained on. Dimension Demonstrations (SFT) Preferences (RLHF/DPO) Labeler task Generate the ideal output Compare two candidate outputs Cost per label High; scales with response length Low; roughly flat in difficulty Skill required Domain expertise plus writing ability Judgement only Quality ceiling The annotator's own writing The annotator's ability to rank What it encodes One point in output space A direction in output space Tacit criteria (tone, hedging, refusal) Poorly — must be written explicitly Naturally — no articulation needed Failure mode Imitates errors; style over substance Optimizes a proxy; reward hacking The Three-Stage Pipeline The canonical recipe is InstructGPT (Ouyang et al., 2022, "Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback"), which established the structure that essentially every subsequent aligned assistant has followed in some form.
