Connect perception and prediction to physical action under uncertainty. How the pieces connect MENTAL MODEL Robotics, world models control — from question to evidence 01 Sense Synchronize calibrated observations and state estimates. 02 Plan Choose a target or trajectory under constraints. 03 Control Close feedback loops within real-time deadlines. 04 Recover Detect uncertainty, stop safely, and replan. Sense → Plan → Control → Recover. Each transition is a place where an assumption can be inspected before the next layer of the system compounds it. The embodied loop A robot senses the environment, estimates state, chooses a plan, and executes control actions. Sensors are noisy and delayed. Coordinate frames, calibration, and time synchronization determine whether observations can be combined. A correct object label does not by itself provide a safe grasp pose. Control operates at multiple timescales A high-level planner may choose a destination while a lower-level controller stabilizes motion. Feedback compares desired and measured state. Model predictive control repeatedly optimizes a finite horizon and executes only the next action before observing again. Latency and actuator limits constrain feasible behavior. Learned policies and world models Imitation learning copies demonstrations; RL optimizes through interaction; world models predict state or observation transitions. Learned dynamics can support planning but suffer compounding error over rollouts. Simulator success requires validation under real sensor, friction, lighting, and contact conditions. Evaluate physical robustness Test recovery, perturbations, new objects, and environment changes. Record collisions, near misses, control saturation, and operator interventions, not only completion rate. Separate a model’s suggested action from the system authorized to actuate hardware. Worked example A controller running at 100 Hz has 10 ms per cycle. A model taking 250 ms cannot directly supply every control update at that rate. A system may use the model for slower plans and a separate real-time controller for stabilization. What goes wrong A video demonstration shows one trajectory, not reliability across the operating envelope. Reset conditions and human interventions can hide failure modes. Check your understanding Why replan after each action in model predictive control? Reveal the explanation New observations correct state estimates and reduce dependence on long, potentially inaccurate open-loop predictions. An operating model for robotics, world models & control Robotics turns model error into physical consequences. A learned perception model may be one component of a safety-critical loop, but it cannot replace coordinate calibration, actuator limits, collision handling, control timing, and recovery. High-level reasoning and low-level control typically operate at very different rates. The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test. Worked system: a correct label cannot close a control loop A vision model recognizes a cup with high confidence. That does not provide its three-dimensional pose, material, grip point, weight, or whether the robot’s arm can reach it without collision. A planner can choose a high-level goal, but a low-level controller still needs calibrated coordinates, timely measurements, actuator limits, and a recovery path when contact differs from expectation. Separate the rates. A model that takes 250 milliseconds may plan the next action; a stabilizing controller may need to run every 10 milliseconds. Test latency, missing observations, lighting shifts, contact, and emergency stops as part of one loop. Physical AI turns prediction error into motion, so the system’s safe behavior matters more than an isolated perception score. The transition from a language model to a model that sees is less dramatic architecturally than it sounds. Almost every production VLM is a decoder-only transformer of exactly the shape described in section 1, fed a token sequence in which some tokens happen to have come from an image rather than a tokenizer. The interesting engineering is entirely in how pixels become vectors that live in the same space as text embeddings, and in what is lost along the way. This section covers the contrastive pretraining that made image-text alignment work at all, the vision encoders that produce the visual tokens, the two competing ways of attaching them to an LLM, and an honest accounting of where these systems are solid and where they are not. CLIP and contrastive image-text pretraining CLIP Radford et al. (2021), Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision is the single most influential result in multimodal learning, and its influence is disproportionate to its apparent simplicity. Its premise: instead of training an image classifier on a fixed label set, train an image encoder and a text encoder jointly so that an image and its caption land near each other in a shared embedding space. # N image-text pairs in a batch I_f = ImageEncoder(images) # (N, d_i) T_f = TextEncoder(texts) # (N, d_t) I_e = l2_normalize(I_f @ W_i) # (N, d) shared space T_e = l2_normalize(T_f @ W_t) # (N, d) logits = (I_e @ T_e.T) * exp(t) # (N, N), t a learned temperature # The N correct pairs are on the diagonal. Symmetric cross-entropy: loss = ( CE(logits, arange(N)) + CE(logits.T, arange(N)) ) / 2 Read the loss carefully the structure is the whole idea. The N N similarity matrix has the correct pairings on its diagonal and N - N incorrect pairings off it. Cross-entropy along the rows asks given this image, which of the N captions is right ; along the columns it asks the reverse. It is the InfoNCE contrastive objective of section 18 applied across modalities, and its defining practical property is that batch size is the difficulty of the task . With 32 in-batch negatives the problem is trivial and the learned features coarse; CLIP trained with batches of 32,768, so each positive competed against tens of thousands of distractors, which is what forces the encoder to encode fine distinctions rather than gist. This makes contrastive pretraining a systems problem the large-batch requirement drives the distributed training and gradient-accumulation strategies of section 21. The data is the second half of the story, and it is deliberately noisy. CLIP trained on 400 million image-text pairs scraped from the web. Alt text is inconsistent, sometimes wrong, frequently uninformative. But it is free at a scale hand-labeling can never reach , and it carries information no fixed label set contains: relations, attributes, styles, proper nouns, compositions. Radford et al.'s framing natural language as supervision is the durable insight. A model trained on the ImageNet label set can only ever express 1000 concepts; a model trained on captions inherits the open vocabulary of language. Zero-shot classification falls directly out of the shared space, and this is what made the paper famous. Because captions and images are embedded comparably, you build a classifier at inference time out of text alone: embed a prompt per candidate class, embed the image, take the nearest. classes = ["a photo of a cat", "a photo of a dog", ...] T = normalize(TextEncoder(classes)) # (C, d) -- the classifier weights i = normalize(ImageEncoder(image)) # (d,) prediction = argmax(i @ T.T) The text encoder is literally synthesizing classifier weights from a class name. There is no training step, no labeled example, and the class list can be changed between one image and the next. CLIP's zero-shot ImageNet accuracy matched a fully-supervised ResNet-50 on a benchmark it had never trained on. The prompt template matters measurably ( a photo of a {class} beats the bare class name, and ensembling many templates beats one), which is a small early sign of the prompt sensitivity that pervades the field. What CLIP is bad at is as instructive as what it is good at. The embedding behaves substantially like a bag of concepts: it knows a cat, a mat, and a on are present, and is unreliable about which is on which . Benchmarks built to test this (the ARO and Winoground lines of work) found CLIP-style models near chance on relational and compositional distinctions. It counts poorly, reads dense text poorly, and encodes spatial relations weakly. The cause is structural: a contrastive objective only needs enough information to pick the right caption out of a batch, and in a batch of random web images, gist suffices nothing in the training signal ever demands compositional precision. These weaknesses propagate into every VLM that uses a CLIP-style encoder as its eyes. Successors refined the recipe without changing the shape. ALIGN (Jia et al., 2021) showed that a billion-scale noisier dataset with a simpler filter worked at least as well, reinforcing that scale beats curation here. SigLIP (Zhai et al., 2023) replaced the softmax over the batch with a pairwise sigmoid loss, decoupling the objective from the batch and removing the giant-batch requirement, which made strong contrastive models trainable at far lower cost. Open reproductions (OpenCLIP, trained on LAION) made the whole line auditable. Vision encoders: ViT and what it changed The Vision Transformer Dosovitskiy et al. (2020), An Image Is Worth 16x16 Words is what let vision reuse the transformer stack wholesale. The mechanism is almost aggressively simple: cut the image into fixed-size patches, flatten each, project it linearly to d_model , add a position embedding, and feed the resulting sequence to a standard transformer encoder. # 224x224 image, 16x16 patches num_patches = (224/16) ** 2 = 196 patch = flatten(16 x 16 x 3) = 768 values tokens = patch @ W_embed + pos_embed # (196, d_model) # then: an ordinary transformer encoder over 196 tokens The load-bearing claim is that convolutional inductive bias is a crutch you can outgrow. A CNN hard-codes locality (a kernel sees only a neighborhood) and translation equivariance (the same kernel everywhere). These are correct priors about images and they are exactly why CNNs win on small datasets the architecture supplies structure the data cannot. A ViT assumes almost nothing: self-attention over patches is global from layer one, and even spatial adjacency must be learned through position embeddings. Dosovitskiy et al.'s finding was that this is a disadvantage below roughly 10 100 million images and an advantage above it . Given enough data the model learns better priors than the ones we imposed, and it also learns to relate distant regions in a single layer, which a CNN needs depth to do. This is the same story as section 1's: a general architecture with weak priors plus scale beats a specialized architecture with strong priors, once the scale is there. It is also why nearly every VLM's vision tower is a ViT trained contrastively usually CLIP's or SigLIP's rather than a CNN. Encoder choice Training signal Strength Weakness in VLM use CLIP / SigLIP ViT Image-text contrastive Features already semantically aligned to language Inherits bag-of-concepts weakness; low native resolution DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2023) Self-supervised, no text Strong dense/spatial features, good localization Not language-aligned; needs more adapter training Supervised ViT / CNN Fixed label set Cheap, well-understood Closed vocabulary; weaker transfer Encoder-free (patches straight in) Trained with the LLM No frozen-encoder ceiling; simpler stack Far more data and compute to reach parity An increasingly common production choice is to ensemble encoders concatenating CLIP features (semantic, language-aligned) with DINOv2 features (spatial, localization-strong) because their failure modes are close to complementary. Attaching vision to an LLM: the projection-adapter approach The dominant way to build a VLM is to take a strong pretrained LLM and a strong pretrained vision encoder, freeze one or both, and train a small module that maps image features into the LLM's embedding space so that visual tokens are simply prepended or interleaved with text tokens. image - VisionEncoder - (196, d_vision) - Projector - (196, d_model) # now LLM-compatible sequence = [ visual_tokens ; text_token_embeddings ] - the ordinary decoder-only LLM, unmodified image patchify 14 14 ViT encoder 196 patches d_vision Projector linear / MLP d_vision d_model the one trained bridge: visual features become vectors the LLM reads as token embeddings one sequence, d_model wide v_1 v_2 v_196 projected image patches "What" "is" "in" "it?" text token embeddings decoder-only LLM (unmodified) text out The LLM cannot tell which positions came from pixels. The projector is the whole trick: it maps vision-encoder features into the LLM's embedding dimension so image patches occupy ordinary token positions interleaved with text, leaving the decoder architecture untouched. LLaVA (Liu et al., 2023, Visual Instruction Tuning ) demonstrated how far the cheapest version of this goes. The projector was a single linear layer (an MLP in LLaVA-1.5), the vision encoder was frozen CLIP, and the training was two-stage: first align the projector on image-caption pairs with everything else frozen, then instruction-tune on visual conversation data with the LLM unfrozen. The instruction data itself was generated by prompting a text-only GPT-4 with captions and bounding boxes to produce conversations about images it could not see a distillation trick that made the whole thing cheap. The result was competitive on visual chat benchmarks for a training run measured in GPU-hours rather than GPU-months, which is why this recipe became the default. BLIP-2 (Li et al., 2023) is the more elaborate variant and its motivation is token cost. A linear projector emits one LLM token per image patch, so a high-resolution image floods the context. BLIP-2 interposes a Q-Former : a small transformer holding a fixed set of learned query vectors (32 of them) that cross-attend to the vision encoder's output and emit exactly 32 tokens regardless of input size. It compresses, and it is trained in stages to extract text-relevant visual information specifically. The tradeoff is direct a fixed bottleneck discards detail that the task might have needed, and for OCR or fine-grained spatial tasks 32 tokens are provably too few. As of the early-2025 literature the field has largely moved back toward simple MLP projectors with more tokens, on the view that compute is cheaper than lost information, though the question is not closed. Connector Tokens emitted Parameters Preserves detail Notes Linear / MLP projector One per patch Tiny Yes nothing dropped LLaVA; simple, now dominant Q-Former (BLIP-2) Fixed (e.g. 32) Moderate Lossy by construction Cheap context; weak on dense detail Perceiver resampler Fixed Moderate Lossy Flamingo; handles variable-size inputs Pixel shuffle / pooling Reduced by a fixed factor None Partially Common high-res compromise Cross-attention layers Zero into the sequence Large Yes Flamingo-style; context stays free Cross-attention and natively multimodal pretraining The adapter approach treats vision as something bolted onto a finished language model. The alternative is to build multimodality into the model, and there are two distinct versions of that. Flamingo (Alayrac et al., 2022) is the early canonical cross-attention design. Rather than inserting visual tokens into the sequence, Flamingo interleaves new gated cross-attention layers between the frozen LLM's existing blocks; text tokens attend to visual features from a Perceiver resampler while the LLM's own weights stay fixed. The gates are initialized so the new layers start as identity, meaning the model begins exactly as the original LLM and learns to use vision gradually a stability trick worth remembering. Crucially, Flamingo trained on interleaved image-text web documents rather than isolated caption pairs, which is what gave it strong few-shot behavior: it had seen sequences where several images and several passages of text alternate, so multi-image in-context prompting was in-distribution. The architectural advantage is that images consume no sequence positions; the disadvantage is added parameters and a less uniform architecture, and self-attention over concatenated tokens has proven simpler and generally stronger at scale. Natively multimodal pretraining is the current frontier direction. Rather than aligning two separately-pretrained towers, train a single model on text, images, audio and video from the start, with a unified token stream. The argument is that adapter-based models inherit a ceiling from a frozen encoder trained on a contrastive objective that discarded exactly the compositional and spatial information downstream tasks need you cannot recover through a projector what the encoder never encoded. The cost is enormous: you forfeit the ability to reuse an existing strong LLM, and the multimodal data mix becomes a first-class research problem, since too much image data measurably degrades text capability. As of the early-2025 literature the frontier proprietary models are widely understood to be natively multimodal while most open-weight VLMs remain adapter-based, and the open evidence for how large the native advantage is remains thin because the confound with training scale is never controlled. Resolution, tiling, and the token-cost problem A CLIP ViT natively takes 224 224 or 336 336 pixels. That is enough to identify a dog; it is nowhere near enough to read a paragraph in a screenshot, spot a defect in a photograph, or interpret a dense chart. Downscaling a 4K screenshot to 336 pixels destroys the text before the model sees it the failure is in the resampling, not the reasoning, and no amount of prompting fixes it. The direct fix is quadratically expensive. Patch count grows as the square of side length, and attention is quadratic in patch count, so vision-encoder cost grows as the fourth power of resolution. Doubling from 336 to 672 is 4 the tokens and roughly 16 the encoder attention cost, and those tokens then occupy the LLM's context and its KV cache for the rest of the conversation. Strategy Mechanism Cost Weakness Fixed low resolution Resize to the encoder's native size Cheapest Small text and fine detail are destroyed Position-embedding interpolation Interpolate the ViT's position embeddings to a larger grid Quadratic in tokens Out-of-distribution for the encoder; needs finetuning Tiling / AnyRes Split into native-size tiles, encode each, plus a downscaled global view Linear in tile count Cross-tile objects split; token count explodes Native dynamic resolution Encoder trained to accept variable sizes and aspect ratios directly Proportional to content Requires training the encoder for it Token merging / pruning Drop or merge redundant visual tokens post-encoding Reduces LLM cost Risks dropping the tokens the question was about Tiling (the AnyRes approach popularized by LLaVA-1.5/1.6 and its contemporaries) is the pragmatic default. Cut the image into native-resolution tiles, encode each independently, and additionally encode a downscaled whole image so the model retains global layout that tiling destroyed. It works well and its arithmetic is sobering: a 6-tile image at 576 tokens per tile is ~3,500 visual tokens, which is a substantial fraction of a mid-size context window spent on one image, and it stays in the KV cache for every subsequent turn. This is the practical reason multi-image and video reasoning is expensive, and it makes visual-token compression a live research area rather than a micro-optimization. Unified any-to-any tokenization The clear trend as of the early-2025 literature is toward one model that takes any modality in and emits any modality out, over a single token vocabulary. The obstacle is that images are continuous and language modeling is over discrete symbols, and the two standard resolutions of that mismatch have different consequences. Discretize the image into tokens. A VQ-VAE or VQ-GAN encodes an image patch to the nearest entry in a learned codebook, turning the image into a sequence of integer IDs that can be extended into the text vocabulary. Then a single autoregressive transformer models text and images identically, and generation is generation regardless of modality this is the lineage from DALL-E's first version through Parti and Chameleon (Chameleon Team, 2024). The cost is quantization loss: the codebook is a bottleneck, reconstruction fidelity caps output quality, and codebook collapse (most entries going unused) is a real training pathology. Keep the representation continuous and use a different head for generation. Understanding uses continuous visual embeddings (no quantization loss), while image output is delegated to a diffusion decoder conditioned on the LLM's hidden states (section 20). This preserves both fidelity and understanding quality but abandons the elegance of one objective, and the two halves can disagree about what a representation means. The empirically important observation is that understanding and generation want different representations. Understanding wants semantic abstraction throw away the exact pixels, keep what the image means. Generation needs the exact pixels back. Training one representation for both creates a documented tension, and several 2024 systems responded by using separate visual encoders for the two paths within one model. That is an admission that unification is not yet solved, only routed around. Video: a distinctly harder problem Video is not images with an extra index; it is a different cost regime and a different set of required capabilities. The token arithmetic is brutal. At 576 tokens per frame and 1 frame per second, a five-minute clip is 300 frames and 172,800 visual tokens, before any text. Sampling at video frame rates is out of the question. Every practical system therefore subsamples aggressively a fixed budget of 8 to 64 frames is typical and the sampling policy becomes a load-bearing design choice: uniform sampling is likely to miss a brief but decisive event, while keyframe or query-conditioned sampling requires knowing what matters before you have looked. The capabilities required are ones image models never needed. Temporal ordering (did A happen before B), causality, action recognition that depends on motion rather than appearance, object permanence through occlusion, and long-range event tracking. A model that scores well by treating video as a bag of independently-understood frames will still fail all of these, and the important part many video benchmarks are answerable from a single frame, so strong reported numbers frequently do not demonstrate temporal understanding at all. Papers that ablate by shuffling frame order and observe little accuracy change have made this point repeatedly. The architectural responses are spatiotemporal patches (3-D tubelets spanning several frames, so motion is inside a token rather than across tokens), aggressive temporal pooling of per-frame features, memory mechanisms that compress older frames while keeping recent ones detailed, and separate handling of the audio track, which frequently carries more of the semantic content than the pixels do. None of these is settled. Evaluation and documented weaknesses Being precise about what VLMs do reliably versus unreliably matters more here than in most sections, because demo quality substantially overstates measured quality. Capability State as of the early-2025 literature Scene description, object presence Solid reliably good on natural images Document / screenshot OCR Much improved and genuinely useful, but degrades on small, dense, rotated or low-contrast text; errors are silent Chart and diagram interpretation Reads labels and trends; unreliable at extracting precise values Counting Weak beyond small numbers; poor with occlusion or clutter Precise spatial relations Weak left/right, above/below, containment are frequently wrong Compositional binding (which attribute on which object) Weak the direct inheritance of the CLIP-era limitation Object hallucination Persistent objects reported that are not present, biased toward co-occurrence priors Fine-grained recognition (species, parts, defects) Varies by domain; specialist models still win Object hallucination has a clean diagnostic and a clean cause. The POPE protocol (Li et al., 2023) simply asks yes/no questions about whether specific objects appear, including objects that plausibly co-occur with the scene but are absent. Models say yes too often. The mechanism is language priors overriding visual evidence: the LLM has learned that kitchens contain refrigerators, and when visual evidence is weak or the visual tokens are diluted, the prior wins. This is the multimodal instance of the general grounding problem, and it is why a VLM's confident description should not be treated as an observation. Benchmark hygiene is worse here than in text. Multiple-choice VQA benchmarks are notoriously gameable a text-only model given just the question and options, with no image at all, scores far above chance on several popular ones, because of answer priors and question phrasing. Any VLM benchmark result without a blind text-only baseline should be discounted. Contamination is severe (public benchmark images are all over the web), and LLM-judged free-form evaluation imports the judge biases of section 13 plus a new one: the judge usually cannot see the image either. What to trust. Evaluations that are hard to shortcut free-form OCR against exact ground truth, held-out document understanding, adversarially-constructed spatial and compositional sets like Winoground, and blind-baseline-controlled VQA are meaningful. Aggregate leaderboard scores on saturated multiple-choice benchmarks are close to noise for frontier-model comparison. Gotcha The recurring misconception is that a VLM sees the image the way you do and then reasons about it. What actually reaches the language model is a few hundred to a few thousand vectors produced by an encoder that was trained usually with a contrastive objective on web captions to make an image similar to its caption, and nothing in that objective ever required preserving which object an attribute belongs to, how many there are, or precisely where they sit. The encoder is an aggressive lossy compressor tuned for semantic gist, and the LLM cannot recover information the projector was never handed. This explains the whole cluster of failures at once: counting, spatial relations, attribute binding and small-text OCR all fail for the same upstream reason, and all of them get worse as resolution drops. Two practical consequences. First, when a VLM misreads a chart, prompting harder rarely helps increase the resolution or crop the region, because the fix is upstream of the language model. Second, treat a VLM's description as a hypothesis rather than a measurement: for anything requiring precise counts, coordinates, or exact text, verify with a specialist tool rather than trusting fluent output that carries no signal about how much the encoder threw away.

Language modeling settled on one paradigm autoregressive next-token prediction more than five years ago and has not seriously revisited it. Continuous-domain generation did not settle. Between 2014 and 2022 the field cycled through variational autoencoders, adversarial networks, autoregressive pixel models and normalizing flows before diffusion displaced nearly all of them for images, and as of the early-2025 literature the formulation is still moving, toward flow matching and toward transformer backbones, with autoregressive token models mounting a genuine challenge for video. This section covers why each earlier paradigm lost, how diffusion actually works, and where the current disagreements are. The landscape before diffusion Every generative model is trying to sample from a data distribution it only sees examples of. They differ in whether they model the density explicitly, whether sampling is one shot or iterative, and what the training objective actually optimizes and those choices determine the failure modes. Family Training objective Sampling Characteristic failure VAE (Kingma Welling, 2013) Evidence lower bound reconstruction plus a KL term One forward pass from a latent Blurry samples; the likelihood term rewards averaging GAN (Goodfellow et al., 2014) Minimax game against a discriminator One forward pass Mode collapse; unstable, non-convergent training Autoregressive (PixelCNN, image tokens) Exact likelihood, factorized over positions Sequential one element at a time Slow sampling; imposed raster ordering Normalizing flow (Rezende Mohamed, 2015) Exact likelihood by change of variables One invertible pass Invertibility constrains architecture; weak sample quality per parameter Diffusion Denoising regression a simple MSE Iterative, tens to thousands of steps Slow sampling (largely fixed); high training cost The VAE's blurriness is a direct consequence of its objective. Maximizing likelihood under a Gaussian decoder means minimizing squared error to the data, and when several outputs are plausible, the squared-error optimum is their average. Averaging faces gives you a blurred face. Nothing is broken; the model is correctly optimizing an objective that does not reward committing to one mode. The GAN's problem is that it has no objective in the usual sense. Generator and discriminator play a minimax game whose solution is a Nash equilibrium, not a minimum, so the loss went down carries no information about progress the two losses are supposed to stay balanced. Two pathologies follow. Mode collapse : the generator finds a small set of outputs that reliably fool the current discriminator and abandons the rest of the distribution, and since it is never penalized for outputs it does not produce, this is a stable strategy rather than a bug. Instability : if the discriminator gets too strong its gradients vanish, if too weak they are uninformative, and the balance is delicate enough that the GAN literature accumulated a large body of stabilization tricks (spectral normalization, gradient penalties, progressive growing) which helped without ever making training routine. At their peak StyleGAN (Karras et al., 2018) and successors GANs produced superb faces and remained hard to train and hard to condition on open-ended text. Why diffusion won. It trades one hard problem for many easy ones. Instead of learning to map noise to an image in a single leap, it learns to remove a small amount of noise, and iterates. The training objective is a plain regression loss stable, monotone, no adversary, no equilibrium. Because it is trained to reconstruct across the entire noise schedule on every real example, it has no mechanism for mode collapse: dropping a region of the data distribution directly raises the loss. It conditions on text cleanly, and it scales predictably with data and compute. The one thing it gave up single-pass sampling is precisely what the last three years of sampler and distillation research has been clawing back. Denoising diffusion, mechanically The formulation traces to Sohl-Dickstein et al. (2015), which framed generation as reversing a gradual noising process borrowed from nonequilibrium thermodynamics. It became practical with Ho et al. (2020), Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM), which simplified the objective into something that trains reliably. The forward process is fixed, has no parameters, and is not learned. Over T steps, Gaussian noise is progressively added to an image until nothing of the original remains: q(x_t | x_{t-1}) = N( sqrt(1 - beta_t) * x_{t-1}, beta_t * I ) # beta_t is a small variance schedule, increasing with t. # The scaling by sqrt(1 - beta_t) keeps total variance bounded. The key algebraic fact is that this composes in closed form , so you never simulate the chain. Defining alpha_t = 1 - beta_t and abar_t as the running product of alphas up to t: q(x_t | x_0) = N( sqrt(abar_t) * x_0, (1 - abar_t) * I ) # equivalently, sampling directly: x_t = sqrt(abar_t) * x_0 + sqrt(1 - abar_t) * eps, eps ~ N(0, I) This is what makes training cheap: sample a real image, sample a random timestep t, sample noise, and jump straight to x_t in one line. Each training example touches one timestep, chosen uniformly, so a single pass costs no more than any other supervised regression. The reverse process is what is learned. Each reverse step is also approximately Gaussian when the forward steps are small this is the property that makes the whole scheme work, and the reason T is large so a network need only predict its mean: p_theta(x_{t-1} | x_t) = N( mu_theta(x_t, t), sigma_t^2 * I ) FORWARD q fixed, no parameters, closed form add Gaussian noise: x_t = abar_t x_0 + (1 abar_t) x_0 clean x_1 slightly noisy x_t x_{T-1} x_T pure noise learned step: predict _ (x_t, t), subtract it, add _t noise REVERSE p_ the neural network; sampling runs right to left Latent diffusion runs this whole chain on VAE latents, not pixels same loop, far fewer values per step. Diffusion as two opposing traversals of the same noise ladder: the forward direction is a fixed Gaussian corruption you can jump to in one step, while only the reverse direction is learned, one denoising step at a time. The crucial reframing: the network predicts the noise, not the image. Ho et al. showed that parameterizing the network to output the noise eps that was added, rather than the mean or the clean image, reduces the variational objective to a plain mean-squared error and works dramatically better in practice: # training step, in full x_0 ~ data t ~ Uniform(1..T) eps ~ N(0, I) x_t = sqrt(abar_t) * x_0 + sqrt(1 - abar_t) * eps loss = || eps - eps_theta(x_t, t) ||^2 # that is the whole objective Why noise prediction beats image prediction, since this is the part that is genuinely non-obvious. The two are algebraically equivalent given x_t and either quantity you can solve for the other so the difference is entirely about optimization. At high noise levels x_t is nearly pure noise and the clean image is almost unconstrained, so an image-predicting network is asked to solve a near-impossible problem and is dominated by loss from that regime. Predicting the noise instead is a task of roughly uniform difficulty across timesteps, so the loss is better conditioned and every timestep contributes usable gradient. There is also an interpretation, made precise in the next subsection, in which predicting the noise is predicting the direction of steepest ascent in data density a local, learnable quantity rather than a global one. Later work introduced v-prediction , an interpolation between the two parameterizations that behaves better at the extreme ends of the schedule and is standard in high-resolution and distilled models. The score-based view Song Ermon (2019), Generative Modeling by Estimating Gradients of the Data Distribution , arrived at essentially the same algorithm from a different direction, and the unification (Song et al., 2020, Score-Based Generative Modeling through SDEs ) is the conceptual center of the field. What a score function is, in plain terms. The score is the gradient of the log-density with respect to the input: s(x) = grad_x log p(x) . Picture the data distribution as a landscape whose height is probability density real images sit on peaks, noise sits in the flat lowlands. The score is the vector, at any point, pointing uphill toward higher density, together with how steep the slope is. Knowing it means knowing, from any image whatsoever, which direction makes it more image-like. That is exactly what a generative model needs, and it is strictly less information than the density itself: because the gradient of a log kills any constant, the score is unaffected by the normalizing constant that makes explicit density modeling intractable. Sidestepping that constant is the single technical reason score-based modeling is easier than likelihood-based modeling. Given the score you can sample by walking uphill with noise Langevin dynamics: x_{k+1} = x_k + (step/2) * score(x_k) + sqrt(step) * z, z ~ N(0, I) # gradient ascent on log-density, plus noise so you sample the # distribution rather than collapsing onto its single highest mode The difficulty Song Ermon identified, and the fix, is why the noise schedule exists. Real data lies on a thin manifold in a very high-dimensional space, so almost everywhere you might initialize, the density is effectively zero and there is no training data the estimated score there is garbage, and a sampler starting from noise never gets near the manifold. Their fix was to perturb the data with noise at many different scales: large noise smears the distribution across the whole space so the score is defined and learnable far from the data, small noise preserves fine structure near it. Train one network conditioned on the noise level, then sample by annealing from large noise to small. That is the same procedure as DDPM, derived from a different starting point. The connection is exact and worth stating. For a Gaussian perturbation, the score of the perturbed distribution is a rescaled version of the added noise: grad_x log q(x_t | x_0) = -(x_t - sqrt(abar_t) x_0) / (1 - abar_t) = -eps / sqrt(1 - abar_t) # So a network trained to predict eps IS a scaled score model. # DDPM's noise prediction and score matching are the same thing. The SDE framing generalizes both. Taking the step size to zero turns the discrete Markov chain into a continuous-time stochastic differential equation, with a corresponding reverse-time SDE that requires only the score to simulate. It also yields a deterministic probability flow ODE with the same marginals at every time, which is what licenses deterministic samplers and the whole toolbox of off-the-shelf ODE solvers. This is the view under which DDPM, score matching, DDIM and (nearly) flow matching are one family with different parameterizations. Samplers: trading steps for quality Training fixes the model; sampling is a separate algorithmic choice made afterward, and it is where most of the practical speedup of the last few years came from. The same trained network can be sampled in 1000 steps or 20. Sampler Nature Typical steps Notes DDPM ancestral Stochastic 250 1000 The original; faithful, slow, noise injected each step DDIM (Song et al., 2020) Deterministic 20 100 Non-Markovian reformulation; enables inversion and latent interpolation DPM-Solver (Lu et al., 2022) Deterministic, higher-order 10 25 Exploits the ODE's semi-linear structure; a strong default Ancestral / Euler-a Stochastic 20 50 Added noise can mask small errors; less reproducible Distilled (consistency, adversarial) Learned few-step 1 8 Requires a distillation run; some diversity loss DDIM is the important conceptual step. Song et al. constructed a family of non-Markovian forward processes with the same marginals as DDPM's, which means a DDPM-trained network can be sampled under any of them without retraining. Setting the stochasticity parameter to zero gives a fully deterministic map from the initial noise to the image. Three consequences follow: sampling can take much larger steps because there is no injected noise to re-randomize, the initial noise becomes a genuine latent code (the same seed always gives the same image, and interpolating seeds interpolates images), and the process is invertible, so a real image can be mapped back to the noise that would produce it which is the basis of most diffusion editing methods. The general tradeoff is that fewer steps means more discretization error. Solving an ODE with fewer, larger steps accumulates truncation error; visually this shows up as lost fine detail, softened texture, and sometimes structural artifacts. Higher-order solvers buy accuracy per step and are why 15 25 steps is now routine where 250 once was. Below roughly ten steps, generic solvers break down and you need distillation consistency models (Song et al., 2023) train a network to map any point on a trajectory directly to its endpoint, and adversarial distillation methods add a discriminator to sharpen few-step output. Distillation reliably costs some diversity, which is easy to miss because the individual samples still look good. Classifier-free guidance Unconditional diffusion produces plausible images of nothing in particular. Making conditioning actually bind so a prompt is followed rather than loosely suggested was the missing ingredient for text-to-image, and classifier-free guidance (Ho Salimans, 2021) supplied it. It is arguably the highest-impact-per-line-of-code idea in the area. The predecessor, classifier guidance (Dhariwal Nichol, 2021), pushed samples toward a class by adding the gradient of a separately-trained classifier one that had to be trained on noisy images at every noise level, since that is what it would see. It worked and it demonstrated that diffusion could beat GANs on ImageNet, but requiring an auxiliary noise-aware classifier was a serious practical burden and does not extend naturally to free-form text. Classifier-free guidance removes the classifier entirely. During training, drop the conditioning at random (typically 10% of examples), so one network learns both the conditional and unconditional score. At sampling time, run both and extrapolate along the difference: eps_hat = eps_uncond + w * ( eps_cond - eps_uncond ) # w = 0 -> unconditional # w = 1 -> ordinary conditional # w 1 -> extrapolate PAST the conditional prediction # typical text-to-image: w in 5..12 The interpretation is what makes it memorable. The difference eps_cond - eps_uncond is the direction that the condition adds whatever distinguishes an image matching this prompt from an image . Amplifying it beyond w = 1 means moving further in the direction of prompt-ness than the model's own conditional estimate. In the implicit-classifier view, this is sampling proportional to p(x|c) * p(c|x)^(w-1) upweighting regions where a classifier would be confident about the condition. The fidelity/diversity tradeoff is unavoidable and directly controlled by w . Low guidance gives varied, sometimes prompt-ignoring images. High guidance gives strong prompt adherence with less variety across seeds, oversaturated colors, blown-out contrast, and eventually cartoonish artifacts. It is not a quality knob but a distributional one: it deliberately samples from a sharpened distribution rather than the true one, concentrating mass on high-probability-of-condition regions and abandoning the tails. The practical costs are two: sampling requires two forward passes per step (roughly doubling inference cost, though guidance distillation folds the effect back into a single pass), and dynamic thresholding or rescaling is usually needed to keep the high-guidance saturation artifacts in check. Latent diffusion and what made high resolution feasible Pixel-space diffusion at 512 512 means the network operates on 786,432 values at every one of many denoising steps. That is why early high-resolution systems used cascades of super-resolution diffusion models generate at 64 64, upsample with another diffusion model, upsample again which works but stacks models and error. Latent diffusion (Rombach et al., 2022, High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models , the basis of Stable Diffusion) makes a clean observation: most of an image's bits are imperceptible high-frequency detail, and a VAE can compress that away almost losslessly to the eye. So train an autoencoder once, then run the entire diffusion process in its latent space: 512 x 512 x 3 pixels = 786,432 values - VAE encoder, f = 8 64 x 64 x 4 latent = 16,384 values ~48x fewer # diffuse and denoise entirely in latent space, then decode once The division of labor is the elegant part. The autoencoder handles perceptual compression texture, grain, the exact pixel values trained with a combination of reconstruction, perceptual and adversarial losses so it stays sharp rather than blurry. The diffusion model then handles semantic composition in a space where every dimension carries meaning, and is no longer spending the bulk of its capacity modeling high-frequency detail the autoencoder can reconstruct anyway. The compute reduction of roughly an order of magnitude is what put text-to-image training and inference within reach of a single consumer GPU, and that accessibility more than any quality gain is why Stable Diffusion's release reshaped the field. The costs are real and visible in practice. The autoencoder is a hard ceiling: anything it cannot reconstruct, the diffusion model cannot generate, which is the underlying reason small text, fine repeating patterns and faces at small scale in an image are characteristically mangled. Higher compression factors are faster but degrade more, and the latent channel count is a genuine quality lever later systems increased it precisely to lift this ceiling. Architecture and text conditioning The U-Net was the original backbone and is a good fit for the task. An encoder path downsamples while widening channels, a decoder path upsamples back, and skip connections carry high-resolution features across at matching scales. Since the network's job is to output something the same shape as its input, with both global structure and fine detail preserved, the skip connections are doing essential work. Diffusion U-Nets add self-attention at the lower-resolution levels (where the token count is affordable) and inject the timestep through sinusoidal embeddings and adaptive normalization, so one network can behave differently at different noise levels. Diffusion transformers replaced it because they scale better. Peebles Xie (2022), Scalable Diffusion Models with Transformers (DiT), discarded the U-Net for a plain transformer over latent patches the ViT recipe of section 19 applied to noisy latents conditioning on timestep and class through adaptive layer norm whose scale and shift are regressed from the conditioning vector (adaLN-zero, initialized so each block starts as the identity). Their central result is the one that mattered: image quality improves smoothly and predictably with transformer compute, the same clean scaling behavior that section 2 describes for language models, and DiT beat the U-Net baselines at matched compute. The consequence is that image generation inherits the entire scaling and distributed-training toolkit built for LLMs, which is why frontier image and video systems as of the early-2025 literature are transformer-based rather than U-Net-based. Text conditioning is cross-attention on frozen text-encoder embeddings. A text encoder produces a sequence of embeddings, and every block of the denoiser cross-attends to them queries from the image latents, keys and values from the text. Which encoder is used matters more than one might expect: Imagen (Saharia et al., 2022) found that a large frozen text-only language model (T5-XXL) gave better prompt adherence than a CLIP text encoder, and that scaling the text encoder improved image-text alignment more than scaling the diffusion model. The reason is intuitive a CLIP text encoder was trained to summarize a caption into one vector for matching, not to represent compositional structure. Later systems commonly concatenate several encoders' outputs to get both alignment and linguistic depth. The persistent weakness of the whole approach is attribute binding: cross-attention supplies a bag of text features without reliably enforcing which adjective attaches to which noun, which is why a red cube on a blue sphere still fails often enough to be a standard test case. Flow matching and rectified flow The formulation increasingly replacing standard diffusion as of the early-2025 literature is flow matching (Lipman et al., 2022) and the closely related rectified flow (Liu et al., 2022). The reframing is simple enough to state in a line: instead of a noising process to be reversed, define a straight path from noise to data and learn the velocity field along it. # Linear interpolation path between noise x_1 and data x_0 x_t = (1 - t) * x_0 + t * x_1 # t in [0, 1] # Target velocity is constant along the path -- it's a straight line v_target = x_1 - x_0 loss = || v_theta(x_t, t) - v_target ||^2 # Sampling: integrate the learned velocity field backwards x = x_1 for t from 1 to 0: x = x - v_theta(x, t) * dt The motivation is trajectory straightness. The probability-flow ODE induced by a standard diffusion noise schedule follows a curved trajectory, and curvature is exactly what forces a solver to take many small steps a straight line can be traversed in one. Flow matching constructs the interpolation to be straight by design, so few-step sampling degrades far more gracefully, and rectified flow adds a reflow procedure that retrains on the model's own trajectories to straighten them further. Its practical appeal is as much simplicity as speed. There is no noise schedule to design, no variance-preserving versus variance-exploding choice, no signal-to-noise reparameterization a linear interpolation and an MSE on velocity. It also generalizes: the endpoints need not be Gaussian noise and data, so the same machinery covers translation between two arbitrary distributions. It is best understood as a different, better-conditioned parameterization within the same continuous-time family as diffusion rather than a rival paradigm; several published formulations are equivalent up to a change of variables. Adoption in major open text-to-image systems from 2024 onward makes it the default for new work. Autoregressive generation, video, and the open questions The competing paradigm is to tokenize images and model them autoregressively , exactly as text is modeled (section 19.6). Quantize patches to codebook IDs with a VQ model, then predict the sequence with a standard decoder-only transformer. The attraction is unification: one architecture, one objective, one inference stack, and native interleaving of text and images in a single stream, plus the full inherited toolkit of KV caching, speculative decoding and continuous batching from section 22. Axis Diffusion Autoregressive tokens Generation order Global all positions refined together Sequential over a chosen raster order Steps Tens (fewer if distilled), each over the whole image One per token thousands for a high-res image Fidelity ceiling Set by the VAE (if latent) continuous, high Set by the discrete codebook quantization loss Text integration Cross-attention on a separate encoder Native same vocabulary, same stream Editing / inpainting Natural condition on known regions Awkward ordering fights partial conditioning Reuses LLM infrastructure Partially (DiT backbone) Fully Masked or parallel-decoding token models (the MaskGIT line, and later work showing autoregressive image models competitive with diffusion at matched scale) blur this boundary by predicting many tokens per step. The convergence question whether continuous-latent iterative refinement and discrete-token autoregression end up as the same thing under different parameterizations is genuinely open, and the honest summary is that diffusion currently leads on image fidelity while autoregression leads on unification and infrastructure reuse. Video is where this contest matters most, and it is hard for reasons beyond scale. The cost is punishing a 5-second clip at 24fps and 512 512 is over a hundred times a single image, and spatiotemporal attention over that is expensive even in a compressed latent, which is why video systems use 3-D VAEs that compress in time as well as space. The quality problems are distinct from the cost ones: temporal consistency (an object must keep its identity and appearance across frames), physical plausibility (objects should not pass through each other, fluids should behave; models frequently produce locally beautiful and physically impossible motion), long-range coherence (something leaving frame and returning should be the same thing), and controllability of camera and subject motion separately. Evaluation is worse than for images, since no automatic metric captures temporal coherence well and human evaluation of video is slow and expensive. Evaluation Generative image evaluation is measurably weaker than the models it measures, and the standard metric is trusted far past what it supports. Metric Measures Known problems FID Fr chet distance between Inception feature distributions of real and generated sets Biased by sample count; Inception features are an ImageNet artifact; insensitive to some visible defects; gameable Inception Score Confidence and diversity of Inception class predictions No comparison to real data at all; largely superseded CLIP score Image-text embedding similarity Inherits CLIP's compositional blindness; rewards prompt keywords over correct scenes Precision / recall for generative models Fidelity and coverage as separate numbers Better diagnostic than FID; sensitive to the feature extractor Human preference (side-by-side, Elo) What people actually prefer Expensive, slow; rewards saturation and stylistic polish over faithfulness FID's specific flaws are worth knowing because it is quoted everywhere. It models both feature distributions as Gaussians and compares only their means and covariances a strong assumption about a distribution that is not Gaussian. It is biased by sample size, so FID computed on 10k samples is not comparable to FID on 50k, and papers using different protocols are not comparable at all. It inherits whatever an ImageNet-trained Inception network considers salient, which correlates imperfectly with human judgment and mis-measures domains far from ImageNet. It can be improved by changes that do not improve perceived quality matching statistics is not the same as generating well and it says nothing about prompt adherence. Human preference evaluation, for all its cost and its own biases toward contrast and saturation, remains the only measure that has consistently tracked real progress. Gotcha Two things get conflated constantly here, and both are worth separating explicitly. The first is that a diffusion model does not learn to turn noise into an image; it learns to estimate the noise present in a slightly-corrupted image, which by the identity in section 20.3 is a scaled estimate of the score the local direction of increasing data density. Generation is a sampling procedure built on top of that estimate, which is why the same trained weights can be sampled in 1000 steps or 20, why deterministic and stochastic samplers both work, and why sampler choice is a deployment decision rather than a property of the model. The second is FID. It is reported to three decimals and compared across papers that used different sample counts, different resampling filters, and different reference sets, none of which are comparable; it is Gaussian-approximated in an ImageNet feature space; it is sample-size biased; and it is insensitive to failures a human notices instantly while being sensitive to statistical differences nobody can see. A 0.4-point FID improvement is not evidence of anything. Treat FID as a coarse regression check within one codebase and one protocol, and require human preference data or a task-specific measure before believing that one model generates better than another.

Make a model a maintainable service with measurable behavior and a rollback path. How the pieces connect MENTAL MODEL MLOps, deployment observability — from question to evidence 01 Package Version model, data transforms, prompts, index, and runtime. 02 Release Shadow, canary, or gate a controlled cohort. 03 Observe Trace quality, latency, cost, drift, and failures. 04 Recover Roll back compatible artifacts and investigate. Package → Release → Observe → Recover. Each transition is a place where an assumption can be inspected before the next layer of the system compounds it. Version the complete release A model artifact is one component. Record weights, tokenizer, preprocessing, prompts, retrieval index, runtime version, and configuration. Releasing a new embedding model without rebuilding a compatible index can break retrieval even when both components work independently. Define service objectives Choose meaningful targets for availability, latency, quality, and cost. Measure first-token and full-response time separately for streaming generation. Track queue time, model execution, retrieval, and tool calls so bottlenecks are attributable. Sample traces carefully to avoid collecting unnecessary sensitive content. Stage the rollout Use offline evaluation, shadow traffic, canary deployment, and controlled experiments where suitable. A rollback must restore compatible artifacts and configuration. Health checks should exercise a real inference path without treating a successful response as proof of semantic quality. Monitor changing behavior Input drift describes changing inputs; concept drift describes a changing relationship between inputs and targets. Delayed labels complicate monitoring. Establish feedback collection, incident ownership, and scheduled evaluation. Alert on user-impacting failures rather than every harmless statistical movement. Worked example A retrieval service’s latency doubles after a release. A trace shows model inference unchanged but index search increased from 30 ms to 400 ms. Rolling back the model alone does nothing; the index configuration and query pipeline are part of the release. What goes wrong A model loading successfully is not an end-to-end deployment test. A public endpoint must be tested through the same route and authentication boundaries users encounter. Check your understanding What makes a model rollback incomplete? Reveal the explanation Restoring weights while leaving incompatible prompts, preprocessing, tokenizer, or retrieval index can preserve the failure or create a different one. An operating model for mlops, deployment & observability A deployment is a configuration of interacting artifacts, not a model file. Tokenizers, feature pipelines, vector indexes, prompts, model weights, tool permissions, and runtime versions can all change behavior. Treat the full configuration as a versioned release unit. The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test. Worked system: a rollback that restores the wrong system A release changes an embedding model but leaves the old vector index in place. The service remains available, requests return answers, and a generic health check passes—yet retrieval quality collapses because query and document vectors now live in incompatible spaces. Rolling back only the model weights may not fix it if the index, tokenizer, prompt, feature definitions, or configuration changed with the release. Version the release as a set of compatible artifacts. A canary should exercise the same authorization, retrieval, inference, and monitoring path as a user. Define rollback before rollout, then rehearse it with a representative request. Availability is necessary; semantic behavior, cost, and evidence quality need their own signals. Notebook: Instrument one request end to end Make rollback a rehearsed operation. Confirm that a candidate release can serve a real representative request through the same route, authorization, and monitoring path as a user. trace = {"queue_ms": queue, "retrieve_ms": retrieve, "prefill_ms": prefill, "decode_ms": decode} assert sum(trace.values()) = latency_slo_ms # Attribute latency before changing infrastructure. What to test next. 1. Package: Version model, data transforms, prompts, index, and runtime. 2. Release: Shadow, canary, or gate a controlled cohort. 3. Observe: Trace quality, latency, cost, drift, and failures. 4. Recover: Roll back compatible artifacts and investigate. The gotcha. A small inspection script proves only the quantities it prints. Preserve units, shapes, versions, and the input fixture beside its output. A rigorous way to practice Package. Version model, data transforms, prompts, index, and runtime. Release. Estimate memory and workload cost with explicit assumptions and measurements. How the pieces connect MENTAL MODEL Capacity planning, latency AI economics — from question to evidence 01 Define demand Specify arrival rate, concurrency, quality, and latency target. 02 Model resources Count memory, compute, links, storage, and queue capacity. 03 Measure utilization Observe saturation and tail latency under load. 04 Choose policy Set batching, limits, autoscaling, and fallback behavior. Define demand → Model resources → Measure utilization → Choose policy. Each transition is a place where an assumption can be inspected before the next layer of the system compounds it. Begin with a workload definition Record input/output lengths, concurrency, arrival pattern, model, precision, and quality constraints. A tokens-per-second number without these settings is not a portable performance claim. Prefill and decoding exercise hardware differently, and aggregate throughput can improve while individual latency worsens. Count all memory Inference needs weights, KV cache, activations, workspaces, allocator overhead, and the runtime. Training adds gradients and optimizer state. Quantization metadata and temporary dequantization can reduce expected savings. Sharding distributes some allocations while introducing communication and per-device overhead. Separate peak from useful capacity Peak arithmetic is a theoretical ceiling under specified operations. Sustained performance depends on kernel shape, memory traffic, links, and occupancy. Reserve capacity for bursts and failures. A service operating at maximum utilization may develop unacceptable tail latency. Compare cost at equal quality Compute cost per accepted task or useful output, not just raw tokens. Include retries, evaluator calls, retrieval, storage, networking, engineering, and human review where applicable. Electricity equals power integrated over time; chip TDP is not a measurement of total facility consumption. Worked example A job using eight GPUs for three hours consumes 24 GPU-hours. At an explicitly assumed rate of 2 currency units per GPU-hour, accelerator rental alone is 48 units. This is a scenario calculation, not a current price quote; add the rest of the system’s costs. What goes wrong Comparing a sparse FP4 headline against dense BF16 throughput conflates precision and sparsity. Cost numbers expire as workloads, prices, and implementations change. Check your understanding Can maximizing batch size harm a user-facing service? Reveal the explanation Yes. Waiting to fill batches or processing larger batches can increase per-request latency even if total throughput rises. An operating model for capacity planning, latency & ai economics Capacity planning converts a vague performance goal into explicit tradeoffs. A service can increase total throughput by batching while making individual responses slower; a cheaper numerical format can reduce cost while changing quality; a larger memory pool can prevent failures while increasing idle spend. The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test. Worked system: a throughput gain that violates the service promise Increasing batch size can raise aggregate tokens per second by keeping an accelerator busy. It can also make an individual user wait for a batch to form, increasing time to first token beyond the product target. The same service can honestly report excellent throughput and unacceptable p99 latency. Long prompts, queue bursts, and KV-cache pressure change the operating point again. Define demand before quoting capacity: arrival pattern, prompt and output lengths, concurrency, quality setting, latency objective, and failure behavior. Then measure queue time, prefill, decode, memory peak, and accepted-task cost separately. Capacity planning is the discipline of making those tradeoffs explicit before users experience them as outages. Notebook: Instrument one request end to end Run a load test with realistic prompt lengths and burst patterns. Report admission behavior, p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, memory peak, error rate, and cost per accepted result. trace = {"queue_ms": queue, "retrieve_ms": retrieve, "prefill_ms": prefill, "decode_ms": decode} assert sum(trace.values()) = latency_slo_ms # Attribute latency before changing infrastructure. What to test next. 1. Define demand: Specify arrival rate, concurrency, quality, and latency target. 2. Model resources: Count memory, compute, links, storage, and queue capacity. 3. Measure utilization: Observe saturation and tail latency under load. 4. Choose policy: Set batching, limits, autoscaling, and fallback behavior. The gotcha. A small inspection script proves only the quantities it prints. Preserve units, shapes, versions, and the input fixture beside its output. A rigorous way to practice Define demand. Observe saturation and tail latency under load. Choose policy. Set batching, limits, autoscaling, and fallback behavior. Run a load test with realistic prompt lengths and burst patterns.
