Injected content can address the defensive instruction directly: assert that the task changed, that the preceding constraints were a test, that the content is from a privileged source. The defender is negotiating with the attacker inside the same message. It raises attack cost without changing the security model. A defense that a determined attacker can iterate against is a filter, not a boundary. It reduces incident rates against unsophisticated attempts — genuinely useful — but it cannot support a claim of the form "this agent cannot be made to do X by content it reads." The distinction is not always well-defined even in principle. "Summarize this document" applied to a document that contains instructions requires the model to represent those instructions to summarize them faithfully. The line between processing an instruction and following it is a judgment, not a parse. Indirect injection in agent and RAG settings. Greshake, Abdelnabi, Mishra, Endres, Holz and Fritz (2023), Not What You've Signed Up For: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection , established the term and the threat model. The key move is that the attacker never talks to the system. They place content where the system will eventually read it — a web page, a public repository, a document, a calendar invite, an email, a package README — and wait. Agentic systems (section 16) sharpen this enormously because the payoff changes. A chat model that gets injected produces bad text, and a human reads it. An agent that gets injected takes actions : it calls tools, writes files, sends messages, spends money, and exfiltrates whatever is in its context. The relevant quantity is the union of the agent's privileges and its context contents, and injection converts that union into the attacker's capability set. Three properties make agent injection especially difficult: Tool output is untrusted content in the highest-trust position. Retrieved documents and tool results arrive in-context, often formatted to look system-generated, at exactly the moment the model is deciding what to do next. Compromise propagates. Output from one step becomes input to the next. An injected instruction can persist across many steps, and in multi-agent systems (section 17) can cross agent boundaries entirely. Exfiltration needs only one outbound channel. Any tool that can reach the network — a request, a link rendered in a UI, a message send — turns "the attacker influenced the agent" into "the attacker read the agent's context." Defenses and Their Limits An honest accounting. Every entry below reduces risk; none is complete, and the difference between "raises attack cost" and "provides a boundary" is the most important column. Defense Mechanism Real limit Boundary or cost-raiser? Safety training (RLHF, Constitutional AI) Train refusal on harmful-request distributions Generalizes imperfectly off-distribution, which is exactly where attacks live (11.2). Trades against helpfulness — over-refusal is a real, measurable cost Cost-raiser Input classifiers Separate model scores the input before the main model sees it A second model with its own adversarial surface. Attacks can be optimized against the classifier too; base rates make false positives expensive Cost-raiser Output classifiers Score the response before it is returned Better positioned — judges the actual harmful artifact rather than guessing intent — but latency-costly, and weaker against streaming or partial-output channels Cost-raiser Constitutional classifiers Classifiers trained on synthetic data generated from explicit written rules, so coverage can be expanded by editing the rules rather than collecting new attacks. Sharma et al. (2025), Constitutional Classifiers , reported large reductions in jailbreak success under extended red-teaming, with attention to keeping over-refusal and compute overhead bounded Universal jailbreaks became much harder to find in that evaluation, not impossible in principle. Bounded to the harm domains the constitution enumerates; adds inference cost. Adversaries adapt Strong cost-raiser Spotlighting / delimiting Mark untrusted spans explicitly — delimiters, datamarking, encoding — so the model can distinguish them Measurably helps and is worth doing. Still a learned tendency, not enforcement: the model may still follow marked content, and delimiter handling is itself attackable Cost-raiser Privilege separation at the harness Constrain what the agent can do , independent of what it decides: least-privilege tool scopes, allowlisted destinations, human approval for irreversible actions, isolating untrusted content in sub-contexts whose output is treated as data Does not prevent the model being fooled; bounds the blast radius when it is. Costs autonomy and adds friction — the more useful the agent, the more privileges it wants The only real boundary in this table Perplexity / anomaly filtering Reject inputs that look unlike natural text Keyed on an incidental property of one attack family; fluency-constrained attacks evade it directly (11.4) Cost-raiser, narrow The design conclusion for agentic systems. Because the model layer offers no boundary, the defensible architecture treats the model as an untrusted component: assume it can be induced to attempt anything within its privileges, and place the security-relevant controls outside it. This is unsatisfying — it caps agent autonomy for reasons unrelated to capability — but it is the only part of the stack where a guarantee can currently be stated. Cascading cost-raisers is genuinely valuable in practice; it is defense in depth, and it should be described as such rather than as a solution. Automated Red-Teaming Manual red-teaming has an obvious scaling problem: it is bounded by skilled human hours, it is unevenly distributed across the risk surface, and it does not rerun cheaply on every checkpoint. Perez, Huang, Song, Cai, Ring, Aslanides, Glaese, McAleese and Irving (2022), Red Teaming Language Models with Language Models , established the alternative — use a language model to generate the test cases, and a classifier to score the responses. loop: red_lm - generate candidate test inputs target_lm - produce responses classifier - score responses for the harm of interest keep the successful cases; use them to steer generation (zero-shot - few-shot on successes - SFT - RL against the classifier) They generated large numbers of test cases and surfaced failure categories including offensive outputs, leakage of memorized training data, and distributional harms — plus the useful structural finding that failures cluster: successful attacks are not scattered uniformly but concentrate in identifiable regions of input space, which is what makes automated search efficient in the first place. The central limitation is the classifier. The whole loop optimizes against the scorer, so it inherits every blind spot the scorer has, and RL against it will find those blind spots specifically — this is Goodhart's law (section 11.2) applied to the red-teaming pipeline itself. Automated red-teaming therefore reliably finds failures of the kinds the classifier already recognizes , and is systematically weakest on novel harm categories, which are the ones most worth finding. The practical posture is a portfolio: automated search for coverage and regression testing, human red-teamers for the categories no classifier has been built for yet, and external/expert red-teaming for specialized domains. The Vision Precedent: A Problem That Was Never Solved The most useful calibration available comes from a literature that predates LLMs by a decade. Szegedy, Zaremba, Sutskever, Bruna, Erhan, Goodfellow and Fergus (2013), Intriguing Properties of Neural Networks , showed that imperceptibly small, deliberately chosen perturbations to an image flip a classifier's prediction with high confidence — and that these perturbations transfer between models trained on different subsets of data. Goodfellow, Shlens and Szegedy (2014), Explaining and Harnessing Adversarial Examples , gave the influential linear explanation: in high dimensions, many tiny coordinate-wise changes aligned with the weight vector sum to a large change in the pre-activation, so adversarial vulnerability may be a consequence of local linearity in high-dimensional space rather than an exotic pathology. They introduced the fast gradient sign method: x_adv = x + epsilon * sign( grad_x L(theta, x, y) ) Small per-pixel change (epsilon), aligned with the loss gradient, summing to a large change in the logits. What happened next is the part to internalize. A decade of intense effort followed, on a problem that is far easier than the LLM case: the input space is continuous, the threat model can be formalized as a norm ball, the task is classification with a well-defined correct answer, and success is measurable without a judge model. The outcome: A long sequence of proposed defenses were broken shortly after publication, frequently by showing that the defense obscured gradients rather than removing vulnerability. Athalye, Carlini and Wagner (2018), Obfuscated Gradients Give a False Sense of Security , systematized this and broke most defenses from a single major conference in one paper. Adversarial training — training on adversarial examples, formalized by Madry, Makelov, Schmidt, Tsipras and Vladu (2017) as a min-max robust optimization problem — became the one method that reliably provides real robustness. It works, and it is expensive, and it delivers robustness within the specific threat model trained against while generalizing poorly outside it. Certified defenses provide provable guarantees, at accuracy costs and within norm-bounded threat models that do not describe realistic adversaries. A documented robustness-accuracy tradeoff persists. On the standard benchmarks, robust accuracy under strong attack remains far below clean accuracy, years on. The inference for LLMs. The easier problem, with a formalizable threat model and a decade of concentrated attention, produced mitigation rather than solution. The LLM version has a discrete input space, no norm-bounded threat model, no crisp definition of "correct behavior," an unbounded semantic attack surface, and evaluation that depends on a judge. Nothing about this suggests it will go better. This is not an argument for fatalism — mitigations demonstrably raise attack cost, and cost matters enormously in practice — it is an argument that the correct target is bounded, measured, decaying risk under adaptive attack , and that any claim of the form "jailbreaking is solved" should be read as a claim about the attacks that have been tried so far. Why These Results Are Hard to Compare Attack success rate (ASR) is the field's headline number and it is far less comparable across papers than its ubiquity suggests. The problems are methodological and mostly unresolved as of the early-2025 literature. Source of incomparability What varies Effect on reported ASR The judge String-matching on refusal phrases, a classifier, an LLM judge with an unstated rubric, or human raters Largest single factor. String-matching counts any non-refusal as success, inflating scores; a strict human rubric on actual harmfulness deflates them. The same transcripts can differ by tens of points Harmful-vs-not threshold Whether "started to comply" counts, or only substantively harmful content Systematic, direction depends on the paper's framing Attack budget Queries, restarts, optimization steps, human iterations — often unreported ASR is a function of budget; a number without a budget is not interpretable Behavior set Which harmful requests are in the benchmark, and their difficulty mix Non-comparable across papers using different sets Defense stack Bare model weights vs the deployed product with its classifiers and system prompt Huge. Open-weight bare-model numbers do not describe deployed systems, and are often reported as if they do Adaptivity Whether the attack was tuned against the specific defense being evaluated Non-adaptive evaluation systematically overstates defenses — the core lesson of Athalye et al. (2018) Standardized harnesses — HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024) is the most widely used — exist to fix exactly this by fixing the behavior set, the judge, and the attack implementations, and are a real improvement. They do not fully solve it: the standard's own judge becomes the definition of success, and methods can drift toward what that judge rewards. When reading any ASR figure, the four questions that determine whether it means anything: which judge, what budget, which behavior set, bare model or deployed system . A paper that does not answer all four has reported a number, not a measurement. Gotcha Claims that a jailbreak class has been "fixed" have not once survived sustained attention from a determined adversary — and the reason is structural, not a matter of insufficient effort. Defenses are evaluated against the attacks that exist when the defense is built; attackers optimize against the defense that exists when the attack is built. That asymmetry is permanent, and the vision literature (11.8) already ran this experiment for a decade on a strictly easier problem and ended in mitigation, not solution. Two specific traps follow. First, non-adaptive evaluation : a defense tested against pre-existing attacks measures how well it handles yesterday's adversary, which is why so many published vision defenses fell to a single paper that simply re-optimized against them. Second, and more consequential in practice, treating prompt-injection mitigations as if they were boundaries : spotlighting, delimiting and defensive instructions all reduce incident rates and are worth deploying, but none establishes a trust boundary, because instructions and data share one channel with no enforced separation. If an agentic system's security argument rests on the model reliably declining injected instructions, it has no security argument — it has a filter. The boundary, if there is one, lives in what the harness permits the agent to do, not in what the model decides.

Evaluation is the least glamorous topic in this reference and has a reasonable claim to being the field's binding constraint. Every other section depends on it: scaling laws (section 2) are fits to measured loss, RLHF (section 9) optimizes a learned proxy for measured preference, reasoning methods (section 10) are justified by benchmark deltas, and alignment (section 11) is definitionally about whether a measured objective matches an intended one. If the measurement is wrong, the optimization is pointed somewhere unintended and the conclusions drawn from it are unsupported. The uncomfortable summary: a substantial fraction of published capability comparisons are not decidable from the evidence given — because of contamination, because the judge is doing more work than the model, or because a 1.5-point delta on 500 examples is inside the noise. This section is about how to tell which claims survive. Why Evaluation Is Genuinely Hard The difficulty is not laziness. It is structural, and worth decomposing, because each cause implies a different partial fix. The output space is open-ended. Classification has a finite label set and an unambiguous correct answer. "Write a function that does X," "summarize this filing," "explain this proof" have unbounded valid answers with no enumerable reference set. Any scoring function is a proxy for a judgment nobody has written down. The quantity of interest is unobservable. Nobody wants to know a model's MMLU score. They want to know whether it is useful for some task distribution, and the benchmark is a sample from a proxy for that distribution. This is the same proxy-versus-target structure as section 11's Goodhart framing, and it produces the same pathology: the harder the field optimizes against benchmarks, the less benchmark scores tell you. The measurement instrument is the object under study. LLM-as-judge means the yardstick is made of the same material as the thing being measured, with correlated failure modes (12.4). The test set leaks into the training set. Pretraining corpora are web-scale; benchmarks are published on the web. Contamination is the default state, not the exception (12.6). Capability is multidimensional and gets reported as a scalar. A single number over a heterogeneous benchmark suite hides the fact that models differ qualitatively, not just in rank order. Evaluation is expensive and unrewarded. Building a rigorous benchmark is slow, unglamorous, and gets cited far less than a model that scores well on someone else's. The incentive gradient points away from the bottleneck. The Benchmark Landscape An orientation to the widely-used benchmarks, what each actually measures, and its characteristic failure. Names and years are given only where they are well-established. Benchmark Domain Format What it actually measures / known weakness MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2020, Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding ) 57 subjects, elementary to professional 4-way multiple choice The long-standing default for broad knowledge. Documented label errors and ambiguous items in some subsets; heavily contaminated by now; effectively saturated at the frontier MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024) Same territory, harder 10-way multiple choice Rebuilt to de-saturate MMLU: more distractors (lowering the guessing floor from 25% to 10%), harder reasoning-heavy items, cleaned labels. Still multiple choice, so 12.3's critique applies GPQA (Rein et al., 2023, A Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q A Benchmark ) Graduate biology, physics, chemistry Multiple choice Deliberately constructed so that domain PhDs score high while skilled non-experts with unrestricted web access score far lower — the "Google-proof" design. The most credible small knowledge benchmark, and small enough (a few hundred items in the diamond subset) that error bars are wide GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) Grade-school math word problems Free-form numeric answer Historically the standard chain-of-thought testbed. Saturated at the frontier and contamination-prone. GSM-Symbolic-style work has probed whether models are pattern-matching templates rather than reasoning, by perturbing names and numbers MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021) Competition mathematics Free-form, LaTeX answers requiring equivalence checking Much harder than GSM8K; answer-equivalence checking is a real source of scoring noise. Largely saturated by frontier reasoning models HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021, the Codex paper) Python function synthesis Execution against unit tests Genuinely objective scoring — a real virtue. But only 164 short, self-contained problems, so resolution is poor and per-item noise is large. Heavily contaminated. Not representative of software engineering MBPP (Austin et al., 2021) Basic Python programming Execution against tests Same shape as HumanEval, slightly larger, same limitations SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2023) Real GitHub issues in real Python repositories Apply a patch; run the repo's own test suite The most ecologically valid coding benchmark: multi-file, real codebases, real test suites. Caveats — some issues are solvable by finding the actual fix in repo history, some tests are underspecified, and scores depend heavily on the scaffold (retrieval, tooling, retries), so "model score" is really "model plus harness score". SWE-bench Verified is a human-filtered subset addressing item quality Agentic / long-horizon suites Multi-step tool use, web tasks, computer use Task completion, often programmatically checked The frontier of eval difficulty (12.9). Environment-dependent, high-variance, expensive, and frequently non-reproducible as the underlying environments drift Safety evals Refusal, harm categories, dangerous-capability probes Classifier or human judged Judge-dominated (section 12.9). Over-refusal must be measured alongside refusal or the metric rewards uselessness Two structural observations about this table. First, the benchmarks with the most objective scoring are the least representative — unit tests and numeric answers are crisply checkable precisely because the tasks were constrained to make them so. Second, the field's response to saturation has been to build harder versions of the same format (MMLU to MMLU-Pro, GSM8K to competition math), which raises the ceiling without addressing whether the format measures the right construct (12.8). Multiple Choice vs Generative Evaluation The format choice is not a detail. It determines what is being measured, and multiple choice measures something narrower than it appears to. Multiple choice Generative / free-form Scoring Exact, deterministic, free Requires a checker, a judge, or a human Reproducibility High Depends entirely on the scoring mechanism Guessing floor 1/k — a 4-way benchmark starts at 25%, compressing the usable dynamic range Effectively zero Task realism Low. Nobody deploys a model to pick among four supplied options High. This is what deployment looks like Gameability High — see below Lower, but shifts the attack surface to the judge Cost Trivial Substantial, sometimes dominating research budgets How multiple choice is gamed, without anyone trying to game it. The answer can be recoverable from the option set rather than the question. Distractors written by a different process than the correct answer leave stylistic signatures — length, specificity, hedging. There are well-documented cases in the QA literature of models scoring far above chance on multiple-choice items with the question removed entirely, which is a direct measurement of how much signal lives in the options alone. Position bias exists here too: answer-order permutation changes scores, which is why careful evaluation reports permutation-averaged results. The scoring subtlety that changes leaderboards. Multiple choice can be scored several ways, and they do not agree: (a) Compare log P(option_text) across options - biased toward shorter / higher-frequency option strings (b) Length-normalize: log P(option_text) / num_tokens - corrects (a) partially, changes the ranking (c) Compare P("A"), P("B"), P("C"), P("D") as single next tokens - tests whether the model can follow the FORMAT as much as whether it knows the ANSWER; sensitive to prompt template (d) Generate freely, then parse the choice out of the response - closest to deployment; introduces parsing failures that are often silently scored as wrong Two papers reporting "MMLU" may be using different methods from this list, with different few-shot counts and different prompt templates. Differences of several points arise from these choices alone. This is a large part of why independently-run evaluation harnesses (the EleutherAI lm-evaluation-harness and its descendants) matter: they make the protocol explicit and fixed, so numbers become comparable within a harness even when they are not comparable across papers. LLM-as-Judge For open-ended generation, using a strong model as the evaluator is the dominant approach, because it is the only one that is simultaneously cheap, fast, and better than string overlap. Zheng et al. (2023), Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena , is the standard reference and, importantly, is the paper that both validated the method and documented its biases. Mechanics. Two configurations, with materially different properties: Single-answer grading: judge(question, answer, rubric) - score in 1..10 + cheap, scales linearly, no pairing needed - scores drift between judge versions; poor calibration; heavy clustering on a few values (7 and 8 do a lot of work) Pairwise comparison: judge(question, answer_A, answer_B) - A | B | tie + far more reliable; relative judgment is easier than absolute + converts to a ranking via Elo / Bradley-Terry - quadratic in candidates; position bias must be controlled by running BOTH orders and discarding inconsistent verdicts Reference-guided grading: judge(question, answer, reference_solution) - score + large accuracy gain on math/reasoning where the judge alone would be unreliable - needs a reference, which is the expensive part Documented biases. These are measured effects, not speculation: Bias Effect Mitigation Residual risk Position bias The judge favors one slot (commonly the first) independent of content Evaluate both orders; count only order-consistent verdicts, or average Well-handled if actually done. Frequently is not done Verbosity bias Longer answers score higher at equal quality — the same bias that drives RLHF length inflation (section 11.4) Length-controlled scoring; explicit anti-verbosity rubric instructions Partial. Length correlates with real quality too, so over-correcting is also wrong Self-preference / self-enhancement A judge scores its own outputs, and outputs stylistically similar to its own, above others. Panickssery et al. (2024) tied this to self-recognition Never judge with the model family under evaluation; use a judge panel; anchor to human agreement Substantial and structural. Judges are frontier models, so the pool of eligible judges is small and correlated Style over substance Confident tone, formatting, headers and lists read as quality Rubrics that name the failure explicitly; reference-guided grading Persistent. Judges are poor at catching confident factual errors in domains they are weak in Limited reasoning capacity The judge cannot verify what it could not produce Reference-guided grading; restricting judging to tasks below the judge's ceiling Hard ceiling — this is scalable oversight (section 11.5) in miniature The circularity, stated precisely. Models are increasingly trained against model-generated preference signal (RLAIF, Constitutional AI, section 9) and evaluated by model judges. When training signal and evaluation signal come from the same family of systems, error is correlated rather than independent, and the loop can converge on a shared notion of quality that drifts from human judgment without any measurement registering the drift — nothing in the loop is anchored. Zheng et al. reported strong judge-human agreement (roughly in the ~80% range on their setup, comparable to human-human agreement), which is the reason to use the method, but that agreement is measured on tasks and against humans of a particular kind, and it should be periodically re-measured rather than assumed. The methodological rule: an LLM judge is only as trustworthy as the most recent human-agreement study on that task distribution. Reporting judge scores without a human-agreement anchor is reporting an unvalidated instrument. Human Evaluation and Arena Rankings Human evaluation is the nominal ground truth, and it has its own well-documented pathologies. Treating it as an unimpeachable reference is its own error. Cost and latency. Orders of magnitude more expensive and slower than automated evaluation, which forces small sample sizes, which produces wide confidence intervals (12.9). Annotator disagreement. Inter-annotator agreement on open-ended quality is often modest. Low agreement caps the achievable signal: if two humans agree 70% of the time, no automated metric can be validated beyond that ceiling on that task. Non-experts judging expert output. The critical failure. A crowdworker rating a graduate-level biology answer, a legal argument, or a subtle security review is rating fluency, confidence and structure, because those are the accessible signals. This does not merely add noise — it adds bias , systematically rewarding plausible-sounding wrongness, and it is the origin of the length and confidence biases that propagate into reward models and from there into model behavior. Preference is not quality. Raters reward agreement with their own views (section 11.7's sycophancy result traced directly to this) and pleasant style. Optimizing measured preference optimizes for satisfaction, which overlaps with but is not identical to correctness or usefulness. Arena-style pairwise ranking. The LMSYS Chatbot Arena (Chiang et al., 2024) collects pairwise preferences from anonymous users on their own prompts, with model identities hidden, and fits a rating system — originally Elo, later Bradley-Terry maximum likelihood, which is better behaved because it does not depend on match ordering. Bradley-Terry: P(A beats B) = sigmoid( r_A - r_B ) Fit ratings r by maximum likelihood over all recorded comparisons. Report bootstrap confidence intervals -- models with overlapping intervals are NOT distinguishable, however they are ordered on the page. What the arena measures well: real user prompts rather than benchmark-shaped ones, blind pairwise comparison (which sidesteps brand effects), a very large sample, and continuous updating. It is genuinely hard to contaminate in the training-data sense, since the prompts are live and unpublished at the time. What it does not measure: correctness on anything the median voter cannot check. It is a preference ranking, and it inherits every property of its voter population — self-selected, skewed toward casual and coding-adjacent prompts, unable to verify expert claims. It is measurably sensitive to style, formatting and length, and there is an ongoing methodological debate about how much of the ranking is explained by those. Style-controlled variants of the ranking exist precisely because this concern was substantiated. And because model providers can test candidate checkpoints and choose which to release, there is a selection channel from arena feedback back into model development that is not present in a clean experiment. Read arena rank as "which model do users prefer talking to," which is a real and important quantity, and not as "which model is more capable." Contamination: The Central Methodological Crisis Pretraining corpora are scraped from the web at trillion-token scale. Benchmarks are published on the web, discussed on the web, and reproduced in blog posts, GitHub repositories, tutorials, papers and Stack Overflow answers. The default assumption for any benchmark more than a year old is that it is in the training data , and the burden of proof is on anyone claiming otherwise. Benchmark published publicly Web corpus papers, repos, blogs, tutorials, paraphrases Pretraining data n-gram filters catch verbatim copies only Score rises memorization, not matching capability Saturates, retired headroom is label noise a harder successor is published and re-enters the same loop Held-out / private eval items never published; only scores are loop never closes branch Cost: no external reproduction, no item-level error analysis. months, not years Publishing a benchmark puts it on the path into the next model's pretraining corpus, so scores rise ahead of capability until the benchmark saturates and is replaced; keeping the items private breaks the loop at the cost of external auditability. Contamination arrives through several channels, in rough order of how hard they are to catch: Channel Description Detectability Direct verbatim The test file itself appears in the corpus Highest — n-gram matching finds it if you have corpus access Reformatted copies The same items in tutorials, papers, translated or restructured Low. Defeats exact n-gram matching entirely Solution leakage Worked solutions and explanations are in the corpus even when the items are not Low Source leakage The benchmark was built from public sources (GitHub issues, exam banks) that are themselves in the corpus Low, and it is arguably intrinsic to the benchmark's construction — SWE-bench's use of real repository history is the clean example Indirect / synthetic Synthetic training data generated by a model that itself saw the benchmark Very low. A growing problem as synthetic data scales Iterative overfitting No leakage at all; the community simply makes thousands of design decisions while watching the same test set Undetectable by any contamination method — it is not contamination, it is multiple-comparisons overfitting at community scale Detection methods and their honest limits. N-gram overlap. Check whether long n-grams from test items appear in the corpus. This is what most decontamination pipelines do. It requires corpus access — which third parties evaluating closed models never have — and it is defeated by paraphrase, reformatting and translation. It sets a lower bound on contamination, never an upper bound. Canary strings. A unique GUID embedded in the benchmark file, so a model that can reproduce it demonstrably saw the file. Elegant, and weak in practice: it only catches verbatim ingestion of the original file, is easily stripped by anyone building a training corpus, and its absence proves nothing. Membership inference. Statistical tests for whether a specific example was in training, typically comparing the model's likelihood on the example against a reference distribution. Research on this has repeatedly found that apparent success often reflects distribution shift between the "member" and "non-member" sets rather than genuine memorization detection, and that at LLM pretraining scale — where most examples are seen once or twice — power is low. Treat positive results as suggestive and negative results as nearly uninformative. Behavioral probes. Ask the model to complete a test item given only its beginning, or to reproduce the item that follows a given one in the canonical ordering. Sensitive to strong memorization; blind to weaker forms. Perturbation testing. The most practically useful family. Rewrite items — change names, numbers, surface structure — while preserving difficulty, and compare. A large drop on semantically-equivalent perturbations is strong evidence of memorization or template-matching. Building a fresh parallel test set of the same difficulty is the same idea in stronger form. Why this is worse than it looks. Contamination is not uniform noise. It inflates scores selectively — for models trained on more data, more recently, with less careful decontamination — which is exactly the direction that produces spurious apparent progress. It is undetectable from outside for closed models, since the corpus is unavailable and decontamination claims are unauditable. And it degrades gracefully into nothing: a model that saw a paraphrase once has a small advantage that no test will detect but that still moves a leaderboard when the margins are two points. Saturation and the Benchmark Treadmill Benchmarks have a life cycle, and it has become notably shorter. A benchmark is released as challenging, models improve, headroom compresses, and near the ceiling the remaining gap is dominated by label errors, ambiguous items and formatting artifacts rather than capability — at which point the benchmark measures noise and is retired in favor of a harder one. This ran over roughly a decade for early NLP benchmarks and now runs in months. Three consequences that matter more than the treadmill itself: The ceiling is not 100%. Every benchmark has an effective maximum set by its label error rate. When reported scores approach it, differences between top models are differences in how they handle broken items. This is a common source of "model A beats model B" claims that are pure artifact — and it is why human-verified subsets (SWE-bench Verified, the GPQA diamond set) exist. New benchmarks are built by people who know what current models fail at , which selects for a specific kind of hardness and can bake in assumptions about where the frontier is. Successive benchmarks are not samples from a stable difficulty distribution. Saturation and contamination are hard to distinguish from outside. A benchmark's scores rising sharply can mean capability improved, or that the benchmark leaked. Perturbation testing (12.6) is the main tool for telling them apart, and it is not run often enough. Construct Validity The deepest problem, and the least discussed. Construct validity asks whether a measurement measures the thing it claims to. It is standard vocabulary in psychometrics, where measuring unobservable constructs from observable responses is the entire discipline, and it is largely absent from ML benchmark practice. The gap between a benchmark and its claimed construct opens in several ways at once: The operationalization is narrower than the construct. "Reasoning" gets operationalized as grade-school word problems. Doing those well is evidence of something, but the construct being claimed is far broader than the evidence supports, and the inference from one to the other is usually left implicit. The format contributes variance unrelated to the construct. Prompt template, few-shot count, scoring method and answer-parsing all move scores (12.3). Variance attributable to the instrument is variance not attributable to the model. Shortcuts exist that satisfy the metric without the construct. Answering from option-set artifacts, matching a memorized template, exploiting a weak unit test. This is Goodhart again — with the twist that the shortcut is often invisible unless someone specifically looks for it. Aggregation destroys information. A single average over 57 heterogeneous MMLU subjects is not a measurement of a coherent quantity; it is a weighted sum whose weights were determined by how many items each subject happened to contribute. Ecological validity is rarely established. The link from benchmark performance to usefulness on real task distributions is usually asserted rather than measured. SWE-bench is valuable precisely because it narrowed this gap deliberately. The practical form of the question, for any benchmark: what would it take for a model to score highly here without having the capability being claimed? If that has a short answer, the benchmark has a construct validity problem, whatever its scores show. Held-Out Evals, Agentic Evaluation, and Statistical Rigor Private and held-out evals are the main structural fix for contamination and community overfitting: the test set is never published, evaluation runs through a submission interface, and only aggregate scores are released. This genuinely prevents training-set leakage and multiple-comparisons overfitting. Its costs are real — no error analysis by outside researchers, no independent verification that the items are good, trust concentrated in the maintainer, and slow gradual leakage through repeated submissions if the number of attempts is not limited. Related partial fixes: benchmarks built from material published after a model's training cutoff (temporally held-out), and freshly-generated parallel test sets used once. Agentic and long-horizon evaluation is where the difficulty concentrates as of the early-2025 literature. Additional problems beyond everything above: the score measures the model plus its scaffold and cannot cleanly separate them; environments drift over time so results are not reproducible across months; variance per task is enormous because a single early error cascades; partial credit is ill-defined; and each run is expensive enough that sample sizes stay small exactly where variance is highest. Sandboxing and safety constraints add further divergence between the eval environment and deployment. Statistical rigor is where most reported comparisons fail, and it is the easiest thing to check. Miller (2024), Adding Error Bars to Evals , makes the case directly and gives the standard machinery. The basics: For a benchmark of n items scored 0/1, with observed accuracy p: standard error SE = sqrt( p * (1 - p) / n ) HumanEval, n = 164, p = 0.9: SE = sqrt(0.9 * 0.1 / 164) = 0.023 - ~2.3 points 95% CI is roughly +/- 4.6 points So a 3-point difference on HumanEval is NOT a result. Two further variance sources usually ignored: - sampling variance from temperature 0 (rerun with several seeds) - prompt/template variance (often larger than either of the above) When comparing two models on the SAME items, use a PAIRED test (McNemar / paired bootstrap). Ignoring pairing discards the correlation between models and needlessly widens the interval. The practical consequences: benchmarks with a few hundred items cannot resolve differences smaller than several points, most published tables report no uncertainty at all, and leaderboards present strict orderings among models whose intervals overlap heavily. Add to this the multiple-comparisons problem — evaluating many models on many benchmarks and reporting the notable cells — and a large share of "model A is better than model B" claims in the literature are not supported by the numbers presented, independent of any contamination concern. Gotcha Benchmark contamination invalidates far more comparisons than the field admits, and the reason is that the debate is framed around the wrong question. Arguments focus on whether a specific benchmark was in a specific corpus — unanswerable from outside for any closed model, since the corpus is unavailable and decontamination claims are unauditable. The right question is what contamination does to the comparison : it does not add symmetric noise, it inflates scores selectively for models trained on more data, more recently, with less careful filtering, which is precisely the direction that manufactures the appearance of progress. And n-gram decontamination — the standard mitigation — establishes a lower bound on contamination and never an upper bound, because paraphrases, translations, worked solutions and synthetic data derived from contaminated models all pass through it untouched. Two working rules follow. First, a benchmark score is a claim about a model plus its evaluation protocol plus its data provenance; two papers reporting "MMLU" may share only the name. Second, when a model's advantage on an established benchmark is a few points, the honest default is that you cannot distinguish capability from contamination from noise, and the only cheap test that separates them is perturbation — rewrite the items while preserving difficulty and see whether the advantage survives. A benchmark result that has never been perturbation-tested and comes with no error bars is a data point about a leaderboard, not about a model.

Every technique in sections 8 through 12 evaluates a model from the outside: give it inputs, observe outputs, score the result. Section 10.8's Sleeper Agents result is the sharpest statement of why that is not enough — behavioral safety training can hide a behavior rather than remove it, and no amount of output inspection distinguishes the two. Mechanistic interpretability is the research program that responds by opening the model up. The goal, stated as its practitioners state it: reverse-engineer the algorithms a network learned into human-understandable components, with a causal account of how those components produce the behavior . The emphasis on causal and algorithmic is the whole distinction. "This neuron activates on Python code" is a correlational observation. "These attention heads copy the token following a previous occurrence of the current token, and ablating them destroys in-context repetition" is a mechanism — it says what the computation is, and it makes predictions that can be falsified by intervention. The analogy the field uses is decompilation. A trained network is compiled artifact: the weights implement algorithms, but in a representation nobody designed for reading. Mech interp attempts to recover source-level structure from the binary, without access to source, documentation, or any guarantee that human-legible structure is there to find. Features and Circuits Two abstractions carry the whole program, and they came from vision before transformers. Olah and colleagues' Circuits thread (2020, in Distill), starting with Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits , laid out three claims about InceptionV1 that transferred directly: Features are the fundamental unit. A feature is a direction in activation space corresponding to a property of the input — a curve at a particular orientation, a dog snout, a token being a specific person's name, code being inside a string literal. The load-bearing word is direction , not neuron : 13.3 explains why those are not the same thing and why conflating them was the field's central early mistake. Features are connected by weights into circuits. A circuit is a subgraph of the network — specific features, specific connecting weights — implementing an identifiable computation. The vision work traced curve detectors composing into circle detectors, and documented high-low frequency detectors and car detectors assembled from wheel and window features at specific positions. These were verified by reading weights, not by pattern-matching activations. Universality. Analogous features and circuits recur across architectures and training runs — curve detectors appear in many vision models — suggesting some learned structure is determined by the data and task rather than by initialization. Universality is a well-supported empirical tendency, not a law; counterexamples and partial failures exist. The transformer-specific program was set out in Elhage et al. (2021), A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits (Anthropic), which gave the algebraic decomposition the rest of this section relies on. Its central move: analyze attention-only transformers exactly, decomposing the computation into paths through the residual stream, and identify which weight products actually matter. The Residual Stream as a Communication Channel The single most important reframing for reading interpretability work: do not think of a transformer as a stack of layers transforming a hidden state. Think of it as a shared memory bus that components read from and write to. The architecture makes this exact. Each block adds its output to the residual stream rather than replacing it: x_0 = embed(tokens) x_{l+1} = x_l + Attn_l(LN(x_l)) + MLP_l(LN(x_l)) logits = Unembed(LN(x_L)) Unroll it, and every layer's contribution is a separate additive term: logits = Unembed( LN( embed + sum_l Attn_l + sum_l MLP_l ) ) Three consequences do most of the work in practice: The stream is a sum, so contributions are separable. You can ask what a single head contributed to the final logits, because its contribution is a term in a sum rather than being entangled through a nonlinearity. This is what makes direct logit attribution — decomposing the output logits into per-component contributions — possible at all. Components communicate through subspaces . Nothing forces a head to read what the previous layer wrote. A head's W_Q , W_K , W_V project the stream down to a low-rank subspace; its W_O writes back into another. Two components communicate when the write subspace of one overlaps the read subspace of another, which sets up the virtual weights picture: the effective connection between two components is the product of the writer's output matrix and the reader's input matrix, even if they are many layers apart. The residual stream is bandwidth-limited and heavily shared. It has d_model dimensions and many more things to carry, so components must pack information into partially overlapping directions. This is the same pressure that produces superposition (13.3), and it is why the stream's basis directions are not individually meaningful. The framework paper also identified the useful factorization of attention into two circuits per head. This is the vocabulary you will hit constantly: QK circuit: W_Q^T W_K (as a d_model x d_model bilinear form) decides WHERE to attend -- which source position each destination position reads from OV circuit: W_O W_V (as a d_model x d_model map) decides WHAT is moved -- how the attended position's content is transformed and written back The head's action factorizes: attention pattern (from QK) x value transformation (from OV) The framework also distinguishes composition types by which part of a later head a previous head writes into: Q-composition (affecting where it looks via queries), K-composition (via keys), and V-composition (affecting what it moves). Induction heads (13.4) are the canonical instance of K-composition — and note that this multi-head interaction is why a one-layer attention-only model cannot form them. Residual stream (d_model dims, shared read/write bus) Attn head L1H4 MLP layer 3 Attn head L5H2 read write Embedding Unembed / logits A circuit = a specific read/write path: head L1H4 writes a subspace that L5H2 reads via K-composition The residual stream view. Attention heads and MLPs are not sequential transformations of a hidden state; they read subspaces of a shared additive stream and write into it. A circuit is a path through this bus, and two components interact only insofar as one's write subspace overlaps the other's read subspace. Superposition and Polysemanticity Early interpretability hoped neurons would be the unit of analysis. They are not, and the reason is now well understood in toy settings. The observation. Individual neurons are polysemantic — a single neuron fires on unrelated concepts. This is not rare; it is typical. It blocked neuron-level interpretation for years and was widely treated as evidence that networks are simply messy. The explanation. Elhage et al. (2022), Toy Models of Superposition (Anthropic), gave a compelling account. A model needs to represent far more features than it has dimensions. In n dimensions there are only n mutually orthogonal directions — but there are exponentially many almost -orthogonal ones (the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma is the formal version). If features are sparse — any given input activates only a few of them — the network can assign each feature its own non-orthogonal direction and tolerate the interference, because collisions are rare. Superposition is the network trading a small, mostly-avoidable interference cost for a large gain in representable features. Setup: represent m features in n dimensions, m n. x (m-dim, sparse) --W-- h (n-dim) --W^T, ReLU-- x' (m-dim) Sweep feature sparsity S and observe the learned W: S low (features usually active) - no superposition. The model keeps the top-n most important features orthogonally and DROPS the rest. S high (features rarely active) - superposition. m n features get non-orthogonal directions; interference is real but rarely triggered, and the expected loss is lower than dropping features. Observed structure: features organize into geometric configurations (antipodal pairs, triangles, pentagons, tetrahedra -- tied to uniform polytopes), and the transition between regimes is not smooth but shows phase-change behavior. Why this reframes everything downstream. Polysemanticity stops being a mystery and becomes a prediction: if features live in non-orthogonal directions that outnumber the dimensions, the standard basis directions — the neurons — are arbitrary linear combinations of many features. A neuron looks polysemantic because it is a projection onto an accidental direction. The corollary is the field's key methodological turn: the right object to look for is a direction in activation space, not a neuron , and finding those directions requires solving a decomposition problem rather than reading off coordinates. Epistemic status, stated plainly. The superposition hypothesis is well-demonstrated in toy models constructed to exhibit it . That is the paper's own framing. The evidence that real language models use superposition the same way is indirect: polysemantic neurons are ubiquitous, feature counts plainly exceed dimension counts, and the SAE results in 13.5 are consistent with the hypothesis. Consistent with is not the same as demonstrated. Treat superposition as the field's best-supported working model, with the toy-model caveat attached. Induction Heads: The Canonical Circuit Induction heads are the field's flagship result — a circuit that was found, reverse-engineered, verified causally, and connected to a macroscopic capability. Olsson et al. (2022), In-context Learning and Induction Heads (Anthropic), building on the 2021 framework paper. The algorithm. Given a sequence containing [A][B] earlier and [A] again at the current position, predict [B] . Prefix matching, then copying — the fuzzy, learned version of a hash-table lookup over the context. Context: ... [A] [B] ......... [A] - current position Predict: [B] Two heads in two different layers, composed: Layer L: PREVIOUS-TOKEN HEAD at each position, attend to position-1 and write the previous token's identity into a subspace of the residual stream. Now position i's stream carries "I am preceded by t_{i-1}". Layer L+k: INDUCTION HEAD query = current token [A] key = the PREVIOUS-TOKEN info written by layer L - attends to the position whose PREDECESSOR was [A], i.e. the position holding [B] OV circuit copies [B] into the output direction. This is K-COMPOSITION: head 1's output enters head 2's KEYS. It requires at least two attention layers -- which is exactly what the empirical formation data shows. Why this result carries so much weight. Four independent lines of evidence, which together are far stronger than any one: The mechanism was read off the weights, not inferred from activation patterns. The QK and OV circuits do what the algorithm says. A visible phase change. Induction heads form abruptly during training, in a narrow window, accompanied by a bump in the loss curve — a small region where the loss deviates from its otherwise smooth power law. A macroscopic training-curve anomaly with an identified microscopic cause is a rare and strong result. The formation coincides with a jump in in-context learning ability, measured as the improvement in loss on late tokens versus early tokens in a context. The circuit appears and the capability appears in the same window. Causal and generalization evidence. Ablating induction heads damages in-context learning. And the heads do more than literal copying: they participate in fuzzier pattern completion, including translation-like and analogical patterns, indicating a general in-context pattern-matching mechanism rather than a string-copy special case. The honest boundary. Olsson et al. argue induction heads are a major mechanism for in-context learning, with the strongest evidence in small attention-only models and correspondingly weaker evidence in large models. The claim is not that induction heads are all of in-context learning in a frontier model. It is that they are a real, verified, causally-implicated mechanism — and, as of the early-2025 literature, the clearest existence proof that learned algorithms can be recovered from weights. Sparse Autoencoders If features are directions and superposition means there are more of them than dimensions, then finding features is a dictionary learning problem: decompose activation vectors into a sparse combination of elements from an overcomplete dictionary. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are the leading approach. Given activation x in R^d (a residual stream vector, or MLP activations): f = ReLU( W_enc (x - b_dec) + b_enc ) f in R^{d_sae}, d_sae d x_hat = W_dec f + b_dec L = || x - x_hat ||^2 + lambda * ||f||_1 ____ reconstruct ___/ ___ sparsity ___/ Dictionary is OVERCOMPLETE: d_sae is typically 8x to 100x+ larger than d. Columns of W_dec are the learned feature DIRECTIONS; entries of f are the per-example feature activations. The L1 term forces each input to be explained by a handful of features -- the operationalization of the sparse, over-complete, non-orthogonal picture from 13.3. Common variants: TopK SAEs (enforce exactly k active features, removing lambda-tuning and L1 shrinkage), gated SAEs (separate the decision to activate from the magnitude), JumpReLU SAEs (thresholded activation). The empirical results. Bricken et al. (2023), Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning (Anthropic), applied this to a one-layer transformer's MLP activations and found features that were dramatically more interpretable than neurons — responding to specific, describable contexts (particular sorts of DNA sequences, tokens in specific syntactic roles, particular languages) rather than the grab-bag mixtures neurons respond to. Critically, they validated causally as well as by inspection: intervening on a feature changed downstream behavior in the way the feature's interpretation predicted, so this was not just relabeling correlations. Templeton et al. (2024), Scaling Monosemanticity: Extracting Interpretable Features from Claude 3 Sonnet (Anthropic), scaled it to a production frontier model — the result that made SAEs the field's central tool. Findings worth knowing precisely: Millions of features extracted from the residual stream of a deployed model, many corresponding to abstract and multilingual concepts rather than surface tokens — a feature fires for a concept whether it is expressed in English, in another language, or in an image. Features form a geometry: nearby directions correspond to related concepts, giving a navigable structure rather than an unordered list. Safety-relevant features exist — features related to security vulnerabilities in code, to deception and power-seeking, to bias — which is the concrete reason interpretability and alignment converge here. Steering works. Clamping a feature to a high value produces the corresponding behavior change, which is causal evidence that the features are used by the model rather than merely decodable from it. The widely-circulated demonstration was clamping a Golden Gate Bridge feature and observing the model's identity and outputs shift accordingly. Limitations, stated as the field states them. These are active problems as of the early-2025 literature, not minor caveats: Problem What it is Why it matters Feature splitting Increasing dictionary size splits one feature into several finer variants. A generic "legal language" feature becomes many specific ones There is no natural stopping point and no principled way to pick d_sae . The number of features you find is partly a hyperparameter, which is uncomfortable for a method claiming to recover the model's actual units Dead features A substantial fraction of dictionary elements never activate on any input and contribute nothing Wastes capacity and suggests the optimization is not finding the best decomposition. Mitigated with resampling and architectural fixes, not eliminated Reconstruction-sparsity tradeoff lambda trades reconstruction fidelity against sparsity. Sparser dictionaries are more interpretable and reconstruct worse The unexplained variance may contain exactly the computation you care about. Interpretability of the found features is bought with fidelity to the actual activations Shrinkage The L1 penalty biases feature magnitudes toward zero, systematically distorting activations The direct motivation for TopK and gated variants Evaluation is unsolved "Interpretable" is judged by human or LLM inspection of top-activating examples, which is biased toward features that look clean and is not a measure of completeness or causal correctness Without a solid metric, comparing SAE methods is difficult and progress claims are soft. Downstream causal metrics are an active area Downstream performance gaps Some evaluations have found SAE-based interventions underperforming simpler baselines on practical tasks The gap between "we found interpretable features" and "these features are the useful unit of analysis" is not closed The open conceptual question. SAEs assume the model's computation decomposes into a sparse sum of linear directions. That assumption is imported from the superposition hypothesis, which is itself best-established in toy models. If real models use representations that are not sparse-linear in this way — nonlinear features, genuinely distributed codes, features that only exist relative to context — SAEs would still produce a dictionary that reconstructs well and looks interpretable, because a sufficiently large overcomplete dictionary can fit a lot. That is the uncomfortable possibility the gotcha below addresses. Causal Methods: Patching, Ablation, Path Analysis The methodological core of the field, and the thing that distinguishes it from earlier interpretability work: intervention, not correlation . A component that activates during a behavior may be causing it, may be a downstream consequence of it, or may be irrelevant. Only intervening distinguishes these. Activation patching (also called causal tracing, or interchange intervention in the causal-abstraction literature) is the workhorse. Build a MINIMAL PAIR of prompts differing in one relevant respect: clean: "The Eiffel Tower is in the city of" - " Paris" corrupted: "The Colosseum is in the city of" - " Rome" Procedure: 1. Run clean, cache ALL internal activations. 2. Run corrupted; note the (wrong-for-clean) output. 3. Re-run corrupted, but at ONE chosen site (layer, position, head, or feature) SUBSTITUTE the cached clean activation. 4. Measure how far the output moves back toward the clean answer. patching effect = metric(patched) - metric(corrupted) normalized by metric(clean) - metric(corrupted) Sweep the site over all (layer, position) pairs - a heatmap of WHERE the distinguishing information lives and moves. Directions matter and answer different questions: denoising (clean - corrupted run): which components SUFFICE to restore correct behavior noising (corrupted - clean run): which components are NECESSARY -- breaking them breaks behavior Necessity and sufficiency can dissociate, e.g. under redundancy. Path patching refines this. Ordinary patching changes a component's output everywhere downstream, so it cannot tell you which downstream consumer mattered. Path patching restricts the intervention to a specific edge — patch the contribution of head A only as it enters head B's queries, leaving A's other paths at their corrupted values. This is what turns a set of important components into an actual wiring diagram, and it is how circuits are established rather than merely localized. Ablation replaces a component's output with a baseline. The choice of baseline is a real methodological decision, not a detail: zero-ablation pushes activations off-distribution and can produce misleading effects; mean-ablation (the average over a distribution) is the usual default; resample-ablation (a value from another input) keeps things on-distribution. Reported ablation effects are only interpretable alongside the baseline used. The canonical worked example. Wang et al. (2022), Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 Small , applied this machinery end-to-end to a real, if small, model. The task: complete "When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to" with " Mary". They identified a circuit of around 26 heads in several functional classes — duplicate token heads, S-inhibition heads, name mover heads, and (notably) backup name mover heads that take over when the primary ones are ablated. That last finding is the important methodological warning: networks contain redundancy that makes naive ablation understate a component's role , because the network self-repairs. Any claim resting on "ablating X barely changed the output, so X does not matter" must rule out backup behavior. Other standard tools. The logit lens (nostalgebraist, 2020) applies the unembedding matrix to intermediate residual stream states to read out what the model would predict if it stopped at that layer — a cheap and revealing view of how predictions form across depth. It is unreliable in places, because intermediate representations are not in the same basis the unembedding expects. The tuned lens (Belrose et al., 2023, Eliciting Latent Predictions from Transformers with the Tuned Lens ) fixes this by learning a per-layer affine probe to map intermediate states into the final-layer basis, giving substantially better-calibrated readouts — at the cost of a trained component per layer, which introduces its own question about what the probe added (a concern taken up in section 15.2). Automated circuit discovery. Manual circuit analysis costs months per circuit, which does not scale to a frontier model. ACDC (Conmy et al., 2023, Towards Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability ) automates the search by iteratively pruning edges from the computational graph whose removal does not degrade a task metric beyond a threshold, recovering circuits similar to hand-derived ones on tasks where ground truth exists. Attribution patching approximates patching effects with gradients, making it possible to estimate every site's effect in a couple of backward passes instead of one forward pass per site — a large constant-factor win, at the cost of a linear approximation that degrades for large interventions. These methods make circuit discovery tractable; they still require a task with clean minimal pairs and a well-defined metric, which is the binding constraint for anything resembling open-ended model behavior. Where the Program Actually Stands This is the part most often oversold, so it is worth stating without hedging in either direction. Genuinely established Promising but unresolved Far out of reach Specific circuits fully reverse-engineered in small models (induction heads; IOI in GPT-2 small) with causal verification SAEs recovering interpretable features at frontier scale, with causal steering evidence A complete mechanistic account of any frontier model Causal intervention methodology — patching, path patching, ablation with proper baselines — as a rigorous toolkit Whether SAE features are the right unit of analysis (13.5) Verifying the absence of a capability or disposition by inspecting weights Superposition as a mechanism, demonstrated in toy models built to test it Automated circuit discovery scaling beyond narrow tasks with clean metrics Reading a model's goals or intentions off its internals Polysemanticity as a ubiquitous empirical fact Whether small-model findings transfer to frontier scale Certifying a model safe on mechanistic grounds The honest summary. Mech interp has produced real, verified, causally-established results — and they are on small models, narrow tasks, and specific circuits. The gap to "we understand what a frontier model is doing" is enormous, and it is not obviously a gap that more of the same closes: the number of circuits scales with the model, the interactions between them are not additive, and no current method verifies that a discovered circuit is the whole story rather than one path among many. Set against that, the field is genuinely young and moving fast, the tooling is far better than it was two years ago, and the SAE results represent a real step from "small models" to "frontier models." The strongest argument for the program does not depend on completeness. Section 10.8 showed behavioral evaluation can be defeated by a model whose training-time and test-time behavior are identical by construction. Any method that inspects only inputs and outputs is defeated by exactly the failure modes that matter most. Mech interp is currently the main research direction that could, in principle, escape that — and "in principle" is doing real work in that sentence. Gotcha The most consequential open question in this section is whether SAE features are the right unit of analysis at all , and it is easy to miss because the method's outputs are so compelling. The logic runs: superposition says features are sparse non-orthogonal directions; therefore sparse dictionary learning should recover them; the recovered features look interpretable and steering them works; therefore we have found the model's features. The weak step is the first — superposition is best-established in toy models constructed to exhibit it , and its application to real models is inference from consistent evidence, not demonstration. If a frontier model's computation is not well-described as a sparse sum of linear directions, a large overcomplete dictionary would still reconstruct activations well and still yield human-labelable features, because a sufficiently expressive basis fits nearly anything and humans are good at finding stories in top-activating examples. Feature splitting is the visible symptom: if the feature count is partly set by your dictionary size, you are not straightforwardly reading off the model's own units. Two guards. First, treat interpretability-by-inspection as generating hypotheses only — a feature earns the description "used by the model" when intervening on it changes behavior as predicted, which is why the steering results in Templeton et al. (2024) matter far more than the feature labels. Second, remember that even a perfectly recovered feature dictionary is a vocabulary , not a mechanism: knowing what is represented is not knowing what algorithm operates on it, and circuits are what supply the second part.

Section 13 pursued a maximalist goal: recover the algorithms a network learned, component by component, with a causal account of each. Section 13.7 was blunt about how far that is from complete on any frontier model. This section covers the alternative bet — that you can get substantial practical value from model internals without understanding the mechanism, by treating the representation space as an interface you can read from and write to. Zou et al. (2023), Representation Engineering: A Top-Down Approach to AI Transparency , named the program and made the framing explicit. The analogy they draw is to neuroscience: cognitive neuroscience made real progress on high-level phenomena by studying population-level activity and lesion effects long before anyone had a circuit-level account of a cortical column. Representation engineering asks the analogous question of a network — where is this concept, and what happens if I change it? — rather than what algorithm computed it? The two programs are complements, not competitors, and the honest comparison in 14.7 is the point of the section rather than an afterthought. The Linear Representation Hypothesis Everything here rests on one empirical regularity: many high-level concepts appear to be encoded as directions in activation space, such that the concept's presence corresponds roughly to the projection of the activation onto that direction . The history is worth knowing, because it explains why the field found this plausible before it had modern evidence: Word embeddings. Mikolov et al. (2013) observed that word2vec embeddings supported vector arithmetic on analogies — the widely-quoted king - man + woman landing near queen . Static embeddings appeared to encode relational structure linearly. Later analysis substantially qualified this: the effect depends on excluding the query words from the nearest-neighbour search, is much weaker on many relation types, and is partly an artifact of the similarity metric. The honest reading is that a real linear structure exists and the famous demonstration overstated how cleanly it does. Probing classifiers in NLP. Through the late 2010s, a large literature showed that part of speech, syntactic structure, sentiment, tense and coreference are linearly decodable from contextual encoder representations, establishing linear decodability as an ordinary property rather than a curiosity. Modern LLM findings. Numerous concepts have been found to have identifiable linear directions in frontier-scale models — truthfulness (14.5), refusal (14.4), sentiment, and abstract properties surfaced as SAE decoder directions (section 14.5), which are themselves a linear-representation claim by construction. Park et al. (2023) worked toward formalizing what the hypothesis even means, noting that the answer depends on the choice of inner product on representation space — a subtlety usually skipped over. Why linearity might be expected rather than surprising. Three arguments, none decisive: the unembedding is a linear map, so anything the model uses to shape output logits must be linearly readable at the final layer; the residual stream is additive (section 14.2), so components compose by vector addition, which makes linear structure the natural currency; and superposition (section 14.3) explicitly posits features as directions. The honest caveat, which matters. The linear representation hypothesis is a useful approximation with substantial supporting evidence, not a proven law . Known qualifications: some concepts are demonstrably not linearly encoded and require nonlinear probes; some are better described by multi-dimensional subspaces than single directions, and there is documented work on circular or multi-dimensional representations for things like days of the week; the direction found for a concept is often context-dependent, differing across layers, prompt formats and distributions; and linear decodability is a statement about what a reader can extract, which — as 14.2 insists — is a different claim from what the model does. Use linearity as a productive working assumption that frequently pays off, and expect it to fail on some concepts you care about. Linear Probes A probe is the simplest possible tool and, used carefully, one of the most informative. Train a classifier on frozen intermediate activations to predict a property of the input; its accuracy tells you something about what the representation contains. Collect a labeled dataset: (input_i, label_i) For a chosen layer l (and token position p): h_i = activations at (l, p) when the model processes input_i -- the model is FROZEN; no gradients flow into it Train: y_hat = sigmoid( w . h + b ) logistic regression Report accuracy on HELD-OUT inputs. Sweep l across layers - a depth profile of where the property becomes decodable. Typical shape: low near the embedding, rising through the middle layers, sometimes falling near the output as the representation specializes toward next-token prediction. Methodological requirements that are frequently skipped. A probe result is worthless without these: Requirement Failure if skipped Keep the probe simple (linear, regularized) A high-capacity probe can compute the property itself from a representation that does not encode it. At the limit, an MLP probe on raw token embeddings measures the probe, not the model Control task / random-label baseline (Hewitt and Liang, 2019, Designing and Interpreting Probing Tasks ) Without knowing how well the same probe fits random labels, you cannot separate probe capacity from representation content. This paper introduced selectivity — real-task accuracy minus control-task accuracy — as the reportable quantity Baseline against a non-contextual or random-weight model Some properties are decodable from an untrained network's activations. If a random transformer scores nearly as well, the trained model's representation is not what you measured Balanced classes and held-out evaluation Standard, and routinely violated in small hand-built probing datasets Confound-controlled dataset construction The most common real failure: the probe picks up a surface correlate — topic, length, formatting, token identity — that co-varies with the label in your dataset. This is a dataset problem no amount of probe hygiene fixes The distinction that resolves most confusion. Three separable questions, only the first of which a probe answers: 1. Is the information PRESENT? - probe accuracy answers this 2. Is it linearly ACCESSIBLE? - a LINEAR probe's accuracy answers this 3. Does the model USE it? - requires INTERVENTION. No probe answers this. Question 3 needs a causal method: ablate the direction, or add it, and see whether behavior changes as predicted (section 14.6's methodology, applied here). This is exactly why activation steering (14.3) is more than a party trick — it is the intervention that upgrades a correlational probe finding into a causal claim. Activation Steering and Control Vectors If a concept is a direction, adding that direction to the activations should push the model toward the concept. This turns out to work often enough to be practically useful. layer L-1 residual activation h at layer L, one position d READ: probe p = ( v h ) + WRITE: steer h = h + v direction v v = mean(h ) mean(h ) from contrastive pairs same v both ways layers L+1 unmodified weights baseline output shifted output too small: no effect too large: incoherent One direction, two operations: project onto it to read the concept, add a multiple of it to write the concept. The linear representation hypothesis in operational form: a concept direction found from contrastive pairs is read off the residual stream by a probe and written back into it by adding alpha times that same direction. 1. Build CONTRASTIVE PAIRS differing in exactly one attribute: positive: prompts exhibiting the attribute negative: matched prompts that do not 2. Compute the direction (difference-in-means is the standard, and is surprisingly hard to beat): v = mean( h_positive ) - mean( h_negative ) Alternatives: the first principal component of the paired differences; a trained linear probe's weight vector; an SAE decoder column (section 14.5). 3. Intervene at inference, at chosen layers/positions: h' = h + alpha * v (steering / addition) h' = h - alpha * v (suppression) h' = h - (h . v_hat) v_hat (directional ABLATION: project the component out entirely, at every layer and position) alpha controls strength. Too small: no effect. Too large: incoherent output. The usable window is often narrow and must be tuned per direction, per model, per layer. Key results. Turner et al. (2023) introduced activation addition ( ActAdd ), demonstrating steering of sentiment and topic from a single contrastive prompt pair with no fine-tuning. Rimsky et al. (2023), Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition , systematized the difference-in-means approach over larger paired datasets and showed steering of behavioral properties including sycophancy — connecting steering to the misalignment measured in section 11.7. Zou et al. (2023) framed the general read/write toolkit and applied it across honesty, power-seeking, morality and emotion. Section 13.5's feature clamping is the SAE-derived member of the same family. The refusal direction result is the sharpest single finding in this literature, and the most instructive. Arditi et al. (2024), Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction , found that across 13 open-weight chat models spanning multiple families and sizes, refusal behavior is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace . Computing the difference in means between harmful and harmless instruction activations yields a direction such that: Ablating it — projecting that component out of every residual stream activation at every layer and position — largely disables refusal, without a broad degradation of other capabilities. It can be implemented as a rank-one weight modification, requiring no fine-tuning and no gradient computation. Adding it to activations on harmless prompts induces refusal on requests the model would normally answer. Both directions of intervention are what make this a causal claim rather than a probing observation — bidirectional control is the strongest available evidence that a direction is genuinely mediating the behavior rather than merely correlating with it. The dual-use implication, stated plainly.
